#7689. Court Blocks W. Va. AG's Subpoena to Environmentalist Nonprofits

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Part of the AG's argument was that the nonprofits relied on a climate change scenario, RCP8.5, that has been recently "retired."

From yesterday's decision by Judge Joseph Goodwin (S.D. W. Va.) in W. Va. Rivers Coalition, Inc. v. McCuskey:

The Attorney General of West Virginia has used the State's power to compel two citizen organizations to open ten years of their files: their drafts and internal arguments, the groups they have funded, the people who serve on their boards, the coalitions they have joined, and what they have told the agencies they petition. Neither organization markets goods nor services relevant to the subpoenas. The Attorney General identifies no consumer who was cheated, no sale, and no purchase made in reliance on anything either group said.

What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia's waters and climate. The State's chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them.

The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.

The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives.

The State wants a decade of what they published, down to a note sent to a single person outside the organization, along with the unreleased drafts and the internal arguments over what to say. He demanded the names of the organizations that fund them and what each gave, and he has now withdrawn that demand. He still wants the groups they paid, the board members they share, the coalitions they joined, and the comments they filed with the agencies they were petitioning. Because the demand period runs to the date of compliance, the subpoenas reach new communications written while they remain outstanding. No demand identifies a consumer, a sale, or a statement anyone relied on. The subpoenas go into how these citizens arrived at their positions on public questions and who helped them get there.

The Plaintiffs in this case, West Virginia Rivers Coalition, Inc. ("WVRC") and 350.org, promote clean waters, reduced carbon emissions, and healthier lives for the people of West Virginia and beyond. They do not sell any service. They do not advertise a certain product of their own. Instead, they promote ideas. Some of that advocacy and some of those ideas are based, in part, on one model. For that, they have been subpoenaed and asked to turn over ten years' worth of information far beyond any use of that one model.

AG McCuskey's actions violate the protections afforded by the United States Constitution. The Plaintiffs, on this record, have only engaged in protected advocacy speech, not commercial speech. The subpoenas issued on the Plaintiffs trespass on their freedom of association, chill their exercise of the First Amendment, and deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

Because Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the subpoenas violate their First Amendment freedom of association, and because the remaining injunction factors also favor Plaintiffs, their Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order, is GRANTED.

Attorney General McCuskey is enjoined from enforcing these investigative subpoenas for the next fourteen days as set out in the Conclusion of this Memorandum Opinion and Order….

Plaintiff WVRC is a river advocacy nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of West Virginia, and its "mission is to promote clean and healthy West Virginia waters for all." The nonprofit is committed to "clean water and healthy rivers through research, public education, policy advocacy, citizen water-quality monitoring, and engagement with state and federal agencies." It has a modest staff of 15 and an annual budget of approximately $2 million primarily funded by foundations and other organizations. WVRC regularly submits comments on proposed legislation, permits, and rules concerning water quality. And as this court is familiar, WVRC is a party litigant in multiple cases across the Fourth Circuit that challenge permits and approvals for infrastructure projects, pipeline projects, injection wells, and toxic discharges. Because of its litigation efforts, WVRC coordinates "with other organizations through shared counsel" about litigation strategy.

WVRC also engages in public education and information campaigns, including "statements about the effects of climate change in West Virginia's waters and communities, and about the environmental effects of fossil-fuel extraction, transport, and combustion." It is a member of multiple different coalitions committed to similar goals. To fund ts work, WVRC "solicits charitable contributions from the public through its website, mailings, emails, and events," but it does not publish the identities of its funders.

Plaintiff 350.org is a nonprofit corporation, and its "mission is to build a grassroots movement to end the use of fossil fuels and to accelerate the transition to renewable energy." The organization publishes information about climate change, organizes public demonstrations, and coordinates with other organizations with similar goals. 350.org also "solicits charitable contributions from the public through grant applications and through its website, mailings, emails, and events." Those grants and contributions are subject to opt-in confidentiality in some cases and agreed upon confidentiality in other cases.

And an excerpt from the court's First Amendment analysis (for more on RCP8.5, see this N.Y. Times article):

[T]he Court applies "exacting scrutiny" to compelled disclosures of protected First Amendment speech and association. To be a permissible intrusion on the First Amendment, "there must be 'a substantial relation between the disclosure requirement and a sufficiently important governmental interest.'" …

The subpoenas … "… concern[ ] an investigation into alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act ('WVCCPA')." State code authorizes the Attorney General, if he "has probable cause," to "subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, adduce evidence, and require the production of any matter which is relevant to the investigation."

Under West Virginia law, "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are … unlawful." Trade or commerce "means the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any goods or services and shall include any trade or commerce, directly or indirectly, affecting the people of this state." "Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices" includes 16 different definitions including "[e]ngaging in any other conduct which similarly creates a likelihood of confusion or of misunderstanding."

Deploying these broad definitions, AG McCuskey's theory is that the Plaintiffs, environmental advocacy groups, published information, made comments, and advocated based on a study, the RCP8.5, that has been determined "implausible." According to AG McCuskey, this reliance, and subsequent advocacy, is a deceptive act or practice that affects the energy marketplace of West Virginia.

Begin with common sense—in what way could WVRC and 350.org violate the WVCCPA? They are not financial institutions, lenders, or creditors. They are not businesses seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. In fact, both are 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. They do not sell services of any kind. As explained, Plaintiffs are advocacy organizations committed to climate issues. Their missions are public education, dissemination of information, advocacy in support of their ideals, and public support of those who align with their beliefs. What little items they sell are merchandise bearing their names and logos. Surely these minimal sales from advocacy organizations are not the transactions the West Virginia legislature sought to protect consumers from….

Plaintiffs do not engage in commercial speech. By virtue of their missions as nonprofit environmental advocacy groups, their interests are not economic. Their interests include public education, funding environmental projects, modeling and projecting the effects of climate change, and contributing to a society that values clean air, clean water, and healthier lives. The fact that their advocacy touches on the economy is insufficient to be commercial speech. Therefore, Plaintiffs' protected speech and advocacy alleged in this case cannot be regulated under the WVCCPA.

Accordingly, I find that the WVCCPA cannot supply a "sufficiently important governmental interest" under the "exacting scrutiny" applied to freedom of association claims. I next turn to the severity of the "disclosure requirement" under the "exacting scrutiny" analysis….

As discussed, the subpoenas broadly assert that a violation of the WVCCPA might have occurred. And in his response, AG McCuskey admits that there may not be any WVCCPA violation. He does, however, have authority to issue subpoenas to investigate "whether a violation … has, in fact, occurred."

That violation, AG McCuskey argues, arises from only a few instances of Plaintiffs using a certain climate projection model, RCP8.5. Any publication born from that model, he asserts, is potentially unfair or deceptive. So to assess the breadth of the subpoenas and the compelled disclosure Plaintiffs are subjected to, the court turns to the subpoenas' demands. It is reasonable to assume that the demands would roughly track the RCP8.5-related violations and the allegations of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

Not so. The subpoenas ask for much more. The 16 categories of demands include every statement Plaintiffs have ever published about a West Virginia energy business with a "Climate Claim." But that demand is not limited to climate-related statements supported by the RCP8.5 model. It includes every climate-related statement that names a West Virginia energy business which is published and supported or informed, at least in part, by any model, study, project, plan, projection, or paper. Demand No. 4 is similarly broad: the subpoena demands every published projection concerning West Virginia and all documents related to those projections, without narrowing it down to those supported by the RCP8.5.

The rest of the demands do not even try to mask their broad and sweeping intentions. Donation requests, payments to third parties, and licensing and funding documents of all projects concerning West Virginia are demanded. Every document projecting costs and damages is demanded, as well as every report, study, model, or paper that the Plaintiffs directly or indirectly supported. Documents pertaining to internal considerations are demanded wholesale. So, too, are all documents pertaining to third-party communication and coordination in any fashion. And even with AG McCuskey's last-minute withdrawal of certain demands for donor information, Plaintiffs will still be obligated to disclose "board affiliation, coalition partners, grantees, agency submissions, internal deliberations and drafts, solicitation totals and targeting."

Plaintiffs call this a fishing expedition. In part, I agree. The subpoenas demand a large share of documents in Plaintiffs' control for the last ten years. But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net. Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.

As stated, compelled disclosure that invades First Amendment protections can only stand if there is a substantial relation between what must be disclosed and a "sufficiently important governmental interest." Here, I find neither a sufficiently important government interest nor do I find a substantial relationship between the compelled disclosure and the government interest….

And the court also briefly notes plaintiffs' retaliation claim, without resolving it:

Plaintiffs have alleged substantial evidence to support their [retaliation] claim. AG McCuskey has publicly disparaged pro-environmental groups and has called for the DOJ to investigate similar groups. He has joined contentious litigation against environmental advocacy organizations. And the chasm between the subpoenas' demands and the purported basis for investigation suggests a retaliatory motive.

This phenomenon of state and federal investigation into the affairs of advocacy non-profits has begun to permeate our culture. The courts have enjoined civil investigative demands on comparable records. [Citations omitted. -EV]

However, because retaliation concerns the Attorney General's motive, I will reserve judgment on Count One until he can present evidence at a hearing for a preliminary injunction. Having already determined that an injunction is warranted on the basis of Count Two (freedom of association), the court declines to address the remaining counts….

Derek Teaney and Amanda Demmerle (Appalachian Mountain Advocates, Inc.) represent plaintiffs.

The title of that 1960s movie came from a message Adolf Hitler sent to his commanding general in Paris in August 1944. He wanted Paris to burn if he couldn’t keep it.

Today, the call isn’t coming from the Führerbunker; it’s from inside the house. It’s not Nazis, but the French—and quasi-French—burning Paris and other French cities.

The Louvre museum in Paris, home to the Mona Lisa, closed Monday “due to a student social movement.” That’s one way to describe the utter chaos overtaking French cities.

In Limoges, rioters set fire to the town hall, destroying its iconic tower. In Marseille, they broke into city hall and vandalized the interior. In Paris, a video circulating online appeared to show young thugs shouting, “Wallah! Kill her!” and “Dirty whore!” [my translation] at a policewoman they chased and threw to the ground—all while trashing property and assaulting people on the streets.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

What’s happening in France is both familiar and new. It’s familiar in that mass protests are endemic to France. They happen every few years when a feckless government tries to balance the books by reforming France’s ruinously generous public benefits. What’s new is the addition of foreign influence and the scale of the violence.

The high-schoolers who kicked off this round of protests are angry about class sizes, dilapidated schools, and access to college. Retirees who joined them say state pensions aren’t enough to live on. Everyone complains about the high cost of living. They all want more state spending to cure their ills.

French protests often turn violent. Torched cars, vandalized property, and looting are common. What has added fuel to the fire this time is the “Casseurs” (breakers), looters, and violent thugs going beyond what was tacitly tolerated in the past. Many seem to be of migrant background, and some carry Palestinian flags or those of the North African countries they or their parents came from.

Videos in French media showed streets of looted stores. Rue Paradis in Marseille has many high-end jewelry and fashion stores, but also many mom-and-pop shops whose owners work long hours for little profit. Dozens of these are now looted shells. Their metal shutters—designed to prevent windows from being broken and stores from being burglarized—lie torn off or broken.

Many of France’s major cities are run by socialists. Marseille’s mayor, Benoit Payan, blames the French government for failing to protect city hall—where his own office is—and local stores. He wants Paris to pay for all the damage. Once again, the French taxpayer is on the hook.

How does this end? Not quickly. The political left is well organized, galvanized, and funded—including with foreign money. We are likely to see more promises of increased spending from lame-duck President Emmanuel Macron, now in the last year of his two terms and unable to run again. He gave a speech condemning the violence on Sunday, but he’s been notably absent as it has unfolded. On Tuesday he stuck with his schedule and flew to the Gulf region.

France has presidential elections next April. Two leading contenders are Marine Le Pen of the right-wing National Rally (NR) and Jean-Luc Melenchon of the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI). Of the two, Le Pen promises to lower migration and limit welfare payments to migrants. Melenchon welcomes mass migration and opposes any reduction in benefits. Le Pen opposes illegal migration, but she hasn’t campaigned on reducing the bloated benefits bill.

>>> France’s Riots Echo 1968. But Macron Is No de Gaulle

But France’s checkbook is tapped out. It hasn’t balanced a budget in 50 years, and this year’s deficit is over 5%. Economic growth is under 1%. Diesel costs about $10 a gallon. National debt is 120% of GDP, and the bond market is getting nervous.

Like other developed countries, France’s fertility rate is below replacement, and the country has allowed in millions of immigrants from its former colonies. On balance, these new arrivals and their children have a lower employment rate than native French, but they get the same social services. Those numbers don’t work, no matter how smart the president in Paris.

Not only is France broke, but it has too few bodies to handle multiple riots at once. France’s national police handle the cities, while the gendarmes enforce the law in the countryside. Both are funded centrally by the French state. Towns have municipal police, but they aren’t equipped or trained for law enforcement, let alone riot control. France has specialized riot-control units, but only so many. The French military is probably Europe’s best, but it is not used for internal operations.

Like France, some of our major cities, New York and Seattle, are now run by avowed socialists. Arguably, administrations in Boston and Los Angeles are also closely aligned with DSA values. And more cities will be in the future.

The DSA wants open borders, nationalized health care, curtailed law enforcement, and higher taxes. If we don’t take heed, France’s present could be our future.

Another key figure in the growing relationship between HOLA and the Chinese-influenced Singham network is HOLA founder Abdolhamid Shahrabi, which the NCRI describes as “one of the Iranian regime’s most important influence operators in Latin America.”

It was Shahrabi who organized Cuban dictator Fidel Castro’s visit to Tehran in 2003. Twenty years later, Shahrabi organized a conference at the University of Tehran attended by the ambassadors of Cuba, Venezuela, Bolivia, and Nicaragua, and Tricontinental’s Prashad.

The NCRI, finally, cites hacked internal records from Press TV, which is Iran’s OFAC-sanctioned English-language state propaganda outlet, which reveal that Press TV contacted by telephone key American partners of Shahrabi ahead of U.S. protests.

“The United National Antiwar Coalition and Workers World Party received no fewer than 260 combined contacts over a 29-month period from 2019 to 2022,” the report said. “Call volume spikes consistently preceded U.S.-based protest surges by roughly one month, indicating that Iranian state media engagement.”

If that doesn’t get our leaders’ attention, not much will.

#7686. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

#7685. ABA tracks new challenges affecting Public Service Loan Forgiveness borrowers

The ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. (Image from Shutterstock)

For lawyers and other student loan borrowers working in public service jobs, the path to having their remaining federal student loan balances discharged under Public Service Loan Forgiveness program after 120 months of qualifying payments is becoming increasingly difficult to navigate.

Under the PSLF program, created by Congress in 2007 with the support of the ABA, borrowers who have made 120 timely payments on their federal direct loans while employed full time in qualifying public service jobs are eligible to receive forgiveness of whatever portion of their loan remains after completing the payments.

But the ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. Issues include processing delays, payment record errors, growing application backlogs, and changes in Department of Education policies and procedures—some implemented with little or no public notice. Significant staffing cuts at the department, including a 40% reduction in Federal Student Aid office staff, have added to concerns about whether problems can be resolved promptly.

For reasons that are not yet clear, many borrowers have not received credit for qualifying loan repayments they’ve made since June, which means those payments cannot yet be counted toward their 120-repayment requirement. The Department of Education has not offered information or explanation on the missing information.

Separately, the Department of Education confirmed in August that it has reduced the number of some borrowers’ qualifying payments, potentially delaying when their remaining loan balances will be forgiven. After initially describing the falling payment counts as a “data issue,” the department subsequently said the changes were intentional, correcting coding errors during the Biden administration that resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers.

For example, some of the PSLF credit reversals may have been for payments made in a repayment plan that didn’t qualify for PSLF, although without an explanation from the Education Department about this process, some borrowers believe their payment counts were removed erroneously.

Without a formal announcement, the department also in July quietly eliminated the Biden-era 15-day grace period on whether PSLF-eligible payments counted as timely. As of July 1, a payment must be made “on or before the due date” to count as a qualifying payment under PSLF.

Also, a “clarification” by the department about the PSLF Buyback program is causing confusion and concern among borrowers.

The PSLF Buyback program allows public service employees to get credit toward the required 120 payments for months their loans were, e.g., in deferment or forbearance and thus not eligible for PSLF. Borrowers can apply to “buy back” those months, however, by paying what they would have paid had they been in repayment during those months.

But under updated Department of Education guidance, borrowers will not be able to buy back credit for payments made while under either of two new repayment plans—the Repayment Assistance Plan or the Tiered Standard Repayment Plan. These two new repayment plans were created in legislation signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025.

Further causing concern is the significant application backlog for the PSLF Buyback program. As of April, the application backlog was between 70,000 to 90,000, but no new data has been released since that time. Even if the backlog has been reduced, some borrowers have waited two years or more to get credit for retroactive payments. The delay requires them to remain in their jobs and repay their loans for longer than required, thus functionally ending the buyback program.

On Oct. 21, the Department of Justice dropped its appeal of two court rulings that stayed the Department of Education’s controversial proposed rules to PSLF, which would have narrowed PSLF eligibility by excluding employees of organizations engaged in activities the department considered as having a “substantially illegal purpose.”

In August, the department had appealed the separate decisions by federal judges in Massachusetts and Washington, D.C., that had vacated the rules.

The ABA vigorously opposed the department’s proposals. In letters to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, ABA Presidents Bill Bay and Michelle Behnke cited a lack of statutory and other legal authority. The ABA House of Delegates reinforced that opposition through adoption of Resolution 505 at its February 2026 midyear meeting, which opposes efforts to politicize this politically neutral program.

“Any perception that benefits are awarded based on political affiliation or ideology undermines the legitimacy of programs such as PSLF, discourages participation, and decreases the requisite public confidence they require to be successful,” the report accompanying the resolution states.

The ABA recognizes the crucial role PSLF plays in encouraging individuals to pursue careers that provide much-needed public services, including public defense services and civil legal aid representation to underrepresented communities such as senior citizens and veterans.

Since the program’s creation, the ABA has consistently responded to attacks and efforts to repeal or cut the program, including direct lobbying efforts through multiple Congresses and administrations; major grassroots campaigns including as a priority at past ABA Day fly-in events in Washington, D.C.; and working alongside its allies in the PSLF Coalition, a collaboration of more than 100 nonprofit and public service organizations.

In all, the ABA has adopted three policies supporting the program, including one in 2002 calling for the program’s creation. The most recent, Resolution 505, urges removal of the requirement that applicants be in qualifying employment at the time of applying for discharge of their student loans—a current program requirement that holds borrowers in limbo, unable to change jobs until the paperwork is filed. Once the required service and payment obligations are met, the resolution states, “there should be no further obligation than to apply for the benefits owed.”

As new issues with the program continue to emerge, the ABA will continue to work with allies to identify issues affecting borrowers and press for solutions. To learn more as significant developments occur, follow us at @ABAGrassroots on LinkedIn.

This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7684. Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

Delaware families and policymakers are wrestling with the same issue troubling Americans nationwide: how to handle artificial intelligence.

In 2024, lawmakers in the Blue Hen State created a committee to study AI. Good thing, because parents and teachers badly need guidance on this issue.

Yet AI technology has advanced rapidly over the past two years, so the committee should prioritize drafting recommendations for K-12 schools.

To date, state officials have set only “voluntary” guardrails around AI use in elementary and secondary schools, according to the Delaware-based Caesar Rodney Institute. In May, legislators considered a proposal to create a pilot program that would allow 12 schools to use AI technology.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI

Still, the final report on the activities would not be due until 2029, and this year’s freshman class will be seniors by then. These students will be gone before lawmakers act on the report’s findings. Instead, lawmakers should focus on helping students in school today.

Besides, given the pace of change in AI technology, this proposal is too little, too late.

Fortunately, legislative models already exist that lawmakers can apply to allow the use of AI in schools, protect student data and prohibit nonacademic AI activities in classrooms.

Heritage Foundation research explains that lawmakers need not explicitly ban or allow the use of AI in schools. For school officials who allow AI in classrooms, however, educators should adopt training programs for teachers and students. These programs should help teachers and students draft prompts and questions for generative AI bots; create media using AI, such as audio, video and pictures; edit student writing; detect biases in AI results; evaluate different AI bots to decide which are the most effective; and protect student privacy.

Local school boards should adopt policies stating that students may use AI for schoolwork only when specifically allowed by teachers.

The U.S. Department of Education is urging state and local authorities to develop solutions. “Research and experience have demonstrated that technology is a valuable instructional tool when it supports strong pedagogy and effective teaching practices,” writes Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary for elementary and secondary education. “The U.S. Department of Education believes these decisions [about education technology] are best made by states and local communities.”

Policymakers should move quickly. Even if self-reported student usage numbers are slightly inflated, the share of students using AI remains remarkable.

Education officials in large school systems such as New York City and Los Angeles are attempting to prohibit the use of AI for this school year. With so many students already using bots, however, a ban on AI will be difficult to enforce.

>>> Meta Abandons Its AI-Generating Tool, but Public-Safety Guardrails Are Needed

Instead of prohibiting AI, policymakers should draw on existing research to select appropriate educational applications of the technology. For example, lawmakers should block the use of companion bots that simulate personal interactions and develop relationships with users.

Instead, educators can give students access to generative bots that use data to summarize complex information. Teachers can benefit from AI programs that help organize lesson plans. When teachers assign students to use AI, students should report how they used the technology.

Parents should have the choice to opt out of these assignments and have students complete the work using other methods.

State policymakers must focus on boosting student outcomes as technology evolves. Federal officials agree. Ms. Baesler writes: “The question should not be whether teachers and students use technology. The question should be whether the technology we ask teachers and students to use improves learning and students’ academic outcomes.”

As Delaware’s AI committee drafts recommendations, officials should focus on student success. Those on both sides of the political aisle—and on either side of AI debates—can agree on this.

Then, parents and teachers can share best practices and offer solutions to help students across all 50 states.

#7683. America 250 at 230 mph

I know nothing about automobile racing, and I confess it at the outset, honesty being the virtue my mother prized above all others save punctuality.

Yet racing has a way of finding a person. When I was a boy in the 1980s and 1990s, my father, on the occasional Sunday afternoon, kept the television tuned to NASCAR. The names drifted through our living room like the smell of pot roast: Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt, Darrell Waltrip, Jeff Gordon.

Once, the athletic director at our Baptist church loaded the youth group into a van and drove us to Atlanta Motor Speedway. There, amid gasoline and thunder, a cluster of drivers signed my cap. Which drivers, I could not tell you; the cap sleeps on the top shelf of my closet. But I remember running into Bobby Cox and Terry Pendleton, of our beloved Braves, and they signed it, too.

I write now from an Indianapolis hotel room, having spent the week with The Mont Pelerin Society. Friedrich Hayek and a few dozen others founded the Society in 1947, gathering beside a Swiss mountain amid the rubble of a world war to keep alive the idea of a free people prospering through free markets. Last year, readers may recall, we were in Morocco. This year, in honor of the nation’s 250th birthday, we came to Indianapolis, home of Liberty Fund, our host and an institution I love.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State

Mont Pelerin meetings are known for their excursions. I once climbed a volcano in Guatemala. This week we went to the Speedway.

It’s an immense place. On race day, some 350,000 souls fill its grandstands and infield while jets tear open the sky. On an ordinary autumn afternoon, with the stands empty and the wind moving through them, it feels like an unroofed cathedral. One stands in it smaller and grateful.

I was told I would be offered a lap with a professional driver. At the entrance waited a stack of liability waivers thick as a family Bible, and my hand trembled as I signed. Then, as if Providence had a hand in the seating chart, I saw Sam Karnick of the Heartland Institute, who missed the conference entirely but arrived from Chicago just in time for this excursion.

I will say only that Sam has stood beside me in matters both personal and professional, which in my life were never quite separate. Sam was riding, too. We would go together.

But first, let me tell you about the museum.

The Speedway opened in 1909. Two years later, Ray Harroun won the inaugural Indianapolis 500 in the Marmon Wasp, a long yellow needle of a car equipped with what may have been the first rearview mirror fitted to an automobile. In the museum stood its replica, along with machines that marked the successive revolutions of racing: the 1914 Delage, the 1928 Miller Special, Bobby Unser’s 1968 Rislone Eagle, the 1972 Sunoco McLaren associated with Roger Penske’s first Indianapolis 500 victory, and the 1982 STP Wildcat in which Gordon Johncock beat Rick Mears by a mere sixteen-hundredths of a second.

Each car tells a story of ingenuity, rivalry, and the restless dissatisfaction that facilitates progress. After World War II, the track lay neglected, its bricks surrendering to weeds, until Terre Haute businessman Tony Hulman bought it in 1945 and restored it. Racing moved from the front-engine roadsters to rear-engine cars, from one mechanical innovation to another, each generation testing the limits left by its predecessor. The record was never allowed to stand for long; someone always thought he could go faster.

Consider the distance traveled in little more than a century. The automobile was still a novelty when the Speedway opened. Now, machines hurtle around its oval at speeds exceeding 230 miles an hour. No central planner conceived this progression, no committee assembled all the knowledge required to produce it. Mechanics, engineers, inventors, drivers and investors each contributed something, often without knowing what the next man would do with it. Some made fortunes; some lost them. The accumulated result exceeded what any one of them could have imagined.

Hayek had a name for the order that emerges from such dispersed knowledge and individual effort: the extended order. The Speedway offered a particularly American illustration: 100 years of rivalry and experiment, ambition and failure, producing an achievement no single mind could have designed.

And so, to the car. Sam and I folded ourselves in and drew the belts tight, and I resolved not to utter a sound, lest some small whimper distract the man whose profession it was to keep us alive. The engine woke. We swept down the straight and up the banking toward the wall, the concrete flashing near enough to touch, the world narrowing to a gray blur and a roar.

I was afraid. I was also, I confess, happy, with that doubled feeling Edmund Burke described when he set the beautiful, which pleases, beside the sublime, which terrifies and exalts at once. Indianapolis Speedway is both. The beauty of a thing well made, and the sublimity of a thing just short of control.

Then the lap was over; silence rushed back. Sam looked at me. He laughed; I laughed.

>>> The Great Migration Remaking Higher Ed

Outside the car, the concrete beneath our feet seemed reassuringly solid. My knees were unsteady, and my heart had not yet settled into its usual rhythm. I thought of Harroun with his rearview mirror, Hulman with his ruined track, and the generations of mechanics and entrepreneurs who had risked money, reputation, and sometimes life itself to see whether a new idea might work.

Their stories differ, but they share a certain disposition: a willingness to act without possessing all the answers, to risk failure without a guarantee of success, and to discover through experiment what no amount of speculation could establish in advance.

That disposition has helped make America what it is. The free society does not promise that every venture will succeed or that every wager will pay. It permits people to try, to compete, to learn from failure, and to build on what others have discovered. Its achievements belong not merely to the celebrated winners but also to the countless people whose experiments, including unsuccessful ones, made the next experiment possible.

Sam and I did little more than occupy two seats for what seemed like a few seconds. We weren’t drivers, engineers or entrepreneurs. We’d simply agreed to the ride, signed the waivers, and climbed aboard. But as we walked away from the track, still chuckling, I thought something was fitting about coming to Indianapolis with a society devoted to liberty and leaving with a fresh appreciation for what liberty makes possible.

The car went around in a circle. The country, over the course of two and a half centuries, has traveled considerably farther.

#7681. Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock

Americans are frustrated with today’s high cost of living, especially fuel prices. Although incomes rose faster than prices last year, it’s been the opposite since February. The only good news is that this inflation will subside when overseas conflicts are resolved, but there is likely more pain to come for consumers until then.

The significant reacceleration of inflation that began in March is due to disruptions in global energy markets. The wars with Iran and in the Ukraine have not only shut off a considerable amount of the world’s crude oil supply, but refined products too, like gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and home heating oil.

Nations worldwide have coped with this reduction in supply by draining energy reserves, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in the U.S., and running refineries at maximum capacity—even delaying critical maintenance. These extraordinary measures blunted but didn’t eliminate the energy shock.

In recent months, Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have reduced Russia’s diesel export capacity by about 90%, effectively taking one of the world’s largest diesel producers out of the market. That additional supply shock has caused diesel prices in particular to skyrocket.

>>> If It’s Good Enough for Wartime, It’s Good Enough for Peacetime 

It’s clear that such energy shocks will affect energy prices, but people often underestimate how much energy affects the price of everything we do and everything we buy. Thus, the energy shock is slowly transforming into an “everything shock,” and it’s showing up in the data.

When someone grabs an item off a store shelf, whether it’s a gallon of milk or a box of screws, that item arrived there on a truck fueled by diesel—and often a train fueled by diesel too. Higher transportation costs put upward pressure on prices everywhere.

Many products are also energy-intensive to produce, like aluminum, where about one-third of its cost of production is electricity. Increasing that input cost makes thousands of items, from soda cans to airplanes, more expensive.

Moreover, energy is a direct input for countless products, from fertilizer to cosmetics to plastics—all synthesized from oil and natural gas. More expensive fertilizer drives up food prices, and plastics are in just about everything today. As elevated energy prices migrate through supply chains, prices everywhere are starting to rise, even if only mildly.

This is a stark contrast to supply-chain data back in January and February, before the Iran war, which indicated prices for many consumer staples would be falling by this time, not rising. That’s still true for some items like certain pharmaceuticals and dairy products, but higher energy prices have simply overpowered any deflationary pressure on most consumer prices this year.

>>> The Red-Blue Energy Divide: How Overregulation Inflates Prices 

Import price data also confirm that today’s inflation is really an energy shock. America has weathered the oil shortage better than most countries because it’s the world’s largest energy producer, pumping a record amount of oil today. Oil prices elsewhere have been higher, which in turn has increased non-energy prices on products and services faster.

Fuel import prices in September rose 4.8% from August and a whopping 34.5% from a year prior. But non-fuel import prices are also rising fast, up 6% over the last 12 months, the fastest annual increase in almost four and a half years. Conversely, non-fuel prices in the U.S. rose at just one-tenth that pace over the same period.

Despite America’s relatively insulated position, the high energy prices since February—especially the high diesel prices more recently—are already spilling into every corner of the economy. Months of elevated inflation are already baked into the cake, so even if the wars in Iran and the Ukraine end immediately, the effects will continue for a while.

Despite that negative short-term outlook, there is some reason for optimism. Since the inflation this year stems from temporary conflicts overseas and not something wrong with the American economy’s fundamentals, energy prices should start coming down once those conflicts end and oil markets normalize.

Until then, however, people will continue to complain about the economy, with negative responses in survey data like consumer sentiment, consumer expectations, and consumer confidence. That’ll remain true even as—or perhaps especially as—the energy shock looks less and less like an energy shock.

#7680. Why the U.S. Air Force Needs More C-17 Globemasters

For decades, the United States has contended with smaller adversaries without the ability to disrupt U.S. aerial logistics. It will not have that luxury in a great-power conflict with China.

In a potential conflict with China, the United States would need to rapidly mass men and equipment throughout the Western Pacific, covering vast distances in a far more challenging geographic environment than the Middle Eastern or European theaters. The success of such efforts will hinge on the airlift capacity of the Air Force—and in particular on the size of the C-17 Globemaster fleet.

The airlift capacity currently offered by U.S. C-17s is plainly insufficient to support large-scale combat operations across the sprawling Pacific theater. To ensure that U.S. forces will be able to stay in the fight against China, the United States must restart C-17 production.

Why the C-17 Globemaster Matters

The C-17 Globemaster is a transport aircraft that delivers large equipment, supplies, and troops to airfields all over the world. It is the second-largest U.S. cargo plane in service, behind only the C-5M Super Galaxy, but is considerably newer than the Super Galaxy and is expected to last far longer.

Boeing, the C-17’s manufacturer, delivered 223 of the aircraft to the U.S. Air Force between 1993 and 2013, out of a total of 279 built for all customers. Today, the Air Force operates 157 active-duty C-17s, with the remaining aircraft being assigned to National Guard and Air Force Reserve units.

Following the completion of the Air Force order, production of C-17s for export continued at Boeing’s Long Beach plant until 2015. The production line was finally closed upon the delivery of the final batch of four Qatar-bound C-17s; it has remained dormant since.

Recent conflicts have placed considerable pressure on the Air Force’s limited C-17 inventory. Between February 28 and June 30, U.S. Transportation Command conducted more than 1,500 air missions into the Middle East. This flight count included frequent periods of high-tempo airlift operations, during which 30 to 40 cargo flights ferried military equipment and personnel into the Middle East each day.

>>> China’s South Pacific Missile Test: Strategic Signaling and Regional Consequences

Air Force C-17s are the linchpin of any major movement of troops and equipment. In the weeks leading up to Operation Absolute Resolve, the seizure of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro from Caracas, open-source data identified 83 C-17 flights arriving at Caribbean bases over a 16-day period. At least 160 transport aircraft were observed moving through Europe, the Mediterranean, and the Middle East in the 13 days before the Operation Midnight Hammer strikes of June 2025.

The intense demand for this overworked transport force is likely to grow in future years. New requirements for mobile radars and improvements to existing weapons systems point to a growing cargo catalogue that C-17s will be tasked with transporting.

In addition to carrying new C-17-standardized cargo, Air Force officials envision employing the aircraft as a strike platform. The deployment of palletized munitions from C-17s may provide U.S. forces with a flexible and affordable way to saturate enemy airspace. However, each combat patrol performed by C-17s will eat away at the Air Force’s aggregate airlift capacity.

America Doesn’t Have Enough C-17s for a Great-Power War

Put simply, as the C-17 fleet ages and its maintenance needs grow, the Air Force is being asked to do more with less. This comes at a time when the nation’s strategic airlift force is already reaching its limits. In 2024, the commander of U.S. Transportation Command testified that a single large-scale combat operation would consume America’s existing airlift capacity.

A conflict with China would demand an airlift far more substantial than the one observed during Operation Epic Fury. U.S. forces fighting in the Western Pacific would depend on consistent deliveries of reinforcements, weapons systems, and munitions into contested and austere environments. China’s heavy investment in A2/AD capabilities will further compound the logistical burden on America’s C-17 fleet. A 2025 transfer of a single Patriot battalion from Asia to the Middle East reportedly took 73 C-17 flights to complete, for example.

>>> Reintroduce Nuclear Weapons to the Pacific To Reduce the Chances of War With China

A 2025 transfer of a single Patriot battalion from Asia to the Middle East reportedly took 73 C-17 flights to complete, for example.

America Can Still Restart the C-17 Production Line

The U.S. has been working diligently recently to ensure that it possesses the requisite warfighters, technology, and equipment required to defend the first island chain. However, these assets can only make an impact if they make it to the fight. To do so, the logic is clear: the United States needs to expand its C-17 fleet.

Restarting the C-17 production line is essential to building the airlift capacity required to sustain flight operations across the Pacific theater. Past small-scale conflicts with inferior adversaries have permitted the U.S. to overlook this requirement. Today, it must once again be prepared to fight a prolonged campaign in the Western Pacific against the rapidly expanding Chinese military.

Reopening the assembly line in Long Beach will not be an easy task. Boeing’s skilled labor force for this system has probably dispersed across California in the 11 years since the plant’s closure. Furthermore, the supply chains providing the materials for C-17 production will need to be re-established. Machinery and industrial equipment will also need to be re-sourced or retooled.

Nevertheless, it is vital that this long process begins now. The Air Force would need expanded airlift capacity the moment conflict were to break out along the first island chain. Delaying action until a crisis emerges may mean failure to deliver the airlift capacity the joint force requires when it is needed most.

#7679. Court finds law protecting judges, officers’ personal information unconstitutional

U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey delivers remarks at a news conference in Newark, New Jersey, on Dec. 19, 2022. (Photo By Kyle Mazza/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images)

A West Virginia law shielding the online publication of personal information belonging to judges and law enforcement officers was ruled unconstitutional by a federal appeals court Tuesday.

The Oct. 27 ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, is the first instance of a federal appellate court overriding a state law protecting the home addresses and unpublished phone numbers of judges and officers since states began safeguarding personal information after a gunman shot and killed 20-year-old Daniel Anderl, the son of U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey, inside their New Jersey home in 2020.

Class action lawsuits filed by Michael Jackson, a retired law enforcement officer, charged Thomson Reuters, Whitepages Inc., PeopleConnect and LexisNexis with violating the state’s Daniel’s Law through online people search services, according to coverage by Reuters.

Bursor & Fisher attorney Philip Fraietta, who represents Jackson, did not give a comment for the article.
