#7664. Poe, the Pandemic and a Halloween Lesson for Catholics and Protestants

For many years, I kept a private rule as some men keep a flask in their coat pocket: one novel always at hand, open somewhere, patient, no matter how the briefs and research and obligations piled up.

Lately, I have broken the rule. I’ve felt its absence the way the tongue keeps returning to the place where a tooth once was. Then, the other afternoon, a television appearance was abruptly canceled, and I found myself holding two unclaimed hours like dollar bills found on the sidewalk. The day was bright and sunny, but it was October all the same. The light had that thin, cidery quality, and the shadows lay longer on the lawn than the clock said they had any right to.

It is, as friends of mine insist, Kirktober. Russell Kirk, the sage of Mecosta, Mich., whose “The Conservative Mind” gave postwar conservatism both its pedigree and its conscience, was born in October, and he loved nothing better than a ghost story told by firelight at Piety Hill, his ancestral house. He wrote them too, and wrote them well, for he believed the uncanny was a moral instrument: it reminds us that the universe keeps rules we did not write.

So, in his honor, I wandered from my usual shelves, took down an old leatherbound Poe whose spine had gone soft as a glove, and let it fall open where it wished. It chose “The Masque of the Red Death.”

>>> Manhattan’s Lost Its Screen Presence

The story is hardly longer than a sermon, and it haunted me in a way Poe could not have intended, because the plague years (yes, I mean COVID are not far behind us. His pestilence is “fatal” and “hideous.” “Blood was its Avatar and its seal—the redness and the horror of blood.” The whole business, from first dizziness to last breath, took half an hour.

And then there is Prince Prospero, whose very name is a boast of good fortune and an echo of Shakespeare’s magician, the one who withdrew to an island and commanded the weather. Poe’s prince gathers a thousand of his gayest knights and dames and retires “to the deep seclusion of one of his castellated abbeys.” The courtiers weld the bolts shut behind them. The external world could take care of itself.

One remembers the photographs from our own season of quarantine: the governors at the fine restaurants, the masks lowered for the cameras of the important, the rules that fell on ordinary people like rain and somehow never dampened those who made them.

Inside the abbey, Poe builds a fever dream. There are seven rooms, each a single color: blue, purple, green, orange, white, violet. The seventh is hung in black velvet, and its windows are scarlet, the deep color of blood. No lamp burns in any chamber; instead, braziers on tripods stand outside the tinted glass, throwing firelight through the panes so that every room swims in its own unnatural hue.

Here the masquerade whirls on. The costumes have much of the beautiful, much of the wanton, much of the bizarre, something of the terrible. A mask is a small lie that promises a large one: that you may become anyone, and so nothing can find you. But in the black room stands a great ebony clock, and on each hour it sounds a note so strange that the orchestra falters, the waltzers freeze, the giddiest go pale. The clock is the one guest who cannot be bribed. The rooms run east to west, dawn to dusk, and everyone knows where the last one leads.

At midnight, an intruder appears: 

The figure was tall and gaunt, and shrouded from head to foot in the habiliments of the grave. The mask which concealed the visage was made so nearly to resemble the countenance of a stiffened corpse that the closest scrutiny must have had difficulty in detecting the cheat. 

Prospero, furious at the insult, chases the figure through all seven rooms with a drawn dagger. In the black chamber, the stranger turns, the dagger drops, and the prince falls dead upon the sable carpet. The revelers seize the masker and find beneath the shroud and the corpse-like mask nothing at all, the garments “untenanted by any tangible form.” The Red Death has come and gone.

Poe knew this guest personally. Tuberculosis took his young mother when he was two, then his foster mother, then his brother. In January 1842, a few months before this story appeared, his wife, Virginia, was singing at the piano when blood came into her mouth. She lingered five years. The Red Death lived among him and his and was not merely the product of fiction.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State

My mother would have shut the book. She hated stories like these and would not let us celebrate what she considered the devil’s holiday, so my brother and I were costumed in innocence: pirates, Batman and Robin, Superman, a clown, a nerd with tape on his spectacles, Auburn football players in orange and blue.

We could trick-or-treat, but as we grew older, we went instead to youth group for the Reformation Celebration, honoring Luther and his hammer on that same last night of October. Only as a grown man did I understand how my Catholic brethren must see such a party: as a festival of the Church’s broken body, a wound that Protestants and Catholics alike ought to mourn.

Kirk himself crossed that divide, entering the Catholic Church in middle age, and I think he would have seen what Poe’s story finally tells us. Prospero believed walls could save him. Not so long ago, all of us believed it, or were told to. We sealed ourselves in our own abbeys, masked our faces, and watched the clock of the daily COVID death count, while the powerful went on dancing in rooms we were not permitted to enter.

The churches went dark that spring, Catholic and Protestant both, and the old quarrel between them seemed suddenly beside the point. The Mass and the Lord’s Supper were suspended alike; the dying went to God alone, with no priest or pastor at the bedside; and Easter came to empty pews on both sides of the Reformation.

For a season, the divided church was united in the one way none of us would have chosen: in absence. Perhaps that was the lesson. Nothing we bolt shut keeps out the stranger at midnight, and the clock strikes for every room. What the dark cannot touch is what we share. All Hallows’ Eve is only the night before All Saints, and the night of masks gives way, at last, to the morning of faces.

#7662. No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Of the many inane comments that socialists have made this year, the one that democracy is “the building block of socialism” might be the most absurd.

Who made the comment? You guessed it: New York City’s boy genius, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In a recent episode of “This Past Weekend,” Mr. Mamdani discussed socialism’s ability to ensure affordability with comedian Theo Von. The interview was replete with Marxian nonsense, but Mr. Mamdani also discussed many Americans’ economic frustrations: homeownership feels out of reach; rent is expensive; childcare is unaffordable; and grocery prices are substantially higher.

Young people increasingly feel that the American dream is “slipping away.”

Recognizing affordability problems, however, is not the same as identifying the causes. Mr. Mamdani avers that the free market system cannot solve these problems and that socialism is the silver bullet.

Consider his assertion about democracy. When Mr. Von brought up the concept, Mr. Mamdani interrupted him and claimed, “That’s the building block of socialism.”

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels would like to have a word.

To them, it was clear that implementing socialism—a word that they used interchangeably with communism—would require the opposite of democracy: tyranny.

In their 1848 “The Communist Manifesto,” the owner’s manual for Marxism, Marx and Engels rightly predicted that people would fight back when the government seized their property—something Mr. Mamdani should bear in mind as he upsets more and more New Yorkers with property-grabbing schemes.

“The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the State,” Marx and Engels wrote. “Of course, in the beginning, this cannot be effected except by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property, and on the conditions of bourgeois production.”

So, no, Mr. Mamdani. Socialism’s pillars are totalitarian, based on forced nationalization and coercive state control.

Now, let us deal with the fanciful claim that socialism is the best way to order society: “Socialism to me means that you have whatever you need to live a dignified life, and it’s the government’s job to deliver on that.”

It sounds compassionate, but what happens when the government assumes responsibility for determining, financing and delivering the necessities of a “dignified life”?

Here, we begin to understand why Mr. Mamdani mixes socialism with democracy. To him, democracy is not just about electing leaders; it is also about letting people choose things that they cannot afford, courtesy of taxpayers.

In line with his big-government agenda, he explained socialism as “the extension of democracy from the ballot box to the rest of your life … your workplace, your home.”

Yet socialists devalue real democracy when they define it as the “right” for people to own what they have not earned. They also devalue the protection of inalienable rights when they insist that 51% of the electorate can suppress individual liberties such as property rights—something America’s Founders called “mobocracy.”

A free society empowers majorities, but it also protects individual rights. More government intervention will neither expand liberty nor make New York City more affordable.

The Big Apple is indeed the most expensive city in the United States and the third most expensive in the world. Mr. Mamdani said that is because “greed is baked into a lot of this economy.” He portrays capitalist profit incentives as a motive for firms to exploit workers, reduce the quality of goods and break the law.

Still, profit and wealth are not social defects to be discouraged; quite the contrary. In competitive markets, signals indicate that entrepreneurs have found ways to provide goods and services that consumers value. These incentives encourage businesses to innovate, produce more, reduce costs and discover better ways to meet people’s needs.

This must be a foreign concept to Mr. Mamdani, who believes that it is the government’s duty to provide the public with everything, from rent to groceries. He ignores commonsense solutions that have worked the world over, such as tax cuts and deregulation—and deportations, for that matter, which would reduce costs for households and businesses alike.

>>> Mamdani Is about to Make Housing Even More Expensive

Instead, Mr. Mamdani turns to central planning, even though government bureaucrats created many of the affordability problems he now insists they will solve.

Take housing. Mr. Mamdani argues that housing costs are central to New York’s economic problems, and many economists agree. Yet the city’s affordability crisis results from decades of restrictive zoning, burdensome permit requirements, development constraints, rent regulation and political barriers that limit housing construction.

The pattern is familiar: Government intervention distorts the market, consumers suffer the consequences, then socialists point to those consequences as evidence of market failure requiring still more state intervention.

Throughout his interview with Mr. Von, Mr. Mamdani framed his socialist ideology as empathetic, not the state-controlled subjugation that it is. Yet remember, the more “necessities” the government promises to provide, the more power bureaucrats require to deliver them.

When the government assumes control over housing, childcare, grocery access, transportation and healthcare, citizens become less self-reliant and more dependent on political institutions.

Americans are right to be concerned about affordability, but the challenge facing them today is how to improve markets with more freedom and opportunity, not socialism.

#7661. Crime Is Down: Why Leadership Matters

For years, Americans were told by the left that rising crime was either exaggerated, the result of poverty, caused by COVID, or simply the unavoidable cost of modern life. None of those assertions is true.

Victims, police officers, prosecutors, and families living in high-crime neighborhoods knew better. They understood that crime is not an abstraction. It is a stolen vehicle, a broken window, a family traumatized by violence, or a neighborhood slowly surrendered to fear.

That is why the preliminary results of the just-released 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) deserve serious attention. The numbers point in one direction: crime fell substantially across nearly every major category measured by the survey.

The results are preliminary, and responsible observers will await final estimates and additional analysis. But the trend is unmistakable—and it coincides with a national agenda that has placed public safety, border security, law enforcement, and support for victims at the center of federal policy.

According to the preliminary estimates from the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the rate of serious violent victimization—violent crime excluding simple assault—fell 25%, from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025. Aggravated assault declined even more sharply, dropping 31% from 4.5 to 3.1 per 1,000.

>>> Americans Lost Over $20 Billion to One Type of Crime. Here’s How We Can Fight It

The property-crime figures are equally striking. Property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 per 1,000 households to 111.2 per 1,000. Burglary or trespassing fell 25%. Motor vehicle theft declined 30%, representing approximately 349,000 fewer stolen vehicles. Other household theft declined 19%, while burglary and trespassing represented roughly 460,000 fewer victimizations.

These are not minor statistical adjustments. They represent fewer people harmed, fewer families disrupted, and fewer communities forced to absorb the economic and emotional costs of crime.

The NCVS is particularly important because it captures criminal victimization whether or not the victim reported the offense to police. Each year, the Bureau of Justice Statistics gathers information from a nationally representative sample of approximately 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

It therefore complements the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting data, which are based primarily on information supplied by law enforcement agencies.

The two measures tell a consistent story. The FBI’s 2025 data showed the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began tracking national crime trends in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter declined by an estimated 18.1%.

The NCVS now provides an important second measure, reflecting the experiences of victims themselves.

What explains the decline? No serious analyst should pretend that a single policy produces every change in national crime. Crime rates are influenced by many factors, including local policing strategies, prosecution decisions, economic conditions, demographics, and community involvement. Preliminary survey results also cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship.

But policy choices matter. A president who makes securing the border a priority, removes violent illegal aliens who are subject to deportation, directs the Justice Department to cooperate with the nation’s approximately 18,000 police departments, 3,400 sheriffs’ offices, and 2,300 elected district attorneys, funds law enforcement, and supports victims is sending a clear message: the government’s first responsibility is to protect the innocent.

>>> Another Win for the Task Force To Eliminate Fraud

That message matters. Criminals should expect enforcement, not indulgence. Police officers should know that federal officials recognize the risks they face. Prosecutors should have the resources and cooperation necessary to hold dangerous offenders accountable. Victims should not be treated as an afterthought in a system more concerned with the comfort of defendants than the security of communities.

“This report is proof that President Trump’s ’Make America Safe Again’ agenda is working,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said, the No. 3 official in the Justice Department.

The statement captures the broader significance of the data, even if conclusions should await final estimates: public safety improves when government treats it as a core mission rather than a campaign slogan.

The lesson is straightforward. Effective enforcement, cooperation among federal, state, and local authorities, secure borders, adequately funded police departments, and meaningful support for victims are not outdated ideas. They are practical necessities.

Americans should celebrate these preliminary gains while remaining vigilant. The goal is not merely to report that crime has fallen. The goal is to ensure that it stays down—and that every community, regardless of size or location, receives the protection its residents deserve.

A lawyer who filed a misconduct complaint against a federal judge in Dallas did so after a hearing during which she repeatedly directed racial insults at him, Bloomberg Law reports.

Documents show that attorney Ezra Young, who represented a Black woman professor suing over a tenure denial, filed the complaint following the April hearing in Dallas. His complaint and the response from U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas were among the documents that Brown circulated in an Oct. 17 email to lawyers, judges and members of the media, Bloomberg Law reports.

Throughout the hearing, Brown, a Black woman with Native American ancestry, accused Young of mistreating Black attorneys, took “judicial notice” of her own background in making findings against Young, and repeatedly referred to Young, who is Latino, as being white.

“I think what’s happening here, quite candidly, is you are very intimidated for some reason, Mr. Young, with Black excellence, in light of your white mediocrity. Yeah. Right?,” Brown said, according to the transcript. “You should write that down. I mean, you—I’m—you look like a white man, right?”

“I’m not white, your honor,” Young replied, adding that he’s Latino.

Young filed the complaint, saying he thought that the judge may be suffering from a mental health condition. A judicial investigation resulted in her temporarily losing her docket earlier this month. #7655. Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein of New York dies at 92

In this courtroom sketch, U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York presides during a pretrial hearing in a drug trafficking case for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on July 22, 2026, in New York. (Photo by Jane Rosenberg via the Associated Press)

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York died Wednesday at age 92.

Hellerstein was known for presiding over the federal narcoterrorism conspiracy case against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, according to a story from Law.com. He also oversaw more than 14,000 lawsuits that were filed by victims of the Sept. 11 terror attacks.

On a personal level, the judge is being remembered for his empathy and morality, which was informed by his Jewish faith.

“He didn’t shy away from pushing the boundaries of the law if he thought they would be unjust otherwise,” Evan Farber, a partner at Loeb & Loeb who once clerked for Hellerstein, told Law.com.

Hellerstein graduated from Columbia Law School in 1956, and he became a clerk for U.S. District Judge Edmund Palmieri of the Southern District of New York, Law.com reports. He was a military lawyer with the U.S. Army and a partner and a litigator at Stroock & Stroock & Lavan before being nominated to the federal bench by then-President Bill Clinton. He was confirmed unanimously in 1998.

He took senior status in 2011, but he never slowed down, Law.com reports.

#7654. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

#7652. Federal Court Rejects Trump Lawsuit Seeking to Block Certification of Alaska Senate Election Results

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court found the administration lacked standing to bring the suit. But there are also major substantive problems with Trump's position.

Today, in United States v. Alaska, federal district Judge Sharon Gleason ruled against the Trump administration's lawsuit seeking to block certification of Alaska Senate election results on the grounds that doing so might be necessary to prevent "voter confusion" caused by the presence of two candidates with very similar names on the ballot. As I have explained previously, Dan J. Sullivan can potentially be confused with Dan S. Sullivan (the incumbent GOP senator). Evidence gathered by the New York Times suggests Democrats may have deliberately recruited Dan J. to run, in hopes of siphoning off votes from Dan S. on this topic.

Today's ruling dismisses the Trump lawsuit on the grounds that the United States lacked standing to bring the suit. Most notably, it failed the standing requirement of "redressability." The remedy requested by the administration - blocking certification until the federal government could further "investigate" the issue, would not actually redress the harm of voter confusion, and certainly could not do so while maintaining legally required secrecy of the ballots. In addition, Judge Gleason emphasizes that the federal government's proposed remedy would likely intrude on the powers of the state government,  create more voter "confusion" than it forestalls:

The Supreme Court "has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election…" "Such late-breaking, court-ordered rule changes can 'result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,' and thus undermine the '[c]onfidence in the integrity of our electoral processes . . . essential to the functioning of our participatory democracy.'"

The United States maintains that it is "not seeking to alter the time, place, or manner of Alaska's election" [which the Constitution generally leaves under state control]. And yet it seeks a court order preventing the State from certifying the election if certain circumstances occur; a court order requiring the State to segregate and preserve certain ballots; and a court order permitting the United States to conduct an investigation into the intent of those voters who cast ballots for Daniel J. Sullivan. These requests certainly involve the time, place, and manner of Alaska's election, which are the responsibilities of the State, not the executive branch of the federal government. Clearly, if this Court were to order that certain ballots will be segregated and subject to a future and as yet unspecified investigation by law enforcement, it would likely result in voter "confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls."Such late-breaking changes to the election rules are strongly disfavored.

In addition to these procedural problems with the Trump lawsuit, it also deserves to be rejected on the substantive merits. I covered some of the reasons why here and here. See also the excellent amicus brief filed by prominent election law scholar Rick Hasen, which goes into these issues in greater detail. Quite simply, there is no federal law giving the administration the power to block certification of election results based on "voter confusion."

As explained in one of my earlier posts about this case, Democrats deserve blame for seeking to deceive voters in this way, even though it is highly unlikely it would cause enough confusion to change the outcome of the election (various aspects of the Alaska ballot and election system reduce the already low odds of that happening). But for reasons summarized in the same post, this kind of thing is far from the worst example of exploitation of voter ignorance. Lies and deceptions about public policy issues are far more significant.

Today's decision may be appealed. But I think it highly unlikely that the appellate court (or the US Supreme Court) will reverse it.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#7646. Supreme Court to Consider Successive Habeas Claim in Capital Case, Twenty Years After the Murder

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

This week, the Court will consider when a death-row inmate may file a second habeas application based on “a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable.”

On Wednesday this week, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in Guerrero, Director of the Texas Department of Criminal Justice v. Dexter Johnson. It is a capital case involving the kidnapping, rape, and murder of Maria Aparece that Johnson committed in 2006. The case does not involve any claim Johnson is innocent of these heinous crimes, but rather how to interpret provisions in the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 (AEDPA).

AEDPA prohibits successive habeas applications by state prisoners with only two narrow exceptions, including for claims that "rel[y] on a new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(A). The question presented seems to answer itself. The Supreme Court has granted cert to decide whether a claim relies on a "new rule of constitutional law, made retroactive to cases on collateral review by the Supreme Court, that was previously unavailable" when the Court announced the rule before the filing of the prisoner's prior federal habeas petition. As Texas persuasively argues in its merits brief, Johnson's Atkins claim (that he should not be executed because, he claims, he is borderline intellectually disabled) does not rely on any new rule of constitutional law. The Court decided Atkins v. Virginia in 2002—long before Johnson filed his initial federal habeas application, before his conviction became final on direct review—and even before he committed the capital murder for which he was sentenced to death.

Instead of a change in law, Johnson's claim relies on a new factual predicate: the publication of a new diagnostic manual by the American Psychiatric Association (the DSM-5), under which he was diagnosed with an intellectual disability. But a claim in a successive application based on a new factual predicate must satisfy § 2244(b)(2)(B), which Johnson's Atkins claim does not, because his new evidence has no bearing on whether the jury would have found him "guilty of the underlying offense." 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(2)(B)(ii).

Surprisingly, a Fifth Circuit panel accepted Johnson's argument that he could pursue relief on this "new" claim. And the Fifth Circuit en banc denied further review by a vote of 9-7. Judge Ho (joined by Judges Jones, Smith, and Engelhardt) wrote a dissent from this denial, pointing out that "[e]xtraordinary delays like this are, alas, extraordinarily commonplace in our criminal justice system. And they are far from costless. Never mind the expense to the taxpayer. Such delays also force the family and friends of victims like Maria Aparece to wait for justice—for over two decades, in this case."

I have filed an amicus brief in the case, along with counsel of record Allyson Ho and her colleagues at Gibson Dunn, Brad Hubbard, Matt Scorcio, Brandon Wolf, and Marquan Robertson. Our brief provides a fuller account of the cost to victims' families—such as the Aparece family—who must wait for justice in capital cases like this one. Here's the introduction to our brief:

Twenty years ago, in the early-morning hours of Father's Day 2006, Dexter Johnson abducted 23-year-old Maria Chrisalee Lopez Aparece—"Sally" to her family and friends—and her boyfriend, Huy Ngo, at gunpoint. After terrorizing them, Johnson raped Sally in the back seat of her car while his accomplice taunted Ngo. Johnson then marched Sally and Ngo into the woods, shot each of them in the head, and left them for dead. Johnson and his accomplices then took Sally's car joyriding and used her credit cards to fund a shopping spree. Earlier that evening, Sally had been at home making a card for her father, Protasio Aparece, while he worked a sixteen-hour shift as a registered nurse. After her murder, Sally's family found the unfinished card. They placed it in their living room, in front of the fireplace, alongside Sally's ashes—where it remains today. Johnson's vicious crimes inflicted unbearable pain on his victims and their families.

But that was just the beginning of their suffering. Johnson's serial litigation has robbed the families of even a modicum of peace or closure. It has been two decades since Johnson brutally murdered Sally, and nineteen years since a Harris County jury sentenced him to death—but justice still has not been served. This Court should vindicate crime victims' "important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence," Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 149 (2019), and "powerful and legitimate interest" in "real finality," Calderon v. Thompson, 523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998), by reversing the judgment below and ending an ordeal that has compounded the suffering of Sally's family for over two decades.

You can read the full brief for the Aparece family here, which discusses how excessive delays (like the one in this case) break AEDPA's promise of finality in capital cases and how research confirms that excessive delays in criminal cases harm victims' families.

I hope the Court reverses the Fifth Circuit's decision and brings the Aparece family one step closer to justice.

#7643. Promise to Apologize Might Be Enforceable—but Court Can't Order Apology if None Was Finally Agreed to

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Judge Mia Roberts Perez (E.D. Pa.) in Souderton Area for All v. Souderton Area School Dist., decided Sept. 28:

This case began as a case about Plaintiffs' exercise of their First Amendment rights by protesting at a Souderton Area School District ("District") school board meeting. It then became a case about keeping promises. Now, it is a case about which promises this Court can enforce.

When Plaintiffs protested the Souderton Area School Board outside a September 2024 meeting, the government officials for whom their message was intended were not the only ones affected. One school board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter as they exited the meeting. In the parking lot, Plaintiffs Christopher Spigel, Helen Spigel, and Patrick Kitt confronted them. Rather than constraining their critical expression to the adult members of the school board, the protesters directed their ire toward the child, who the District has consistently maintained was frightened by the adult Plaintiffs' conduct.

Here are plaintiffs' allegations as quoted in an earlier decision:

According to the Complaint, in August 2024, Plaintiffs and other District community members learned that then-member of the Board of School Directors of Souderton Area School District (the "Board") William Formica posted lewd comments on social media about Vice President Kamala Harris, disparaging teachers and non-English speakers, and deriding diversity programs. In response, Plaintiff Souderton Area For All ("SAFA") encouraged its members to attend District Board meetings to protest and demand Mr. Formica's resignation.

The August 29, 2024 Board meeting saw high attendance of community members opposed to Mr. Formica's remarks, as well as a rally organized by SAFA to protest. But the Board did not allow SAFA or its members to demonstrate on District property, requiring them to gather on a public sidewalk 80 feet away from where the meeting was held.

At the same time, the Board permitted supporters of Mr. Formica to gather and counter-protest directly outside the meeting's entrance on District property. Due to increased attendance, the Board began requiring meeting attendees to provide photo-ID so that they could prioritize seating for District residents. Several individual Plaintiffs were excluded from meetings as a result of this new rule.

On September 26, 2024, as Board members exited a Board meeting, Plaintiffs Patrick Kitt, Christopher Spigel, and Helen Spigel protested by making cricket noises and accusing the Board of being complicit in Mr. Formica's misconduct through its silence. One Board member was accompanied by her teenage daughter, who was upset and intimidated by the protesters directing questions and accusations to her.

Two weeks later, the District issued cease and desist letters to Plaintiffs Kitt, Spigel, and Spigel, informing them they could not be on school property for the remainder of the school year, including for public meetings. On November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed this lawsuit, alleging the District's actions violated their rights to free speech and due process. In addition to the Complaint, on November 20, 2024, Plaintiffs filed a Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order ("TRO"), seeking to enjoin the District from enforcing its ban on Plaintiffs from entering school property for the remainder of the 2024–25 school year and allowing Plaintiffs to enter school property to attend school board meetings and other events on the same terms as other members of the public….

[T]he Court enforces the settlement promises …: continued livestreaming and archiving of Board meetings; rescission of the cease-and-desist letters; completion and maintenance of the designated protest/gathering area consistent with applicable law; and payment of the attorneys' fees already authorized.

What exactly was allegedly said to the daughter? According to a letter from the school district's lawyer attached to the Complaint,

It is my understanding that you … began screaming erroneously believing that [Board member Kim Wheeler's] daughter was Bill Formica's daughter. You screamed: "Tell your father he's an asshole" and "Tell her dad he's a fascist and needs to resign."

We are also advised that Jim Wheeler admonished you not to speak to her daughter because she is just a child and Bill Formica was not her father. You once again began yelling at Kim Wheeler's daughter to: "Then tell your mother to stop saying silent and she's just as bad as Bill."

On the other hand, the plaintiffs' counsel describes matters differently (in response to an e-mail from me):

As to the plaintiffs' position regarding what was said at the September 26, 2024, school board meeting, Chris Spigel recalled asking "does the child know her dad is a fascist?" and Patrick Kitt recalled that he called Board Member Formica a "coward" and a "beta male" but did not say anything to Board Member Wheeler's daughter, who was 15 at the time.

The e-mail also disputes other claims in the letter from the school district's lawyer, related to how close some of the plaintiffs were to Formica and her daughter; it cites surveillance video at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Th8y29iZjY0 (though noting that the video has no sound).

And now back to the Sept. 28 decision on the apology:

After the District retaliated against Plaintiffs and Plaintiffs brought this lawsuit, the parties engaged in lengthy settlement negotiations. At all times, the settlement terms included a promise by Plaintiffs to issue an apology to the child who was personally, adversely affected by their conduct.

The settlement negotiations ultimately broke down, and this Court granted the District's motion to enforce the settlement agreement on promissory estoppel grounds. The Court found that Plaintiffs promised to dismiss the lawsuit and apologize to the child, that the District relied on those promises when it took definite and substantial action to fulfill its own obligations under the settlement agreement, and that it would be unjust to allow Plaintiffs to walk away after the District's actions in reliance.

Plaintiffs move for reconsideration of one part of the Court's order, which was sealed due to the confidential nature of the parties' agreement. The Sealed Supplemental Order required Plaintiffs to keep their promise to apologize to the board member's teenage daughter, an innocent bystander who no one disputed was caught in the crossfire of the protest and experienced emotional distress as a result.

As adults, as community members, and as parents, people recognize the importance of teaching children by example: showing them kindness and respect, and taking accountability for their choices so that their children may follow those examples in their treatment of others. It is not controversial to acknowledge that the ethical thing to do when an adult harms a child is to apologize to that child, even if the harm was inadvertent.

The First Amendment, however, limits the Court's ability to compel an apology. A party may waive First Amendment rights through an agreement, but courts presume against waiver of fundamental rights. Any waiver must be voluntary, knowing, and intelligent, and supported by clear and compelling evidence.

Here, the record does not establish such a waiver. The proposed apology changed throughout the negotiations—including who would issue it, what it would say, and how it would be delivered—and Kitt's willingness to apologize was conditioned on resolution of all other settlement issues, a condition that was not met. For these reasons, and those discussed more fully below, Plaintiffs' Motion for Reconsideration is granted….

Plaintiffs argue the Sealed Supplemental Order violates their First Amendment right against compelled speech. Defendants oppose, asserting that the Order at issue here merely enforces a promise Plaintiff Kitt made, through which he waived his First Amendment right….

[G]enerally applicable laws do not offend the First Amendment simply because they have incidental effects on speech. See Cohen v. Cowles Media (1992) (finding that allowing promissory estoppel action based on promise not to disclose confidential source's identity did not violate First Amendment despite incidental consequence of inhibiting truthful reporting because "the First Amendment does not confer on the press a constitutional right to disregard promises that would otherwise be enforced under state law"). "First Amendment rights can be limited via contract."

However, there must be "'clear' and 'compelling' evidence of waiver and that waiver is voluntary, knowing, and intelligent." "[C]ourts must indulge every reasonable presumption against waiver of fundamental constitutional rights." In the context of the First Amendment, a waiver must also be "freely given."

Typically, courts lack the power to order litigants to apologize. See Devonish v. Atl. Cnty. Justice Facility (D.N.J. 2010) (collecting cases and dismissing claim for injunctive relief directing an apology because "the remedy of 'apology' is not cognizable, either within the meaning of a Section 1983 action or as a general legal remedy that a court has the power to order, under any provision"); see also Woodruff v. Ohman (6th Cir. 2002) (finding district court exceeded its equitable power when ordering defendant to apologize for gender discrimination because "[t]he apology will not provide any remedy … for which the damages imposed have not already accounted," and there was no authority "that would permit a court to order a defendant to speak in a manner that may well contravene the beliefs the defendant holds"); Ali v. Barton (N.D. Fla. 2020) (noting that the Court lacks the power to order defendants to issue "an unconditional apology")….

Throughout the settlement negotiations, the parties themselves disagreed about the nature of the apology. The apology was first raised as a term of the settlement at the settlement conference on January 16, 2025. The parties initially agreed that Plaintiff Stephanie Barnett Jamison would deliver the apology to the minor. The minor thereafter expressed that she would not accept an apology from Jamison because Jamison was not directly involved in the actions that frightened her. As of February 5, 2025, the parties were still negotiating the specifics of the apology.

Plaintiffs eventually agreed that Kitt was willing to provide the apology "so long as all other issues in the case are resolved." The issues were not fully resolved. Between February and May 2025, the parties continued exchanging drafts of the settlement agreement and making changes to certain provisions, including whether the parties would issue a joint press release, individual press releases, or no press release at all. That term was never resolved because the District did not accept Plaintiff's final proposal that the agreement be silent as to a press release until the offer was terminated. The Court already found that term material to the agreement.

As this Court previously explained, each of the drafts the parties exchanged contained materially different terms. Each constituted an offer or counteroffer, such that there was no settlement agreement that the Court could enforce under traditional contract principles. The Court agrees with Plaintiffs that Kitt could not knowingly, voluntarily, and intelligently waive his First Amendment right to be free from government compelled speech when his promise was conditioned on the parties' resolution of all other issues—a condition that was not met….

I am looking into getting unsealed the sealed supplemental order and the briefing related to objections to that order.

Emily Morgan and Joy Ramsingh (Ramsingh Legal, PLLC), and Solomon Furious Worlds and Sara J. Rose (ACLU of Pennsylvania) represent plaintiffs.

#7642. When the Supreme Court blessed zoning

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

James Metzenbaum was stuck on a train from Washington – slowed by a snowstorm – convincing himself that his opponent had successfully persuaded the Supreme Court against his position within the last few minutes of oral argument. He had just argued in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty in defense of the city’s zoning plan. The poor weather meant he might not get back to his office in time to send a telegram asking Chief Justice William Howard Taft for more briefing before the weekend. So he improvised – opening the train car door, making eye contact with a man shoveling snow near the tracks, and tossing him a telegram wrapped in cash. The shoveler seems to have understood what was intended. He sent off the telegram, and a few days later the court granted Metzenbaum permission to file another brief.

Not long after that, the court granted a full rehearing, which was followed by a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions. In a 6-3 decision, the court sided with Metzenbaum and in favor of Euclid’s power to pass comprehensive zoning, and against a local developer who had argued the town’s plan exceeded the city’s police power and destroyed the property’s value. Three justices dissented, though they never said why.

It was an odd start to the birth of modern zoning, and it happened almost exactly 100 years ago.

Many people think the term “Euclidean zoning” takes its name from the Greek “father of geometry.” Instead, it takes its name from Village of Euclid, which upheld the power of cities to zone.

But the city at the center of that lawsuit was, in fact, named after the ancient mathematician. In 1796, six surveyors working in the Western Reserve in Ohio demanded better terms for their punishing work. Together they secured an agreement to jointly own a township in return for settling a few dozen families there. They named it for the man regarded as their profession’s patron saint. And while they eventually abandoned the town’s frigid winters, the name endured.

By the early 20th century, nearby Cleveland had become an industrial metropolis and Euclid was positioned to develop alongside it. Ambler Realty owned 68 acres between Euclid Avenue, a major road for storefronts, and the Nickel Plate railroad, a hub of industrial freight – meaning the property had enormous industrial potential. But in 1922, Euclid adopted an ordinance dividing the village by use, height, and area. Near the avenue, Ambler’s land could accommodate single- and two-family dwellings, but not apartments, shops, or factories, which were relegated farther back toward the tracks. The company alleged that land worth $10,000 an acre for industry would fetch no more than $2,500 for residential use.

Ambler challenged the ordinance under the Ohio Constitution and the 14th Amendment’s due process and equal protection clauses. Government could protect health and safety, Ambler said, but it could not confiscate an owner’s freedom to use its property when the property itself posed no danger to the public.

Comprehensive zoning was still a relatively new experiment. New York City’s influential 1916 resolution, which (among other things) sought to regulate the size and height of the city’s buildings, was only a decade old when Euclid reached the Supreme Court. To supporters, zoning promised to bring scientific order to urban growth. To opponents, it entrusted the future of a city to officials who could mistake their preferences for the public welfare or succumb to lobbying.

Ambler retained Newton D. Baker, a former Cleveland mayor and Woodrow Wilson’s secretary of war during World War I. In overlapping litigation, he represented a Jewish orphanage seeking to build in University Heights, Ohio, where land-use restrictions became a tool of ethnic exclusion. Baker was thus acutely aware that a debate about the “residential character” of the city might actually be a debate about the people who wanted to reside there. Euclid’s attorney, meanwhile, was James Metzenbaum, who had helped draft the ordinance he was defending and lived on Euclid Avenue himself.

The first round went to Baker. Federal District Judge David Westenhaver, Baker’s former law partner, struck down the ordinance in 1924. According to Westenhaver, the ultimate effect of Euclid’s plan was “to classify the population and segregate them according to their income or situation in life.” But in defending the rights of both the poor and property owners, Westenhaver revealed his own prejudices: He argued that Euclid’s plan could not possibly be constitutional given that the Supreme Court had just struck down exclusionary racial zoning, which he believed was even more beneficial.

The village took advantage of a rule allowing it to appeal directly to the Supreme Court, which heard argument on Jan. 27, 1926, in the old Senate chamber (the court would move to its current location in 1935). Only eight justices were present, since George Sutherland was resting in Charleston, South Carolina, with high blood pressure.

Neither party requested a transcript, so no one knows exactly what was said at argument. But Metzenbaum later recalled a lighter moment. After Chief Justice William Howard Taft asked why Metzenbaum alternated between the term “realtors” and “real estate men,” Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes interjected that, judging from a case heard the previous week, one received more money than the other. Metzenbaum responded, “I presumed the distinction was about the same as that which exists between a statesman and a politician.” In Metzenbaum’s recollection, Taft shook with laughter, repeating the comparison.

By the time Baker finished his turn arguing, however, Metzenbaum’s good humor had evaporated. His anxiety followed him onto the train home, and, believing that Baker had misrepresented certain facts, he composed the telegram which would reach Taft by way of the snow shoveler. His worries were evidently justified. Justice Harlan Stone’s records show a 5–3 conference vote against the ordinance. But the court later agreed to hear the case again, perhaps so that Sutherland could sit for argument. The case was reargued on Oct. 12, almost exactly a century ago.

Additional argument admitted additional briefing. Cincinnati lawyer and planning advocate Alfred Bettman had missed the original amicus deadline. He sought permission to file late from Taft, whom he knew personally, and the court granted it, allowing his brief to be considered before the next argument date.

Bettman’s theory differed from Metzenbaum’s in important ways. The village’s lawyer argued for an expanding understanding of the state’s police power that would allow the government not just to regulate for public health and safety, but to promote the general welfare. Bettman, by contrast, argued that zoning was just like other nuisance laws, except it allowed localities to prevent nuisances from occurring in advance. Bettman’s theory threatened to say the quiet part out loud: certain defenders of zoning considered some people, rather than their property, a nuisance.

On Nov. 22, 1926, Sutherland announced the decision upholding Euclid’s ordinance. Taft joined him, along with Justices Holmes, Louis Brandeis, Edward Sanford, and Stone. Justices Willis Van Devanter, James McReynolds, and Pierce Butler dissented, but left no written opinion explaining why.

Sutherland’s most memorable illustration came from nuisance law: “A nuisance may be merely a right thing in the wrong place—like a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” It was not exactly a flattering analogy for those who wanted to live in the type of higher-density housing banned by Euclid’s zoning ordinance. Later, Sutherland described an apartment “very often” as “a mere parasite,” benefiting from the surroundings its presence would undermine. Apartments could obstruct air and sunlight, generate traffic and noise, diminish the attractiveness of neighboring homes, and reduce the area’s residential character, he said. Though the plan would burden some businesses and owners who were not nuisances themselves, such overbreadth didn’t render the law unconstitutional on its face. (Interestingly, Sutherland mentioned how suppressing density was a means of suppressing fires, a rationale that San Francisco had used to systematically exclude primarily Chinese-owned laundries from the area and that was rejected by the Supreme Court.)

While Ambler had argued the plan was diverting industrial development away from Euclid, Sutherland concluded it had merely confined that development to certain areas. And while Euclid was engaging in a relatively new and more intrusive form of regulating property, Sutherland (quoting another opinion) responded that, “[w]ith the growth and development of the State, the police power necessarily develops … to meet the changing conditions.”

At the same time, the majority left room for future challenges. Sustaining the ordinance’s general framework did not validate every zoning plan or every application. Two years later, Sutherland himself wrote for a unanimous court in Nectow v. City of Cambridge, invalidating a residential restriction where the factual findings showed no substantial relationship to public health, safety, convenience, or welfare.

But since then, courts have overwhelmingly approved zoning and afforded localities considerable deference in crafting it.

Baker died on Christmas Day in 1937. The law firm that he helped found and that bears his name, Baker Hostetler, is one of the largest firms in the country, and buildings ranging from a public high school to a college dorm to a veteran’s hospital are named in his honor.

Metzenbaum turned his victory into a lasting professional identity, publishing “The Law of Zoning” in 1930. His wife, Bessie, had died in 1920, and he reportedly died on New Year’s Eve in 1960 trying to free his car from a snowbank while visiting her mausoleum.

Despite Euclid’s best laid plans, Ambler’s property eventually went to industrial use after all. During World War II, the federal government acquired the site to put up an aircraft engine and landing gear factory. The industrial complex now known as Nickel Plate Station sold for $18.5 million in June 2026. Apparently zoning could not predict what the community would need in the future.

A century after Euclid, the battle over zoning rages on. Proponents of zoning, as in Euclid, see it as a critical means of promoting public welfare and the surrounding environment. Opponents point to ample evidence that zoning has been used to exclude “undesirable” populations from certain parts of town, all while suppressing dynamism and inflating the cost of housing.

We have seen several Supreme Court cases establishing limits around zoning. In cases like Nollan v. California Coastal Commission and Dolan v. City of Tigard, the court limited the types of demands the government can make of property owners who apply for a development permit. And in Moore v. Cleveland, the court invalidated a zoning restriction that prevented a grandmother from living with her grandchildren. While the majority relied on the sanctity of the family, Justice John Paul Stevens wrote separately to emphasize that Euclid had “vastly diminished the rights of individual property owners,” but had not “totally extinguish[ed] them,” and thus zoning restrictions must have a meaningful relationship to the public welfare. But Euclid itself remains on firm ground, its holding having produced no written dissents but perhaps a century of consequences worth dissenting from.

Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

Recommended Citation: Anastasia Boden, When the Supreme Court blessed zoning, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 26, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/when-the-supreme-court-blessed-zoning/

#7641. Some Surprisingly Tolerant Judges out There in Pennsylvania

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Commonwealth v. Outlaw, decided Thursday by Pennsylvania Supreme Court Justice David Wecht, writing for a unanimous court:

In June 2022, Philadelphia County Court of Common Pleas Judge Roxanne E. Covington was holding a hearing on a motion to suppress evidence in Marquis McClain's criminal case. Seated in the gallery of the courtroom was McClain's acquaintance, Basile Outlaw. After Judge Covington announced that she would be denying McClain's suppression motion, Outlaw stood up and said "the judge is a cocksucker" loud enough for Judge Covington to hear. Judge Covington responded, "What did you say?" Outlaw replied: "Never mind. I'm leaving." Outlaw then exited the courtroom.

A deputy sheriff and a court employee began searching the building for Outlaw. The trial court recessed the suppression matter to allow McClain's defense attorney to confer with his client in the wake of the court's suppression ruling. The court subsequently adjourned, but Judge Covington asked McClain's attorney to "stick around for another moment … just in case." Around this time, Outlaw came back to the courtroom on his own, at which time he was taken into custody for direct criminal contempt.

Outlaw was tried and sentenced "to fifteen to thirty days' incarceration"; he served thirty days. But the Pennsylvania Supreme Court reversed the conviction:

Specifically at issue here is Subsection 4132(3) [of the Pennsylvania Crimes Code]. A conviction under that Subsection "requires proof beyond a reasonable doubt: (1) of misconduct, (2) in the presence of the court, (3) committed with the intent to obstruct the proceedings, (4) which obstructs the administration of justice." This Court has held that, "[f]or conduct to constitute an obstruction of the administration of justice, it must significantly disrupt judicial proceedings." This means that "[r]emarks that are injudicious, or even disrespectful, will not, without more, justify a summary conviction for contempt of court." To illustrate these principles, consider Williams v. Williams, where a pro se attorney in a custody dispute reacted injudiciously to a trial judge's evidentiary ruling:

Opposing Counsel: I heard him say that you are such a fucking asshole. I heard it as an officer of the court. And the stenographer is nodding her head. That's exactly what he said, "He is such a fucking asshole." And he said it under his breath. And as an officer of the court, I am standing here, and I am testifying that that's exactly what he said.

The trial court held Williams in contempt. On appeal, however, this Court held that Williams' remark did not obstruct the administration of justice because, although "there was a momentary break in the proceedings" due to Williams' comment, "the hearing resumed quickly," "[t]he entire incident encompassed just three and a half pages of hearing transcript," and "[s]uch a transient delay is not an obstruction of justice." Expounding upon the statutory requirement that the contemnor must "obstruct[t] the administration of justice," we explicitly stated that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)."

Consistent with Williams is Behr v. Behr, where a pro se litigant brought to family court a box of documents that had the word "DEATH" scrawled on it in faint orange highlighter. The box remained under the litigant's table for the entire hearing, and only after the proceeding concluded did anyone notice it. The trial court held the litigant in contempt, but this Court reversed, concluding that the litigant's conduct did not significantly disrupt the judicial proceeding. We also rejected the trial court's suggestion that a significant disruption occurred when the presence of the box triggered an investigation and subsequent contempt hearing. We called this "circular reasoning" because, if we accepted the argument, it would mean that "any time a court reconvenes a hearing to investigate alleged misconduct, the alleged contemnor has automatically obstructed the administration of justice." …

The circumstances of this appeal are analogous to those in Williams. The insult that Outlaw directed at the court here ("the judge is a cocksucker") is offensive in a manner similar to the remark made in Williams ("He's such a fucking asshole."). Both comments fall well below the expected standard of courtroom decorum, and both contemnors made their comments in response to judicial rulings with which they disagreed. Furthermore, the delay to the proceedings in this case was limited to the judge asking Outlaw "What did you say?", followed by Outlaw responding "Never mind. I'm leaving." This is the exact sort of "transient delay" or "momentary break in the proceedings" that we held in Williams cannot serve as the basis for a conviction under Subsection 4132(3). …

[A]t common law, judges had broad authority to impose contempt for insulting remarks that undermine the court's authority with the public. This sweeping authority continued to be enforced well into the twentieth century. In Appeal of Levine (Pa. 1953), for example, we affirmed the contempt conviction of a District Attorney who responded to a scheduling misunderstanding by saying to a trial judge: "that's the way with this court, always mixing things up; everything is set on one day." Upholding the contempt conviction, this Court described the inherent contempt powers possessed by trial courts in extremely broad terms, saying that: "[g]enerally speaking, one is guilty of contempt when his conduct tends to bring the authority and administration of the law into disrespect."

Appeal of Levine represents perhaps the zenith of judicial contempt authority in the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. The Appeal of Levine Court itself admitted that the judicial power to punish all disrespectful conduct committed in the court's presence is "arbitrary in [ ] nature and liable to abuse." Following Appeal of Levine, the judicial contempt powers were codified and limited by the General Assembly's enactment of 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132. Our decisions interpreting that statutory codification, including Williams, Behr, and Campolongo, retreated from Appeal of Levine's maximalist approach and stressed that "[i]nappropriate and even ill-mannered conduct which does not obstruct or delay the trial falls short of the misbehavior punishable under 42 Pa.C.S. § 4132(3)." These decisions also emphasized that "trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment, and they must be on guard against confusing offenses to their sensibilities with obstruction of the administration of justice."

The OAG's [Office of the Attorney General's] argument cannot be squared with these contemporary precedents. Under the OAG's proposed approach, virtually all disrespectful remarks or profane language would be contemptuous, so long as the comment can be said to risk undermining the court's authority in the minds of the public. Indeed, the OAG maintains that "spewing" vulgar language of any kind while court is in session constitutes an obstruction to the administration of justice (even if it does not delay the proceedings) because such language "weakens the public's faithful adherence to a court's judgments and rules of decorum." The OAG's view of the law is not compatible with this Court's precedent, which holds that there can be no obstruction of the administration of justice within the meaning of the Judicial Code absent a significant disruption to the judicial proceeding. …

Justice Sallie Updike Mundy concurred, joined by Justices Kevin Dougherty and Kevin Brobson:

[W]e have not been asked to reconsider our holdings in [cases such as Williams], and absent such a request, this Court must adhere to these decisions…. I write separately to emphasize my agreement with Chief Justice Emeritus Saylor's dissent in Williams:

While not every intemperate remark will cross the line which separates zealous advocacy from contemptuous conduct, in my view the vulgar and insulting language at issue was appropriately punishable summarily as direct contempt. [Williams'] remarks were not only injudicious and disrespectful-the epithets directed at the Court were an affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal and thus alone sufficient to constitute interference with the due and orderly administration of justice.

Like my esteemed former colleague, on a clean slate, I too would have found Williams' conduct punishable under Section 4132(3).

In fact, I find the use of the word "significant" throughout the majority in Williams, amongst other cases, when discussing disruptions that constitute "obstruction of the administration of justice" to be nebulous and subject to disparate interpretations. Merriam-Webster defines "significant" as, inter alia, "having meaning[,]" "large enough to be noticed or to have an effect[,]" and "having or likely to have influence or effect." Clearly, the trial court found the interruption caused by Outlaw's vulgar outburst to be "large enough to be noticed[.]"While I understand "that trial judges are supposed to be persons of fortitude who are able to thrive in a hardy environment," I find the act of calling a judge a "cocksucker" to be an "affront to the authority and dignity of the tribunal[,]"which was historically adequate to support a finding of contempt….

Keisha Nicole Hudson and Aaron Joshua Marcus (Defender Association of Philadelphia) represent Outlaw.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T.
