#7640. Firing for "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" Post Upheld

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

In Johnston v. County of Gila (D. Ariz.), Judge Dominic Lanza rejected, on procedural grounds, plaintiff's challenge to a Gila County Personnel Commission decision upholding his firing from his job as "a legal secretary with the Gila County Attorney's Office"; here's the factual and legal analysis from the Commission decision (see exhibit 10):

On September 10, 2025, at around 2:00 p.m. Arizona Time Appellant posted "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" on/via his Facebook account.

Multiple GCAO employees, including some who are not Appellant's Facebook friends and/or who do not personally use Facebook, saw and otherwise learned of Appellant's post on September 10 and in the days that followed. Multiple GCAO employees discussed the post with each other and complained about the post to GCAO's Chief Deputy Joseph Collins as well as to Gila County Attorney Bradley Beauchamp.

Beauchamp believed that the post appeared to condone murder based on the victim's political viewpoints and statements and became concerned that this post and perception would reflect on GCAO in the public's eyes and thereby undermine the public's trust in GCAO's official duty to prosecute homicides without bias and without regard to a victim's views, statements, or affiliations. Several other GCAO employees shared the perception that Appellant's post appeared to condone the murder of someone based on their statements and views and shared the concern that this would reflect poorly on GCAO and undermine public trust.

Multiple GCAO employees reported being offended or otherwise bothered by the post. Appellant's post resulted in immediate meetings and changes to office practices due to concerns of disharmony within the office and the effects it would have on GCAO operations.

Appellant's Facebook account was reportedly set to 'private' which Appellant believed would limit his post to only being seen by his existing Facebook friends and that all his friends had to do if they were upset by his post was 'unfollow' him. Notwithstanding Appellant's Facebook account setting and his belief as to the setting's effect on post-exposures, his post apparently reached multiple witnesses within a short timeframe, including some who either were no t his Facebook friends or did not use Facebook at all….

The evidence introduced in this matter demonstrated that Respondent's decision to dismiss Appellant for Appellant's social media post "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" was based on the following:

Accordingly, Respondent's reason for dismissing Appellant did not appear to have been decided at random or on a whim, to be founded in prejudice, or to lack a reasonable basis.

With regard to Appellant's assertions that his dismissal violated his rights under the 1st Amendment to the United States Constitution, the evidence presented in this hearing did not support Appellant's claim, particularly in light of the close direct nexus between the central mission of Respondent's office—the fair and impartial prosecution of all criminal matters without regard to a crime victim's personal views, opinions, or affiliations and Appellant's post about a public homicide victim, Appellant's role in the office and exposure to members of the public, Respondent's concerns regarding inferences the public would make based on Appellant's post, the fact that almost immediately multiple parties complained regarding Appellant's post and their perception that it condoned murder and reflected poorly on the office, the immediate disruption it caused in Appellant's office, and the immediate and widespread knowledge of Appellant's post.

Here's a slightly adapted version of my analysis of the general First Amendment issue that I posted right after the Kirk shooting:

In such cases the government is acting as employer, and in that capacity it has more latitude to discipline and fire employees than it does to imprison or fine them. Generally speaking, the government may discipline an employee based on the employee's speech if

There is no categorical exception even as to government employment for speech that praises violence; indeed, Rankin v. McPherson (1987) (which Johnston cited in his arguments to the Commission) held that the First Amendment was violated by the firing of a law enforcement clerical employee for saying, after President Reagan was wounded, "if they go for him again, I hope they get him":

[The statement] plainly dealt with a matter of public concern. The statement was made in the course of a conversation addressing the policies of the President's administration. It came on the heels of a news bulletin regarding what is certainly a matter of heightened public attention: an attempt on the life of the President. While a statement that amounted to a threat to kill the President would not be protected by the First Amendment, the District Court concluded, and we agree, that McPherson's statement did not amount to a [punishable] threat … or, indeed, that could properly be criminalized at all.

The inappropriate or controversial character of a statement is irrelevant to the question whether it deals with a matter of public concern. "[D]ebate on public issues should be uninhibited, robust, and wide-open, and … may well include vehement, caustic, and sometimes unpleasantly sharp attacks on government and public officials." "Just as erroneous statements must be protected to give freedom of expression the breathing space it needs to survive, so statements criticizing public policy and the implementation of it must be similarly protected."

But Rankin stressed that the speech actually didn't create much upset or disruption for the office, whether because of an internal reaction or an external one. To quote the concurrence by Justice Powell,

There is no dispute that McPherson's comment was made during a private conversation with a co-worker who happened also to be her boyfriend. She had no intention or expectation that it would be overheard or acted on by others…. The risk that a single, offhand comment directed to only one other worker will lower morale, disrupt the work force, or otherwise undermine the mission of the office borders on the fanciful.

Interference with work, personnel relationships, or the speaker's job performance can detract from the public employer's function; avoiding such interference can be a strong state interest…. [But w]hile McPherson's statement was made at the workplace, there is no evidence that it interfered with the efficient functioning of the office…. Constable Rankin testified that the possibility of interference with the functions of the Constable's office had not been a consideration in his discharge of respondent and that he did not even inquire whether the remark had disrupted the work of the office.

Nor was there any danger that McPherson had discredited the office by making her statement in public. McPherson's speech took place in an area to which there was ordinarily no public access; her remark was evidently made in a private conversation with another employee. There is no suggestion that any member of the general public was present or heard McPherson's statement.

Nor is there any evidence that employees other than [her boyfriend] who worked in the room even heard the remark. Not only was McPherson's discharge unrelated to the functioning of the office, it was not based on any assessment by the Constable that the remark demonstrated a character trait that made respondent unfit to perform her work.

Here, the Personnel Commission found that there had been disruption, based on "Testimony from multiple witnesses attesting to staff disharmony and disruptions occurring almost immediately after, and in the days following, Appellant's post—including staff complaints, colleagues being bothered and offended by Appellant's post, an office meeting, and an immediate change to office standards regarding political debate to avoid further disharmony and staff complaints." And the post, unlike McPherson's statement, was made to a considerable number of people; even if it was a Facebook page set to private, a lot more people were aware of it.

If one looks at later lower court cases, they have routinely turned on whether the speech created enough controversy, with the public or with coworkers. When the government is administering the criminal law or civil liability, such a "heckler's veto" is generally not allowed: The government generally can't shut down a speaker, for instance, because his listeners are getting offended or even threatening violence because they're offended. But in the employment context, the Pickering balance often allows government to fire employees because their speech sufficiently offends coworkers or members of the public. (The analysis may differ for public university professors, though it's not clear how much; see this post for more.)

This conclusion by lower courts applying Pickering might, I think, stem from the judgment that employees are hired to do a particular job cost-effectively for the government: If their speech so offends others (especially clients or coworkers) that keeping the employees on means more cost for the government than benefit, the government needn't continue to pay them for what has proved to be a bad bargain. Maybe that's mistaken. Maybe it's so important to protect public debate, including on highly controversial matters, that public employers should have to keep on even the most controversial employees (see this article by Prof. Randy Kozel, which so suggests in part). But that appears to be the rule.

We see this, for instance, with statements that are allegedly racist, sexist, antigay, antitrans, etc.: If they cause enough public hostility, or seem highly likely to do so, then courts will often allow employees to be fired based on them. But if they largely pass unnoticed except by management and perhaps just a few people who file complaints, then courts are much more likely to hold that the firings may violate the First Amendment (see, e.g., this post and this post, though there are many other such examples).

There are other factors that courts consider, to be sure: For instance, if the employer can show that a person's speech shows they are unsuited to the job, that makes it easier for the employer to prevail. (That seems to be part of the county attorney's justification here.) But even there the magnitude of public reaction is relevant, because one common argument is that one trait required for certain employees is the ability and willingness to instill confidence and respect in coworkers and clients, rather than to produce outrage and hostility.

And while some have tried to distinguish, say, racist speech from other speech on the grounds that it shows the speaker is likely to unfairly treat clients or coworkers who belong the groups he condemns, one can say that about many kinds of speech: Speech praising the killing of people who publicly advocate for certain views may be said to show the speaker is likely to unfairly treat members of the groups. (Such unfair treatment may often be illegal, especially by public employees, but in any event will often be unethical and contrary to the employer's mission.) As a result, the magnitude of the public reaction, which is often measurable rather than speculative, ends up playing a major role.

This creates an unfortunate incentive: Like any heckler's-veto-like rule, it rewards would-be cancellers, whether among the public or just among coworkers, if they only speak out often enough and with enough outrage. But rightly or wrongly, that is how these cases generally shape up.

Ashley E. Caballero-Daltrey, Derek Ryan Graffious, and Michele Molinario (Jones Skelton & Hochuli PLC) represent the County.

#7639. The Supreme Court as agent of the people

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In my first two entries for this column, I focused on the president’s removal power and Congress’ power to make law. This third entry focuses on our third branch of government and explains why the Supreme and inferior federal courts are properly conceptualized as faithful agents of We the People – not faithful agents of Congress. Recognizing the distinction helps explain why the Supreme Court can, and should, exercise the power of judicial review – something which, while an acknowledged part of the Supreme Court’s power for well over two centuries, has recently come under question.

Although many schools of interpretation can embrace the idea that federal courts are faithful agents of We the People, that conception of the judicial role has become a prominent feature of modern textualism. In 2017, then-Judge Amy Coney Barrett explained that “[t]he textualist commitment” to interpreting laws according to the perspective of an ordinary reader “might be explained by a … conception of faithful agency … that understands courts to be the faithful agents of the people rather than of Congress.” For support, she noted that Justice Antonin Scalia “did not think that a commitment to legislative supremacy casts courts in the role of Congress’s agents,” as he “characterized courts as agents of the people rather than agents of Congress.”

More recently, in an opinion joined by Justice Samuel Alito, Justice Neil Gorsuch defended the major questions doctrine – a canon of interpretation that requires administrative agencies to identify extra clear statutory authority before regulating in economically or politically “major” ways – by quoting then-Professor Barrett for the proposition that “clear-statement rules help courts ‘act as faithful agents of the Constitution.’”

As an initial terminological matter, there is not currently a meaningful difference between conceptualizing courts as faithful agents of the People and conceptualizing courts as faithful agents of the People’s Constitution. The Constitution’s Preamble describes the Constitution as being enacted on behalf of We the People. So under our present constitutional order, acting as a faithful agent of the People’s Constitution is a means of acting as a faithful agent of the People.

Although that conception of the judicial role has been widely held, it is nonetheless mistaken for at least three reasons.

First, the three federal branches are coequal; none is a principal or agent of the others. Second, and as I recently explained in this column, the Constitution does not empower Congress to ordinarily make law alone. Instead, Congress makes law through a multi-branch lawmaking process that includes the president. A federal jurist who claims to be a faithful agent of Congress therefore approaches statutory interpretation from a starting posture that mistakenly favors one of the two political branches that the People’s Constitution tasks with collectively making law.

The third reason why it is mistaken to conceptualize courts as faithful agents of Congress is that Congress can sometimes work with the president to make unconstitutional statutes. In those situations, federal judges who conceptualize themselves as faithful agents of Congress would seem to be required to dutifully give legal effect to Congress’ unconstitutional statutes. But that is not what courts should do if they wish to respect the Constitution’s limits. Instead, when courts are faced with constitutionally defective statutes, courts should exercise judicial review and demonstrate that the courts are themselves constitutionally prohibited from treating unconstitutional statutes as valid law. By doing so, courts demonstrate that they are faithful agents to the People’s Constitution, not Congress.

Federal courts’ power of judicial review is no doubt familiar to most lawyers, given Chief Justice Marshall’s 1803 decision in Marbury v. Madison. Less than 15 years after the ratification of the Constitution that vested “judicial Power” in the Supreme and inferior federal courts, Marshall explained that “[i]t is emphatically the province and duty of the Judicial Department to say what the law is,” and that if “the Constitution is superior to any ordinary act of the Legislature, the Constitution, and not such ordinary act, must govern the case to which they both apply.”

The familiar form of judicial review reflected in Marbury is consistent with the idea that federal courts are faithful agents of the People. Nevertheless, in an important new book, titled “Supremacy: How Rule by the Court Replaced Government by the People,” law professors Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan challenge the Supreme Court’s ability to review the constitutionality of federal legislation. The book offers an important argument against judicial review of federal statutes. And that argument would no doubt be of interest to constitutional framers working on a clean slate. But when it comes to working within the constitutional system already established on behalf of We the People, the book’s argument against judicial review is problematic.

The core of the problem with Bowie’s and Renan’s argument against judicial review of federal statutes is their suggestion that Congress has seemingly unlimited discretion to define its own constitutional limits. Bowie and Renan highlight, for example, the claim that “the only power the Constitution gives judges is ‘the judicial Power,’ which is a term that historically referred to British judges’ power to enforce, not second-guess, laws passed by Parliament,” and they contend that “[t]he most straightforward method of overcoming judicial supremacy would be for Congress to enact a statute that prohibits courts from enjoining or declining to enforce a federal law on constitutional grounds.” But as I have noted in earlier scholarship, such arguments risk conflating the “distinction between a supreme English Parliament and a legally constrained, coequal Congress.”

As the English constitutional theorist A.V. Dicey explained, “[t]he principle of Parliamentary sovereignty means” that “no person or body is recognised by the law of England as having a right to override or set aside the legislation of Parliament.” To recognize in Congress a power to statutorily prohibit the courts from declining to enforce a federal law on constitutional grounds would be to recognize in Congress a power that is not meaningfully distinguishable from the aspect of sovereignty that Dicey ascribes to Parliament. But as Justice Clarence Thomas has explained, “one of the fundamental differences between our Government and the British Government” is that although “Parliament was supreme[,] Congress is not.”

To be clear, conceptualizing federal courts as faithful agents of the People would not require accepting a form of judicial supremacy – or the idea that, even outside of the bounds of federal courts’ jurisdiction, every judicial opinion is binding law on the other two branches. To the contrary, the Constitution’s supremacy clause encodes a form of legislative supremacy into our constitutional order; so long as federal statutes are “made in Pursuance” of the Constitution, those statutes qualify as the “supreme Law of the Land” and thus can legitimately constrain executive and judicial decisionmaking.

But to conclude the Constitution establishes a form of legislative supremacy is distinct from concluding that the Constitution establishes a form of congressional supremacy. Unlike the sovereign Parliament, which Dicey described as having the “right to make or unmake any law whatever,” the non-sovereign Congress cannot enact whatever legislation it wants. Rather, Congress is constrained by the People’s Constitution. The supremacy clause illustrates this by, as mentioned, only treating some statutes – namely, those “made in Pursuance” to the Constitution – as the “supreme Law of the Land.” Courts thus act as proper agents of the People when they distinguish between statutes made in pursuance to the Constitution, which courts must treat as supreme law, and statutes that violate the Constitution, which the courts should set aside for purposes of resolving the case at hand.

One might nonetheless contend that judicial review of federal legislation is somehow inappropriate on democratic grounds. One version of that objection might contend that courts should act as agents of the democratically elected Congress – meaning that courts should enforce whatever statutes survive the democratic lawmaking process, even if a court concludes that the statutes violate the Constitution. Bowie and Renan, for example, argue for “democratic constitutionalism,” which they say means “a Constitution whose questions are decided not by the Court but by the people’s elected representatives through federal statutes.”

That type of argument has at least two key weaknesses.

First, federal judges are themselves selected and supervised through democratic means. To wit, federal judges are selected by a politically accountable president and confirmed by a politically accountable Senate. Federal judges may be impeached through the political impeachment process. Federal judges’ statutory rulings can largely be overruled through the democratic process with new legislation. And federal judges’ constitutional rulings can be overruled through the constitutional amendment process.

Second, and more fundamentally, the fact that federal judges do not stand for election is a constitutional feature, not a bug. In establishing the federal government, We the People tasked three coequal branches to act as the People’s agents; two branches (i.e., Congress and the president) stand for regular elections, while the third (i.e., the judiciary) does not. The fact that federal judges do not stand for election does not mean those judges are somehow not agents of the People. To the contrary, it simply means that the courts make up a different class of agents. And political minorities no doubt recognize the wisdom in empowering at least one class of agents to operate outside the daily whims of majoritarian politics.

Finally, it is of course the case that federal judges can get the law wrong – and as human beings, judges (like other humans) have the capacity to act immorally. (Bowie and Renan demonstrate as much by highlighting grave errors made by the Supreme Court throughout its history.) But Congress and the president can make legal and moral errors as well. So imposing a form of congressional supremacy would not fix the underlying problem that humans (even those that serve in Congress) are not angels. Part of the wisdom behind our Constitution’s structure is that it addressed human nature by limiting the consequences attributable to any one branch’s errors. And the courts play an important role within that constitutional design by exercising judicial review.

In sum, it is mistaken to conclude that accepting the validity of judicial review requires accepting rule by the courts rather than rule by the People. The courts, like Congress and the president, are agents of the People. And the courts rightfully act as agents of the People when they decline to give legal effect to statutes that violate the People’s Constitution.

Chad Squitieri is an Associate Professor of Law at The Catholic University of America, where he researches and teaches about federal administrative law and the Constitution's separation of powers.

#7638. It’s OK to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in court, judge says

A Wisconsin county judge is allowing people to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in county courtrooms to celebrate the team’s recent World Series victory.

Following the Milwaukee Brewers’ historic World Series victory Wednesday, a Wisconsin county judge issued an order allowing people to wear Milwaukee Brewers attire in county courtrooms through the end of the official victory parade.

Waukesha County Presiding Judge Michael P. Maxwell, who consulted first with the chief judge and the clerk of court, issued the order after the Brewers captured their first-ever World Series title in franchise history, defeating the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday, Fox6 News Milwaukee reports.

“While every day our courts deal with very serious issues, like child custody disputes and holding criminals accountable, the last few weeks have seen Brewer fever in many off-the-record conversations between lawyers, parties and court staff,” Maxwell wrote in a statement.

“We thought that this could be one small way we could recognize this historic achievement by the Milwaukee Brewers organization and let folks in the court system participate in celebrating with all Wisconsin,” he added.

#7637. Firing of R.I. Governor's Staffer for Pro-Gaza-Ceasefire/"End to the Occupation" Post Violated First Amendment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Sanchez v. Almond, decided Wednesday by Judge John McConnell (D.R.I.):

Mr. Sanchez began working at the office of Rhode Island Governor Daniel J. McKee in May 2021 as a "constituent services" staffer. The office is "the first point of contact with the public for the Governor's office" where employees handled calls, emails, letters, walk-ins, constituent problems, requests, and questions about the Governor's positions.

Mr. Sanchez was not a member of senior staff, and did not formulate policy, or policy developments. While the scope of his employment is shaded differently by the parties, they all agree that his duties involved, among other things, helping Rhode Islanders access public benefits and triaging their concerns by referring them to the appropriate departments. The office received roughly 500 calls and 400 emails per month.

Mr. Sanchez's direct supervisor was David Barricelli, who reported to Joseph Almond, Senior Deputy Chief of Staff, who in turn reported to Antonio Afonso, the Chief of Staff in charge of hiring and firing in the Governor's office, including Mr. Sanchez. Mr. Sanchez's performance was never called into question, and he was never disciplined before his termination….

Sanchez was also a Providence City Council member (and his superiors had not objected to his running for local office).

On October 7, 2023, Hamas attacked Israel killing roughly 1,200 people and Israel responded with fierce military actions in Gaza, whose population is overwhelmingly Palestinian. That day, the Governor's office issued a statement condemning "the abhorrent acts of terrorism by Hamas against innocent civilians in Israel" and expressed solidarity with Israel.

The same day, Mr. Sanchez posted on his personal social media a call for "respect of all human rights, especially the Palestinian people who faced atrocities for decades[,] and at the same time condemn all attacks on civilians." Ten days later, Mr. Sanchez posted that the United States was "actively aiding in a genocide" and called for "immediate deescalation and cease-fire."

On October 22, 2023, while off duty, he posted on the platform "X" (formerly known as "Twitter"):

"prov did not disappoint … yesterday, I marched with thousands of people calling for an immediate ceasefire and a [sic] end to the occupation"

The video attached depicted scores of people marching in Providence, Rhode Island. Some members of the Governor's staff thought that rally participants had chanted "from the river to the sea." That said, nothing suggests that Mr. Sanchez adopted or repeated that phrase nor is there evidence to suggest he endorsed that chant, or is in favor of violence. {No one disputes Mr. Sanchez's account "@MSanchezPVD" represents his employment as a City Councilman not his employment at the Governor's office suggesting that he was acting outside his capacity in the Governor's office.}

The post led to concern at the Governor's office, and to media questions:

On October 23rd, the Governor's Director of Legislative and Intergovernmental Affairs, Rico Vota, counseled Mr. Sanchez not to make new posts reflecting his opinion, to keep a low profile, to speak to Mr. Afonso, and to tell the communications team about any media inquiries. He did not, however, ask him to remove the posts. Mr. Vota notified Matthew Sheaff, the Governor's Senior Advisor for Communication, who likewise recommended that Mr. Sanchez keep a low profile, which Mr. Sanchez did.

That same day, two media outlets, NBC 10 WJAR and The Providence Journal's Katherine Gregg, asked the Governor's office about the rally but did not mention Mr. Sanchez or his posts. In response, the Governor issued a statement that he "unequivocally condemn[ed] the despicable acts of war and terror perpetrated by Hamas against the people of Israel."

The next day Ms. Gregg asked the Governor's communications team to confirm that Mr. Sanchez worked for the Governor and Mr. Sheaff replied that "… [a] member of our senior staff has spoken with the individual, and the situation is under review." Ms. Gregg also contacted Mr. Sanchez, but he did not respond to her and instead told Mr. Sheaff about her inquiry, apologizing for "dragging you guys into this."

On October 25th, Ms. Gregg published an article identifying Mr. Sanchez as a Constituent Services associate; NBC 10 WJAR and a WPRO radio host then asked the office about him, and NBC 10 reported on the post. A state legislator asked Mr. Vota whether the employee in the article "worked downstairs."

On October 26th, Mr. Barricelli reported to Mr. Almond that Constituent Services had received three emails and two phone messages about Mr. Sanchez's post, all after Ms. Gregg's article. Mr. Almond did not consider these "to be a lot," and they did not interfere with the office's operations. Mr. Almond testified that addressing such matters was within his own regular duties, and Mr. Barricelli testified that fielding such comments is the associates' job.

Afonso and Almond demanded that Sanchez take the post down, but he refused; he was then fired. Sanchez sued, and the court held that Sanchez's First Amendments rights were violated (and so clearly that the defendants weren't entitled to qualified immunity):

The First Amendment protects the right of a public employee to speak on matters of public concern, and that right "is not lost when an individual chooses to work for the government." Public employees' speech on matters of public concern, on their own time, is speech long understood to "occup[y] the highest rung of the hierarchy of First Amendment values." Nonpolitical public employees do not "surrender" their First Amendment rights by accepting government employment. …

The Court "must balance the interests of the employee, as a citizen, in commenting upon matters of concern and the interest of the State, as an employer, in promoting the efficiency of the public services it performs through its employees." "This balancing act is commonly referred to as the Pickering balancing" after the Supreme Court's decision in Pickering v. Board of Ed. (1968)….

On Mr. Sanchez's side, speech on public issues occupies the greatest of First Amendment protection, and the stronger the speech interest, the stronger the justification the employer must offer. {The interest by the employee and the public is heightened when the employee is also an elected official, as was Mr. Sanchez.} …

On Defendants' side, legitimate interests include avoiding unnecessary disruption and inefficiency, maintaining discipline and harmony in the workplace, and protecting close working relationships that depend on loyalty and confidence. A reasonable prediction of disruption receives significant weight, and an employer need not wait until disruption becomes manifest before acting. Courts are more willing to credit such a prediction where some disruption has occurred….

Defendants contend that the post sent "a mixed message on the Governor's public stance." Mr. Afonso testified that some constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's view with the Governor's. Even so, there was little room for genuine confusion. Mr. Sanchez's account identified him as a city councilor and never mentioned the Governor. The press, not the post, connected him to the Governor's office.

Crediting Mr. Afonso's testimony, nothing in the record shows that constituents conflated Mr. Sanchez's position with the Governor's that was traceable to the post itself. Mr. Sanchez's account cannot be reasonably understood as speaking on behalf of the Governor such that it would cause confusion in either the Governor's office or the public's perception….

[As to actual disruption, c]rediting Defendants' version of the record, in the five days between the post and the termination, the Governor's office received: one Providence Journal inquiry following up on the social media posts; three emails and two telephone messages from the public; a question posed by a state legislator in the elevator to Mr. Vota; and a few other questions from NBC 10 and a WPRO radio host. The Court also credits Ms. Darocha's recollection that the Governor was asked about Mr. Sanchez at press gaggles that week; Mr. Sheaff's testimony that the matter "encompassed [his] day"; testimony that time spent on the matter was time not spent elsewhere; and the decision not to put an optional event on the Governor's calendar.

Mr. Almond testified the inquiries were not "a lot" and "did not interfere with the operation of the office" and Mr. Barricelli testified that handling such communications was essentially his associates' job. By its own account, that office spends roughly "85 percent" of its time responding to current events and media inquiries. Better said by Mr. Sheaff, "[i]t's very common that the Governor gives a statement or his thoughts on news of the day …[;] [i]t's just part of the job of being a governor." This is the ordinary business of a governor's office and nothing in the record suggests that the post affected the Governor's own work, his relationship with his staff, or the office's ability to serve constituents in an unusual way. Balancing these facts, and considering the Defendants' burden on this issue, the Court settles this score firmly against Defendants.

{Defendants also point to Mr. Sanchez's later acknowledgment that he had "put[ ] the [G]overnor in a tough situation" and that, "given my day job, these kinds of things can get messy quickly." Though affecting the Court's calculus, an employee's recognition that his speech is affecting his employer does not supply Defendants with the artillery they think it does.} …

Brian W. Haynes (Casner & Edwards, LLP) and Edward H. Trent, Gene C. Schaerr, and Miranda Cherkas Sherrill (Schaerr Jaffe LLP), and James A. Ruggieri (Higgins Cavanagh & Cooney, LLP) represent plaintiff. Note that I'm a part-part-part-time academic affiliated with Schaerr Jaffe LLP, but I didn't work on the case, and was indeed unaware of it until it came up in a Westlaw query of mine; no-one asked me to blog about it.

NEXT: Firing for "Rot in Hell Charlie Kirk" Post Upheld

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. #7636. My New Dispatch Article on the Legal Case Against Trump's Section 338 Tariffs Targeting Canadian Imports

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

It explains why the Section 338 tariffs are illegal, and part of a broader pattern of tariff power grabs.

Today, The Dispatch published my new article on the case challenging Trump's Section 338 tariffs against Canada. Here is an excerpt:

Courts have already ruled against two avenues President Donald Trump used to impose his tariff regime. That hasn't stopped his efforts to attempt to deploy obscure or outdated trade law provisions to justify new import levies.

His latest tool is the Smoot-Hawley Tariff Act of 1930, the notorious legislation that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression.

Section 338 of that law is the basis of Trump's massive 50 percent tariffs on a variety of Canadian imports, including motor vehicles, furniture, dairy products, and more. On October 20, Gellert Global Group Corp., a major food importer and producer based in New Jersey, filed the first lawsuit challenging those tariffs before the U.S. Court of International Trade, the federal court with jurisdiction over tariff cases.

Gellert, which imports Canadian cheese subject to the tariffs, is represented by the Liberty Justice Center, a public interest law firm I worked with on the case challenging the massive tariffs Trump imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). It resulted in the tariffs' invalidation in February by the Supreme Court, which not only ruled that IEEPA doesn't authorize tariffs but also emphasized that tariffs are a congressional power, and that the president does not have the power to "impose tariffs on imports from any country, of any product, at any rate, for any amount of time." The Section 338 tariffs are a similar power grab.

They are illegal for multiple reasons, part of an ongoing effort by this administration to usurp Congress' constitutional authority over tariffs. In addition, they harm the U.S. economy and poison relations with a key ally. Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act has never been used by a president to enact tariffs before; Philip Zelikow, a conservative trade policy expert and former Bush administration official, has shown that Section 338 was superseded by legislation enacted in 1962 and 1974.

Even if Section 338 is still operative, Trump's tariffs on Canadian goods violate its requirements. As the complaint explains, the Canadian trade measures cited by Trump as justification for the new tariffs do not discriminate against U.S. goods; Section 338 can only be used against discriminatory policies. Some of the Canadian measures retaliate against previous tariffs imposed by Trump. Most do not actually treat U.S. goods less favorably than imports from many other countries. In addition, the Section 338 tariffs go well beyond "offsetting" Canadian measures, violating another requirement of the law….

The administration's interpretation of Section 338 also runs afoul of the major questions doctrine, which requires Congress to "speak clearly" when authorizing the executive to make decisions of "vast economic and political significance." Under Trump's approach, Section 338 can be used to impose 50 percent tariffs whenever a trading partner imposes any restrictions on U.S. goods, or simply chooses not to buy them. And the resulting tariffs need not be calibrated to those they are supposed to "offset." This is a blank check to impose massive tariffs against almost any imports at any time—exactly the kind of power the Supreme Court, in its ruling on the IEEPA case, determined the executive cannot have…

If Section 338 is still valid and does grant the kind of nearly unlimited authority Trump claims, that would violate the constitutional "nondelegation" doctrine, which restricts delegation of legislative power to the executive…

The Section 338 tariffs are part of an ongoing series of import taxes Trump has instituted in the wake of the IEEPA decision, seeking to again usurp the unlimited tariff authority the Supreme Court denied him. He previously tried to use Section 122 and Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to essentially replicate the IEEPA tariffs. In both cases, he sought to transform a narrowly limited tariff authority into a blank check to impose massive tariffs at will…

In addition to illegally usurping Congress' authority under the Constitution, these tariff actions raise prices for consumers, greatly reduce economic growth, would impose some $700 billion in new taxes on Americans over a 10-year period, and have failed to increase manufacturing employment, despite Trump's claims that they would achieve that goal.

The tariffs against Canada—combined with Trump's repeated threats to make Canada the "51st state"—have also poisoned U.S. relations with a key ally. The percentage of Canadians with a favorable view of the U.S. has fallen from 54 percent in 2024 to only 33 percent this year—a worse rating than even China's authoritarian regime…. Alienating a key ally and trading partner doesn't make America "great again." It makes us weaker, poorer, and more isolated.

NEXT: Firing of R.I. Governor's Staffer for Pro-Gaza-Ceasefire/"End to the Occupation" Post Violated First Amendment

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7635. Alysandra Dutton on Writing Historical Noir and Investigating Ancient Roman Crimes

In 753 BCE something happened to the Sabine Women. Romulus, fresh off of founding Rome, could not make marriages for himself and his men, who were considered little more than a gang of particularly nasty bandits. He opted for stealing his brides from neighboring Sabinum during a festival, cementing Rome’s legacy in their wombs.

And when I was fourteen, sitting in the audience of a local high school production of Seven Brides for Seven Brothers, a romantic comedy retelling of the Abduction of the Sabine Women, listening to the cast sing jovially about how those women kissed and cried all over that Roman countryside, a feeling welled in me that I would later associate with the need to clear my desk and get writing: indignation. Or maybe, spite.

Ever since, the Sabine Women have haunted me, much the way true crime stories haunt my generation of American women; their pain felt cautionary, their story morbidly compelling, as they showed up again and again in my drafting notebooks. Sure, the crime was solved. We know who took the Sabine Women, and we know why.

But in time I realized I wasn’t able to let them go because the injustice was ongoing; historians writing seven hundred years after the founding of Rome claimed the women were happy to be kidnapped and in love with their captors, marking perhaps one of the earliest incel arguments that women secretly desire to be overpowered, that rape is not that violating after all. And until the record said otherwise, I couldn’t not write.

The Stolen Women came together for me, probably not surprisingly, as I discovered an interest in detective literature. I already felt like an investigator, cynical and working against the grain for my victims; it made sense to take years of notes and half-started stories and filter them through classic noir conventions.

My favorite noirs are about fighting—often futilely—against the system. That seemed to me a fitting framework by which to see a young Sabine woman, pitted against Rome. As contemporary readers, we know what’s coming—we know Rome wins.

But in noir, the the tragic end—often as foregone a conclusion as Rome—is an aside. The story is about what drives a person to leave their well-earned cynicism at the door and fight anyway. I wanted to give the Sabine that story.

Soon, Safinia appeared on the page. My classic, hard-boiled detective; at first, all she wants is to be left alone to put food on the table and protect her sisters. But then, the femme fatale, a woman in danger, in tears, draws her into the twisting, atmospherically moody world of a mystery.

The disappearance of an ex-lover, answers that lead to more questions, and a sidekick classical historians will immediately recognize as keeping vital secrets—it was all there. I may as well have given her a pipe to smoke on as slats of light shine through her dusty office (she does, at one point, smoke hemp in the fashion of the ancient world—one of my favorite scenes, and a send-up I couldn’t resist). But what would happen when her investigation led to Rome?

As Safinia descended further into her obsessive pursuit of mysteriously disappeared women, I also began to feel obsessive, my research notes looking more like a murder board every day. By this point, I was living in Rome, as a member of the awards-holder cohort at the British School at Rome. Before this moment, I had written a lot about trauma; my history necessitated it. Writing about violence, about violation, was my way of making sense of my own past.

In Safinia, I found cathartic satisfaction in her quest for answers and subsequent fight for survival. But what began as an intimate story about gendered violence began to take a larger shape during my days at the BSR. Suddenly, I realized I was writing a book not only about violence—but about violence in Rome. And the qualifier mattered.

Any contemporary archeologist will tell you that the study of Rome is also the study of fascism. I’ve written before about how it is impossible to extract fascism from its birthplace, and the reason for this is practical and material: fascism mucked up a lot of crime scenes in its day. Or, I should say, excavations.

Mussolini’s thirst to associate himself with the image of the Roman Empire meant large swaths of history were greedily uncovered, poorly documented, and then left to rot. Far from the conservation practices of archeological excavations today, even the Colosseum Mussolini was determined to see from his balcony, tearing down a historic medieval neighborhood to achieve this, was neglected by the 1970s. It was a known site for drug-users and criminals (and underground cinemas and raves, but that’s a story for another day), crumbling dangerously around its edges.

I note the irony in an essay at the back of The Stolen Women: Mussolini wanted to see the colosseum Emperor Domitian built so that he could feel like a God, too. But Emperor Domitian, my research found, proudly displayed an impossible to verify family tree that tied him to the original kidnapped Sabine Women, eight hundred years before his reign. This was the brag of important men in Rome, their Sabine ancestors promoted from victims to propaganda that proves a family’s interests in the Eternal City.

From here, my tact had to change; a moody, forget-it-Jake-it’s-Chinatown ending had no place in this world. I’d been so consumed by the crime of kidnapping, and the futility of Safinia’s hopes for solving it, that I was missing the crime of history, of rhetoric; not of how you tell the story of an Empire, but of how you justify it.

Ancient historians edged around the Sabine Women, acknowledging the crime but inventing, in the same breath, an ending that renders their kidnapping palatable. Titus Livius—Livy—claims in his histories that the women kept their freedom of choice and chose to stay with their Roman captors; Dionysius of Halicarnassus praises Romulus’ bold foreign policy in his decision to kidnap them in the first place. And Mussolini, in Italy’s fascist era, rips the protective shell off of history and lays it bare and eroded, absent any context that doesn’t spell empire.

In these days of writing and drafting, Safinia’s task looked enormous, insurmountable. But if nothing else, she taught me how to move doggedly, determinedly through history; to trust the way the Earth churns up new answers and new mysteries. They will never have all of you, a historian tells her at a low moment, and he’s right.

Alysandra Dutton attended the University of Arkansas for her MFA, where she was awarded a dizzying number of fellowships and prose awards. Her short fiction appeared in Catapult, Electric Literature, and The Sun, and she wrote The Stolen Women with support from The Elizabeth George Foundation. Currently, she lives in Minnesota and is a teaching artist with The Loft Literary Center, where she leads regular historical fiction workshops and neurodivergent writing groups, Interlochen Arts Camp, and the ALS Association.

#7634. Law firms face increasing AI-fueled cyberattacks, new report says

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise. (Image from Shutterstock)

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise.

These attacks have doubled since 2023, according to cybersecurity company CrowdStrike’s 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which was released Wednesday.

The report shows that between August 2025 and August 2026, cyber adversaries named 455 legal entities as hacking targets, an increase of 39% from the prior year.

While CrowdStrike did not name specific firms or other legal groups as the victims of attacks, Reuters has reported that Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr and Seyfarth Shaw are among those that have experienced cyber breaches in recent months.

“What we’re seeing across the broader threat landscape, more and more threat actors are using agentic technology ⁠to democratize hacking,” said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president for counter adversary operations. “It’s going to get a lot worse before it gets better.”

#7633. What should you watch this weekend? (Oct 30 – Nov 1, 2026)

A mystery lover’s guide to what’s new to streaming this weekend.

Dexter: Resurrection, season 2 (Paramount)

If you haven’t been keeping up on the expanded Dexter universe, this is the spinoff / continuation series that’s actually really good! (For a full guide to the spinoff universe, Olivia Rutigliano has you covered here.)  Resurrection has a knack for using guest stars extremely effectively (like the original series did, season to season) and this time around, it’s Brian Cox bringing a jolt of electricity to the story of Dexter’s days in New York City.

Liev Schreiber and Stephen Graham star in this new serial killer / FBI agent cat-and-mouse thriller. It’s a very Hannibal Lecter setup, but with a few dark twists of its own along the way. For fans of the genre, this is well worth the time: a high-quality production with all the trappings we expect from a story about a serial killer mastermind.

It’s Halloween weekend, so I’m assuming most people looking to stream a movie at home will be looking toward the horror and supernatural ends of the genre. But I’m going to get way more specific than that and recommend a duo of witchy Massachusetts set movies, starting with The Crucible (Prime), the 1996 film from director Nicholas Hytner, working off a script by Arthur Miller himself. starring Daniel Day-Lewis as John Procter and Wynona Ryder as Abigail Williams. Filming was done in Massachusetts and Nova Scotia, and the whole production has that wind-swept woebegone Bay Colony atmosphere down perfectly. From there, it’s a short trip over the marshlands to The Witches of Eastwick (HBO), starring Jack Nicholson, Cher, Susan Sarandon, Michelle Pfeiffer. It’s of course based on the John Updike novel, back in a simpler time when America was still fascinated by adultery and middle aged sexual awakenings. Also, there’s some magic involved, and rituals, so it works for Halloween viewing.

#7632. Fifth Circuit Will Decide En Banc Whether § 230 Preempts Texas Mandates on Social Media Platforms

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The Fifth Circuit ordered en banc rehearing Wednesday; here's an excerpt from the long panel opinion (Computer & Comm. Industry Ass'n v. Paxton), decided in July by Fifth Circuit Judges Dana Douglas and Patrick Higginbotham (I posted about the case then):

[1.] [Texas] H.B. 18 … imposes requirements on DSPs [Digital Service Providers]…. With the exception of its age-verification requirement, H.B. 18 applies only to DSPs whose digital service "connects users in a manner that allows users to socially interact with other users on the digital service," "allows a user to create a public or semi-public profile for purposes of signing into and using the digital service," and "allows a user to create or post content that can be viewed by other users of the digital service," including via a message board, chat room, or other "landing page, video channel, or main feed that presents to a user content created and posted by other users."

{H.B. 18 exempts from its coverage state and local government websites, financial institutions, medical websites, small businesses, higher education websites, employee management software, school education software, and e-mail and direct messaging services that provide only those services. H.B. 18 also exempts digital services that "primarily function[ ] to provide a user with access to news, sports, commerce, or content primarily generated or selected by the [DSP]" and provide only incidental social functions.}

H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement mandates covered DSPs to develop and implement a strategy to prevent known minors' exposure to "harmful material" and other content "that promotes, glorifies, or facilitates" "suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders"; "substance abuse"; "stalking, bullying, or harassment"; and "grooming, trafficking, child pornography, or other sexual exploitation or abuse." "Harmful material" is defined with reference to its definition in the Texas Penal Code [to refer to obscene-as-to-minors sexually themed material]….

[2.] Consistent with other courts of appeal, we have interpreted Section 230 to provide DSPs with "broad immunity" from "all claims stemming from their publication of information created by third parties." … Building on Doe v. MySpace, Inc. (5th Cir. 2018), where we had previously held that Section 230 "shielded MySpace from negligence liability for publishing communications between a minor and an adult who later sexually assaulted her," in Free Speech Coalition, Inc. v. Paxton (5th Cir. 2024), we held that an age-verification requirement for pornographic websites was different, and not preempted, because it did not pertain to "immuniz[ing] web service providers from harm caused by unremoved speech on their website," which is "the point of Section 230."

We distinguished between liability "reliant on the harm done by third-party content," which is preempted by Section 230, and "liability purely based on whether plaintiffs comply with the statute," which is not. "[T]he nature of Section 230's protections," we observed, is "to protect a provider from speaker-liability stemming from the speech it hosts." …

[T]he monitoring and filtering requirement requires covered DSPs to "implement a strategy" to prevent known minors' exposure to "harmful material"—that is, material obscene to minors as it is defined by Texas law—and other content "that promotes, glorifies, or facilitates" "suicide, self-harm, or eating disorders"; "substance abuse"; "stalking, bullying, or harassment"; and "grooming, trafficking, child pornography, or other sexual exploitation or abuse." It provides for enforcement for "violation[s]" by the Consumer Protection Division of the Attorney General's Office or by actions for a declaratory judgment or an injunction brought by the parent of a "known minor affected by" a violation.

Actions to enforce the monitoring and filtering requirement are claims stemming from DSPs' actions as publishers, that is, from their monitoring, screening, and deletion of content, and are thus squarely preempted by Section 230. Although H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement is framed as a matter of affirmative obligations rather than direct penalties for published content, this is not conclusive under our precedent.

"[I]f the claim seeks to hold the defendant liable for 'deciding whether to publish, withdraw, postpone, or alter content[,]' the claim treats the defendant as a publisher or speaker and is barred by section 230." The requirement would hold DSPs liable for their failure to adhere to state-set publication standards, not only "treat[ing] [them] as … publisher[s] or speaker[s]," but treating them as publishers subject to sweeping state controls. Enforcement is triggered by failures to adequately filter according to a complex array of prescribed practices, as ascertained by the Texas Attorney General's Office and by the parents of minors "affected"—in other words, harmed—by these failures. The monitoring and filtering requirement thus imposes a "duty" that "'would necessarily require an internet company to monitor[, alter, or remove] third-party content.'"

As we observed in Free Speech Coalition, "publishers do not filter audiences; they filter content." Unlike the age-verification requirement we addressed in that case, H.B. 18's monitoring and filtering requirement is all about filtering content, and is thus preempted….

[3.] The Attorney General contends that the Supreme Court's recent recognition of the DSPs' own free speech interest in curating the content they display in Moody v. NetChoice, LLC (2024) means that Section 230's broadly-interpreted rule against "treat[ing]" the DSPs "as the publisher or speaker of any information provided by another information content provider" does not apply to claims that simply seek to hold social media platforms liable for their own speech, such as the methods they use to curate content.

We hesitate to read Moody to render Section 230 so easily avoidable, as if speech could not be both protected by the First Amendment and subject to preemption on the grounds that the speaker may not be treated as a publisher. Such a narrow view of Section 230 preemption would conflict with the statute's purpose "to maintain the robust nature of Internet communication and, accordingly, to keep government interference in the medium to a minimum." It would also conflict with the text of § 230(c)(1), which, in spite of its often-discussed connection with specific instigating judicial decisions, "cannot be ignored": "Congress grabbed a bazooka to swat [a] fly."

Given that "First Amendment values … drive the CDA," it should be no surprise if the two protections overlap. As we recognized in MySpace, drawing on the Fourth Circuit's influential Zeran decision, "[digital] service providers … subject to liability only for the publication of information, and not for its removal … would have a natural incentive simply to remove messages upon notification [of a possible harm,] whether the contents were [actually harmful] or not." This would have an obvious "chilling effect on the freedom of Internet speech," implicating basic First Amendment freedoms as well as Section 230's more specific protections for internet speech.

Viewing our Section 230 precedent together with Moody, the First Amendment protects the DSPs' editorial discretion from unconstitutional government regulation, and Section 230 protects those same decisions from civil liability based on third-party content. The argument that we must choose between them presents a false choice….

Because we hold that the monitoring and filtering requirement is preempted by Section 230 of the CDA, we do not reach the constitutional issues presented here.

Judge James Ho dissented as to that analysis:

[1.] Section 230 is triggered only when a provider is treated as the "publisher" or "speaker" of content provided by "another" information content provider. So it does not apply when a provider is held liable for its own content—including its curation of third-party content….

[C]uration of third-party content is fundamentally different from publication of third-party content. A digital service provider may choose to publish content created by third parties. But the providers engage in their own speech when they curate that content. The Supreme Court has so held. See Moody v. NetChoice (2024)….

[To quote Doe ex rel. Roe v. Snap, Inc. (2024) (Thomas, J., dissenting from denial of certiorari),] when "platforms organize users' content into newsfeeds or other compilations," they claim that they are "engage[d] in constitutionally protected speech." Yet "[w]hen it comes time for platforms to be held accountable for their websites, however, they argue the opposite." "In the platforms' world, they are fully responsible for their websites when it results in constitutional protections, but the moment that responsibility could lead to liability, they can disclaim any obligations and enjoy greater protections from suit than nearly any other industry." …

Consistent with Justice Thomas's observations, … we concluded that "section 230 does not provide a general immunity against all claims derived from third-party content." To the contrary, "providers of interactive computer services may be held liable for speech or conduct that is properly attributable to them, even if third-party speech exists somewhere upstream." …

[2.] The Securing Children Online through Parental Empowerment Act (SCOPE Act) … protects children from the dangers of social media. It does so by requiring digital service providers to implement [reasonable steps] to prevent children from being exposed to "harmful material"—namely, content that promotes suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, substance abuse, stalking, bullying, harassment, grooming, trafficking, child pornography, and other sexual exploitation or abuse…. And if a platform fails to take such steps, parents may seek declaratory or injunctive relief against the provider….

[T]he Act simply imposes a duty on social media companies to meet certain standards for curation—that is, for their own speech. It imposes no penalty based on the publication of third-party speech.

So if third-party content leads to harm to children, the SCOPE Act does not hold social media companies liable, so long as they have met its standards for curation…. [T]he SCOPE Act considers the curation decisions made by social media companies—not the harm caused by the third-party content itself….

[3.] As for the First Amendment challenge to the SCOPE Act not reached by the panel majority: "States have a profound interest in protecting the innocence of children," and "[n]othing in the First Amendment prevents states from taking steps to shield children" from harmful content. I would have simply certified the questions regarding the proper interpretation of the SCOPE Act to allow the Supreme Court of Texas to clarify the meaning of state law….

Thanks to the Media Law Resource Center (MLRC) MediaLawDaily for the pointer.

#7631. Nika Grace on finding remains in deserts and writing a serial killer novel

It is a truth universally acknowledged that if you hike across the desert, intently looking at the ground, you will eventually find a dead body.

Let me back up a step to explain why an otherwise mentally healthy thirty-something woman would be hiking across the remote desert for so many thousands of trailless miles. It was because of #VanLife, actually, though this occurred before I understood how to use a hashtag (do I yet understand how to use a hashtag? Don’t answer that.) And, of course, I was never quite affluent enough to purchase a van.

The year was 2010. My husband and I had gotten married, acquired a mortgage, a master’s degree, and a matched set of Real Actual Careers. Reader, I lasted six months.

After that, I decided that business casual blouses and working for the weekends wasn’t for me, and we went on the run. We moved into a Toyota Tacoma truck nearly as old as we were, and worked seasonally to pay for enough ramen to keep rock climbing until we were too old and too square to get up the cliffs anymore.

After a short stint on the ice in Antarctica—a tale for another time—we landed in the Mojave Desert, tracking desert tortoises across the desiccated landscape. When I first got the job, I thought the stories of other tortoise bios finding dead bodies were some kind of urban myth. A form of hazing the new girl that was probably blown out of proportion thanks to mis-identified coyote bones and having too much time to think. Until we found a finger.

A woman’s finger; painted fingernail. No blood. No body.

It was found by a cheerful ex-raft-guide from Flagstaff, one crew over from where I was walking survey lines in the desert just outside of Las Vegas.

The chills that went up my spine followed me all the way home to where I was camping in the—unlockable—camper shell of my Toyota Tacoma, the dusty wind howling around its thin metal shell all night.

Listen, I wanted to make money for road tripping as much as the next girl, but exactly where did that finger come from? And where was the rest of that woman’s body? And why—where—but—didn’t they have police down here?

The questions were more plentiful than the answers. As the years in the Mojave cropped up and the body count rose along them, we never did hear the stories behind any of the human remains we turned in. Not the multiple skulls, not the drifter we found outside of Nipton with his uncashed welfare check in his pocket, not the “suicide” that I still swear was a very thinly-veiled mob hit (details redacted for the safety of the bios who found it). There were so many bodies found by tortoise biologists that eventually Outside Magazine did a feature on the phenomenon, though they didn’t cover half the tales I could have told.

One that stuck with me was three graves, complete with crosses and mounded dirt, armored with river-smoothed stones. We found them near an abandoned compound that used to house a meth lab, and a cult. Since five girls had gone missing in this area the local police in this case actually sent a crew out to exhume the sites. They dug them all the way to bedrock and found nothing, which always tickled my imagination.

I understand setting up crosses for a memorial, perhaps, but why go to the trouble to mound the dirt? Why lug so many stones in such a sweaty climate if you weren’t faking the graves for someone else’s benefit? I couldn’t stop thinking about it, and I never got answers, so I ended up writing a flash fiction story to give myself the resolution that reality was reluctant to allow me.

The sluggishness of the authorities when it came to following our GPS coordinates to the corpses gave me a healthy respect for how much easier it was to get away with murder than I had previously thought, at least in the Mojave. The desert always felt like a place real adults had forgotten. What with its abandoned and half-burnt trailers jutting up alongside the sand-drifted highways and the graffiti laced bones of defunct water parks.

That’s why when I decided to write a book about a female serial killer, I set her story in the Phoenix desert. Because I wanted the metaphorical resonance of her rising from the ashes of her past, sure. But mostly because I wanted somewhere to hide the bodies.

I started writing this book in a desert, of course. When I was working a job outside of Barstow fence monitoring. Just me walking miles of fence to look for distressed tortoises not used to having their habitat chopped up by the dividing lines of men. On a day when I’d just written one of the first chapters from my serial killer’s POV, I found two murder weapons.

Do I know they were murder weapons? Of course not. When I called the police, they said it was county jurisdiction and hung up on me. The two young county sheriffs who eventually responded had to borrow a set of my latex gloves for tortoise handling just to take the guns into evidence, and never followed up with me about the results of the investigation, if they even did one.

But guns like these cost hundreds to thousands of dollars. Why toss them out the window unless you had to?

I never learned who the guns belonged to, or how they got there. What I did learn was that if you want to get away with murder, you better do it in the desert.

Nika Grace loves writing fight scenes and kissing scenes and is always on the lookout for a story idea wild enough to include both. By day, she works as a writing coach with Sanctuary Editorial, and on the weekends, she and her husband love to disappear into the labyrinth of the canyon country in the American Southwest. Her home base is in Moab, Utah, but her muse lives in New Orleans. She is the author of Serial Killer Wanted.
