#7629. Prof. Francesca Gino's Contract and Discrimination Claims Against Harvard Business School Dismissed

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

"In 2021, allegations were brought against [Gino] claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty," and eventually to her tenure being revoked and her being fired.

Some short excerpts from the long decision by Judge Myong Joun (D. Mass.) today in Gino v. President & Fellows of Harvard College:

Plaintiff Francesca Gino is a former tenured professor at Harvard Business School ("HBS") and brings this action against Defendants President and Fellows of Harvard College ("Harvard") and Defendant Srikant Datar ("Dean Datar"). In 2021, allegations were brought against Plaintiff claiming that she committed research misconduct, which triggered an approximately 18-month long inquiry and investigation by HBS administrators and faculty. In March 2023, the investigation committee found, by a preponderance of the evidence, that Plaintiff committed research misconduct…. In May 2025, Harvard revoked Plaintiff's tenure and terminated her appointment with HBS.

Plaintiff claims that Harvard breached its obligations under various policies and procedures governing the investigation of the research misconduct allegations and the tenure revocation proceedings. Specifically, Plaintiff argues that a jury could find that Harvard deviated from its policies and procedures such that Harvard could be found in breach of those agreements, and that Harvard did not carry its burden of proving research misconduct or grave misconduct. Plaintiff also alleges that the proceedings and related findings, including the adverse employment actions taken against her, were pretext for gender discrimination….

In approximately June of 2021, three professors—Leif Nelson, Joseph Simmons, and Uri Simonsohn, who publish under the name "Data Colada"—presented their allegations against Gino to HBS Professor Max Bazerman during a 90-minute Zoom call…. [Eventually, a Harvard] Investigation Committee issued its 41-page Final Report with nearly 1,200 pages of supporting documents, finding by a preponderance of the evidence that Plaintiff committed research misconduct intentionally, knowingly, or recklessly with regard to all five allegations.

The Investigation Committee's Final Report considered and rejected Plaintiff's contentions that unnamed "bad actors," research assistants, or other co-authors might have instead been responsible for the data anomalies. The Investigation Committee concluded that Plaintiff's "repeated and strenuous argument for a scenario of data falsification by bad actors across four different studies," involving "different co-authors, different journals, different lab personnel, and different home institutions" and spanning eight years, was "highly implausible." The Investigation Committee recommended corrections of the scientific record, putting Plaintiff on unpaid leave, and initiation of steps leading to termination of employment….

The court granted summary judgment on all these issues, in Harvard's favor. Here's an excerpt of the discussion of her breach of contract claims:

Massachusetts courts enforce contractual promises made by private universities, while according appropriate respect to their academic and disciplinary judgments. The Third Statute [a Harvard academic policy] permits removal of an officer holding a teaching appointment "only for grave misconduct or neglect of duty." I hold that this is a substantive, enforceable limitation on removal, not a merely aspirational statement.

The limitation does not, however, confer a right to have a federal jury independently determine scientific authorship, data provenance, or the correct weight of forensic evidence after an academic tribunal has considered those matters. Judicial review asks whether Harvard reached its determination honestly and reasonably, upon a rational evidentiary foundation, and in compliance with its enforceable contractual procedures. This is meaningful review: the University's decision does not prevail merely because a committee announced it.

This standard respects both the contractual restriction on removal and the institutional responsibility to adjudicate research-integrity matters. A court may not uphold a decision procured through dishonesty, resting on no reasonable evidence, or reached through a material violation of promised procedures. It also may not choose among plausible competing forensic interpretations merely because a reasonable factfinder could have drawn different scientific inferences. Gino bears the burden of proving breach in this action. The Third Statute Procedures separately placed on Harvard's complainant a clear-and-convincing burden of establishing grave misconduct or neglect of duty; the record must be examined for whether Harvard applied that burden, not treated as though the civil burden had transferred to Harvard….

Harvard's decision had a substantial contemporaneous evidentiary basis. The record describes forensic examination of anomalous data in four research papers; analysis of the history and characteristics of relevant datasets; consideration of Gino's explanations; a faculty investigation finding misconduct by a preponderance of the evidence, and; a subsequent hearing committee finding, by clear and convincing evidence, of misconduct grave enough to warrant revocation. These are not independent judicial findings that Gino altered any data. They establish that Harvard investigated defined allegations and articulated an evidentiary explanation for its decision. The committees' findings alone would not rescue a decision shown to be knowingly false or irrational; the investigative materials, considered together with the contrary submissions, provide the relevant basis for review.

Gino denies intentionally falsifying research data, relies on favorable accounts from coauthors and colleagues, and challenges aspects of the forensic inferences and evidence of access or authorship. I credit these disputes and draw permissible inferences in her favor.

But the question under the contract is not whether a jury could reject some of Harvard's inferential steps or prefer an alternative forensic account. Gino must identify evidence from which a reasonable jury could conclude that Harvard did not honestly believe its determination or lacked a rational basis to make it.

The identified differences over inference, attribution, and scientific weight do not establish that the peer decisionmakers knowingly adopted a false conclusion or acted without a reasonable evidentiary foundation. Accordingly, no triable breach arises merely from the competing interpretations of the underlying research record….

And from the court's rejection of Gino's sex discrimination theory:

Plaintiff points to the following pieces of evidence that she argues supports evidence of discriminatory animus: (1) Harvard deviated from and breached its policies and procedures; (2) Harvard and Dean Datar have historically subjected women to less favorable treatment; (3) Harvard has treated allegations of research misconduct against male professors differently than the allegations against Plaintiff, and; (4) certain statements made by Harvard employees were false and otherwise constitute discriminatory remarks….

Plaintiff relies on similar arguments she raised in support of her breach of contract claims that Harvard deviated from its policies with respect to investigating research misconduct. "Evidence that the employer deviated from its standard procedure or policies in taking an adverse employment action against a plaintiff may be relevant to the pretext inquiry." As discussed, Plaintiff's evidence does not support a finding that Harvard breached its policies. Furthermore, Plaintiff provides no evidence that any purported deviations from Harvard's policies are connected to gender bias….

Plaintiff argues that there is evidence that Defendants have historically treated women less favorably than men. This evidence includes Plaintiff's own testimony and testimony from Plaintiff's colleague at HBS. Plaintiff provided testimony in a sworn declaration that she "personally observed that it was more difficult for women to obtain tenure at HBS than men. Indeed, about three times as many male professors get promoted as compared to female ones. In the Accounting & Management Unit, it's worse: closer to four times as many." She also stated that in 2022, she participated in an Appointment Committee meeting in which "gendered language was used to discuss the work of one female professor in the Accounting & Management Unit." When Plaintiff raised the issue to senior colleagues, one of them told Plaintiff that it "has been that way for a while." Plaintiff's declaration also states that "there had not been a single tenured woman in the Accounting & Management Unit for more than 20 years." Plaintiff's colleague, Professor Frances Frei, also testified to evidence that Dean Datar attempted to prevent another female professor from obtaining tenure.

Plaintiff's evidence is plainly insufficient. This evidence is made up of Plaintiff's own conclusory allegations that it is more difficult for women to obtain tenure, a statement made by an unknown female colleague supporting Plaintiff's belief that obtaining tenure is more difficult for women, vague allegations that unspecified "gendered language" made by unknown speakers was used when discussing an unspecified female professor, and an unsubstantiated statement from a colleague that Dean Datar attempted to "counsel out" another unspecified senior lateral hire. There are no other non-speculative facts—documents, communications, data, or otherwise—that support these conclusions or that tend to show a pattern of gender bias. Indeed, when pressed for further information about Dean Datar's alleged "pattern" of disfavoring women, Professor Frei could not provide a response.

Further, the record does not demonstrate any other evidence of a pattern or practice of discriminatory conduct or unfavorable treatment that can be applied to reasonably infer gender bias against Plaintiff….

Plaintiff points to evidence that Harvard has treated allegations of misconduct against male professors differently than allegations against Plaintiff. Plaintiff points to two examples where male professors were treated differently…. "To successfully allege disparate treatment, a plaintiff must show that others similarly situated to her in all relevant respects were treated differently by the employer." … Here …, there are important differences. For instance, in both the case of Mr. Serafeim and Mr. Soltes [the two examples pointed to by Plaintiff -EV], Harvard found that the complained-of conduct did not fall within the definition of research misconduct….

Additionally, the allegations against Mr. Serafeim had to do with a misleading footnote that was later admitted and explained to be an error, and the allegations against Mr. Soltes had to do with his conduct in connection with subjects that he interviewed. In contrast, the allegations against Plaintiff involved thirteen allegations of data falsification and fabrication in nine papers co-authored by Plaintiff, and after a preliminary assessment, five of those allegations were found to be sufficiently credible to fall within the definition of research misconduct. In short, it is Plaintiff's "burden to connect the dots" between the facts and circumstances surrounding the allegations against her and those of her male colleagues, such that a jury may find that they are similarly situated. Plaintiff has not met that burden here….

Plaintiff points to allegedly false statements made by Dean Datar and other Harvard leaders, as well as a gendered remark by a member of the Investigation Committee, as evidence of unlawful animus. Plaintiff alleges that the following false claims were made: (1) Dean Datar falsely claimed under oath that he did not make any "deal" with Data Colada and Data Colada's allegations against Gino were not brought to his attention until after the Interim Policy was created; (2) Dean Datar falsely denied telling Dean Pisano that Data Colada was pressuring HBS to move the investigation along and accusing it of "whitewashing"; (3) Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino; (4) Professor Amabile falsely claimed under oath that, during the time of the investigation, she was not aware that the allegations brought against Gino were raised by Data Colada, and; (5) RIO Bonacossa falsely claimed under oath that he was not aware of Data Colada's allegations against Gino at the time he was asked to serve as RIO and he did not tell Gino she could not obtain a forensic expert….

The facts presented by Plaintiff regarding the false statements do not prove that the adverse employment actions Harvard took against Plaintiff were motivated by gender bias or that the justification offered by Harvard was a sham. The allegedly false statements about what Dean Datar, Dean Cunningham, RIO Bonacossa, or Professor Amabile knew or when they knew it are not relevant to the reasons offered by Harvard that support their adverse employment decisions.

Additionally, the other fact disputes—whether Dean Datar made a deal with Data Colada and was pressured by Data Colada to move the investigation along, and whether Dean Cunningham falsely stated that she did not ask Professor Frei to counsel out Gino—are not material. The investigation that led to the adverse employment actions taken against Gino took place over nearly 18 months, involved several rounds of review by several different committees, including 26 professors, administrators, and trustees who evaluated documents, research, data, and conducted witness interviews. This investigation concluded in a 41-page report detailing the allegations, investigation process, and reasoning supporting the findings. The Third Statute Proceedings were similarly thorough and resulted in in-depth findings of fact and recommendations. Plaintiff has offered no evidence to demonstrate that Harvard's reasoning is a sham or a pretext for gender bias.

Finally, Gino points to a committee member's observation that she may have experienced professional and personal pressure after her husband lost his job. Although Gino characterizes the comment as reflecting an assumption about gender and family roles, I assume for purposes of the motion that it could carry such an implication. That does not end the inquiry: the remark must be assessed in context, including the speaker's role, whether it informed a disputed factual finding, and whether the record connects it with any adverse decision because of sex. Viewed together with Gino's other evidence, the quoted remark does not, without such a connection, establish that Harvard's stated reasons were a pretext for sex discrimination.

Considering the evidence cumulatively rather than in isolated categories, Gino identifies criticism of the procedures, comments concerning women's advancement, two male faculty members accused of different forms of impropriety, challenged statements by institutional actors, and the committee member's remark. The asserted procedural irregularities do not, without a supported causal connection, compel or permit a reasonable finding that the decisionmakers acted because of her sex. The comparator matters identified above concern materially different charges and screening decisions.

Even assuming that Gino meets the modest prima facie threshold and that some administrative statements are disputed, the total record cited does not raise a genuine dispute that Harvard's articulated research-misconduct basis was a cover for sex discrimination under federal law. Count I's selective-enforcement theory separately fails because the identified male comparators do not demonstrate selective pursuit of comparable allegations on the basis of sex. The Title VII and Title IX claims are against the institution insofar as authorized by the respective statutes; any individual liability asserted against Dean Datar must be evaluated under the applicable state-law provision rather than presumed from the federal employment claims….

Douglas E. Brayley, Jenny K. Cooper, Elena W. Davis, Stephanie D. Porges, and Laura G. Hoey (Ropes & Gray LLP) represent defendants.

#7628. Remembering Mark Pryor, beloved crime novelist and iconic Austinite

On October 8th, we lost Mark Pryor, a great craftsman of entertaining mysteries and thrillers, and an active and much loved member of the crime fiction community. He conceived unique heroes and anti-heroes with vivid settings. Not only was he a writer we admired, he was one we called a good friend.

His story was cool before he was even born. His father travelled on motorcycle across America on holiday from Britain where fell in love and brought the American lady home to marry. Mark and born and grew up in England with a love of soccer, where he studied journalism, then law. He used his dual citizenship to make a home in Austin, Texas where he practiced law as a prosecutor, mainly in Juvenile Court, and later as a defense attorney. He most valued his time with juvenile law, feeling he had leeway to hopefully get the perpetrator’s life back on track as well as get justice. However, what he valued most was his wife Sarah and three children, Blake, Henry, and Nicola.

His first novel, The Bookseller, he introduced us to Hugo Marston, the character he wrote about the most. Hugo, a former FBI profiler from Texas, worked as the chief of security for our embassy in Paris. When not indulging in his love of collecting and reading books, he finds himself dealing in mysteries often involving international intrigue. He is often assisted by his wild card of a CIA-connected buddy, Tom Green, his sometime girlfriend, French journalist Claudia Roux, and Parisian cop Lt. Camille Laurens, one of the first reoccurring trans characters in a mystery series to be written with dignity.

“He didn’t give readers a superficial tourist’s version of France,” explains James Ziskin, a friend who started out with him, roughly the same time when they were label mates at Seventh Street. “He wrote details that only an habitué would think to include. He knew the locations, the history, the language, and day-to-day minutiae that make a foreign setting ring true. Second, he was fearless in drawing his characters, for example Camille Laurens, a transgender police lieutenant who appears in several of the Hugo Marston books. It would have been much safer to write a policewoman or policeman. Then there’s his knowledge of the law, his sense of justice, and the expert plotting that runs through all his books. He was a gifted wordsmith, too.”

“His imagery was always so vivid,” adds friend and fellow writer, Puja Guha. “He could set the scene of where things were in a case, or how something happened along the Seine, or anywhere else, in a way that just made you see it in your head so clearly.”

Mark presented Hugo with just a few touches on his background, then revealing a little more with each book. However, he proved to be fully formed as Puja explains. “Hugo’s a great hero. Strong, capable, but also vulnerable and emotional. A really well-rounded character. I always just wished he could find real love in the series!”

His next protagonist, Dominic,  proved to a complete opposite. Like Mark he worked as a juvenile prosecutor in Austin, but he was also a musician, as well as a dangerous sociopath. The books are a bitter, but oh so sweet, a dark chocolate mix of Richard Stark, Jim Thompson, and Patricia Highsmith. (For the record, Mark had only read Highsmith before he wrote the first book, Hollow Man.) When the two of us had dinner one night with noir queens Megan Abbott and Alison Gaylin, he listened intently while we talked about the genre. He later told me he was taking notes that evening for the book. When I asked if he ever thought of doing a book where he pitted Hugo and Dominic in a book, he told me if he was being true to the characters, Hugo could probably survive two chapters.

His last series lead, Henri Lefort, turned out to be his most complex. Introduced in Die Around Sundown, Henri, a homicide detective with a past, works the streets of recently occupied Paris. With small historical details and rich characterizations, he depicts the emotions and humiliation of living in a conquered society. He does have fun putting him in the same apartment Hugo will reside in in the future.

Recently, he returned to Hugo with The Most Mysterious Bookshop in Paris. Hugo retires from the embassy to open up his own bookshop. It opens with a beautiful passage with Hugo taking a morning stroll to the store, taking in the poetic glory of the city that reflects mark’s love for it. Of course, his old skills and reputation pull him in when he is asked to help a chocolate maker faced with blackmail. He delves into the making of the confections with fascinating detail. Many of the supporting cast returns. Pryor finished a second book, A Vintage Murder In Paris, that will be published in spring.

Mark was one of the most sociable writers I ever worked with. He often asked to tag along for dinners I’d have with authors who came into town for book events. One of these dinners led to a strong friendship he had with Phillip Kerr. He was a mainstay at Bouchercon, beloved by both authors and fans, all drawn to his charm and dry wit. To be around the god natured ribbing between James and Mark of who was the better author was hilarious. “I loved sparring with Mark. Of course, Mark landed more blows than he received, I can tell you that. He could slice you to pieces with his wit, and make you laugh at yourself anyway. We used to insult each other publicly whenever we got the chance, but it was all in good fun.“

Fellow Austin author, Mike McCrary described his personality in a nutshell. “Mark was the person you wanted to sit next to at that boring dinner. The one you hoped would be at the thing you didn’t want go to because he’d make it fun. He always made me laugh and rarely caught him without a smile.”

“He had the most mischievous smile,” says Ziskin.  “That English accent. His generosity. His willingness to protect victims and champion the underdog. And, of course, his sense of humor. Everyone liked Mark.”

Mike recalls his mischievous one evening. “Noir at the Bar in Austin. A great example of his wit and his never-ending push to play with the unexpected. He went up on stage before me and he knew I was next. As he wrapped up he turned to the audience and said, “Be nice to Mike. He’s not used to crowds this big.”

One of my favorite memories of Mark is when I hung out with him at a Bouchercon opening party. He had a little too much to drink that evening and was feeling pretty loose. When he saw me the next morning he said with all sincerity and Cary Grant charm, “You were with me most of the night, who do I need to apologize to?”

“I feel like we became close friends after our first couple of conversations,” recalls Puja. “He always made sure no one felt left out and brought people into the discussion.”

He encouraged his fellow authors, reminding us that we were all in this together and we should take pride in what we can do in crime fiction and if you were friend, you knew you had someone who always had your back. He often helped out people who had legal questions about there book. He used Mr. Ziskin’s skills to do both a map and fictional family tree in two of his Hugo books. “Mark mentioned that he liked a map that had appeared in one of my books, so I told him I’d drawn it and offered to do one for him if he wanted. He told me which landmarks he wanted to include and I did my best. The family tree must have come about in the same way. It was something you do gladly for a friend.”

He used his books as a way to show his love for others. He often roped his kids into making funny promo videos. Many of his friends’ names popped up in his books for characters. I believe one of the reasons he turned Hugo into a bookseller was so he could namecheck his colleagues and promote their books in his own. With Mark, everyone was welcome in his world, whether the real or fictional one.

A legendary crime bookseller, Scott Montgomery runs The Hard Word blog, https://www.thehardword.me. Always a crime fiction fan, Scott Montgomery worked on the sales staff of the acclaimed and influential The Mystery Bookstore in Los Angeles for four years.

#7627. A Writer’s Night at America’s Most Haunted Hotel

Book tours have taught me to expect the unexpected. There was the couple in Texas who kindly housed me but warned about their vicious late-night, door-opening, biting cat, and the time a prominent politician’s son asked me to edit his “fictional novel,” a thinly-veiled story about his father’s real-life exploits. But nothing prepared me for what happened in Eureka Springs, Arkansas.

I’d recently met the fabulous writer Stephanie Storey while she was touring her beautiful debut novel Oil and Marble. Stephanie grew up in Arkansas, and I’m pretty sure she told the director of the literary festival, Books in Bloom, about me. I received an invitation to be a featured author at the festival in the spring of 2018. I’d never been to Arkansas and was excited to experience both the town and this celebration of literature. My communication from the director stated I’d be staying at the Crescent, a historic hotel founded in 1866. The town was as adorable and welcoming as advertised, a Victorian village with rumored healing springs, and everyone I met exuded warmth and hospitality. The thriving literary community radiated kindness and engagement.

My room was comfy and oddly shaped, the kind of space that had clearly remained much as it was in the 1800s. The quirks of the layout only added to its charm. It wasn’t until I checked in that day that I noticed a sign proclaiming the hotel to be “America’s Most Haunted Hotel.” I’m not easily spooked, but I do have a healthy curiosity and respect for possibilities.

That evening, after going out for dinner with several other authors from the festival, I took the stairs rather than the elevator to get some exercise as I made my way back to my room. When I reached my floor, I noticed a throng of people blocking the hallway. As I got closer, I realized they were listening with rapt attention to a hotel employee leading them on the nightly ghost tour. And then it hit me: they were standing directly outside my room. The tour guide was calling my room the most haunted room in the hotel.

I looked around, half-expecting someone to jump out and shout, Gotcha! You shoulda seen your face! But no. I eased closer to listen, catching fragments of the guide’s narrative: something about a secret pregnancy, a woman who had mysteriously fallen—or perhaps jumped—from the window of the very room where I’d be sleeping that night. The group murmured, a young girl chewed her nail, a man snapped a photo of my door, and then they moved on down the hall, leaving me standing there. I said aloud to no one, Are you kidding me?

That night, I settled into bed, read for a while, and then turned off the lamp. I wasn’t particularly concerned about the ghost tour’s commentary. After all, the guide was doing his job, creating atmosphere and mystery to justify the tour fee. My room was cozy and funky, and I liked the bed. I nestled into the sheets, closed my eyes, and drifted off.

Then, almost immediately, I sensed a cat hopping onto the bed. Now, I know that sounds wacky. And I can’t exactly articulate the sensation. Still, if you’ve ever had a cat, you know that particular feeling—the gentle padding of paws, the slight shifting of the comforter, barely perceptible but unmistakable. This felt so real, so present, that I jumped up and turned on the lamp, sending my reading glasses flying off the nightstand. There was no cat on my bed. I looked underneath, checked the bathroom, searched the corners of the room, all the while calling Here, kitty kitty, my suspension of disbelief tested. Absolutely nothing.

I got back into bed, turned off the light, and lay there, mind racing, acutely aware of every shadow and sound. I thought of my youngest child, a seventh grader, back home in South Carolina. He had a big math test the next day. I turned the lamp back on and grabbed my phone to text him a good luck, good night text. Not eager to get back out of bed to retrieve my glasses, I squinted and pecked out my message.

“Night, buddy. Proud of you. You got this! Love you so much.”

I hit send, turned off the lamp, then, oddly enough, slept soundly. The next morning, I awoke early and absentmindedly picked up my glasses, only to realize, with great embarrassment, that my late-night text had not been to my son Will, but to my longtime OB-GYN, Dr. Robert. Mortified, I typed a quick explanation. I kept it simple: “Oops. Wrong recipient. Meant for my son.” He replied with a crying-laughing emoji. Thank goodness my gynecologist had a sense of humor.

I opened my laptop and prepped for my session at the festival later that morning. Sipping my coffee, curiosity got the better of me. On a whim, I googled “ghost cat of Crescent Hotel, Eureka Springs,” not really expecting to find anything.

There was, in fact, a ghost cat at the Crescent Hotel—and it had a name: Morris. He was a real orange tabby who had lived at the hotel for twenty-one years, supposedly serving as its unofficial general manager. He had an office with his title on the door and a custom cat-door cut into the lobby so he could move freely through the hotel. When Morris died in 1994, over three hundred people attended his funeral. He was buried on the hotel’s East Lawn with a headstone.

According to what I found, Morris apparently loved his job too much to leave. Guests and staff continued to report his presence—a cat brushing past ankles, faint meows in empty hallways, and, you guessed it: a gentle weight on the bed.

I hadn’t experienced the ghost of a tragic woman in the most haunted room, but I may have experienced Morris.

As I left the hotel that morning to start my day at the festival, I stepped outside and visited Morris’s grave. Standing there, I thought about what it means to be a writer—to remain open to possibilities, to imagine. Morris’s late-night visit had broadened my lens. And as unexpected situations tend to do, the experience made me consider a new what-if. A cat so devoted to his purpose that he transcended death itself to continue his work? There was a story in that.

There always is, if you’re willing to see it.

Fig Days (on-sale April 6, 2027; Regal House Publishing)

Born in Charleston and raised on Johns Island, Michel Stone is part of the 11th generation of her family to hail from the South Carolina Lowcountry. She is the author of the novels Fig Days, forthcoming from Regal House Publishing on April 6, 2027, Border Child (Doubleday), and The Iguana Tree (Hub City Press). She is the winner of the Mary Frances Hobson Prize for Distinguished Achievement in Arts and Letters, the Patricia Winn Award for Southern Literature, and the South Carolina Fiction Award. Michel’s novels have been widely, favorably reviewed from The San Francisco Chronicle to The New Yorker. She holds a BA in English from Clemson University and an M.Ed. from Converse College. Michel is a Fellow of the Aspen Global Leadership Network, a Liberty Fellow, and a Ucross Fellow. She spends as much time as possible in her beloved Lowcountry with her family and Boykin Spaniel. Visit Michel online at michelstone.com and on Instagram @michel.stone.writes.

#7626. Firm partners in Silicon Valley paid more than NY partners, new survey shows

In a reversal that could reflect the artificial intelligence-fueled technology industry boom, law firm partners in Silicon Valley earned more on average than partners in New York last year, according to a new survey. (Image from Shutterstock)

In a reversal that could reflect the artificial intelligence-fueled technology industry boom, law firm partners in Silicon Valley earned more on average than partners in New York last year, according to a new survey.

Compensation for Silicon Valley partners was $2.57 million on average in ​2025, 4% more than partners in New York, according to a survey of large firms.

The survey was released this week by legal recruiting agency Major, Lindsey & Africa and included more than 1,000 respondents, according to a story by Reuters.

Average partner compensation throughout the top 200 largest U.S. firms increased 10% to $1.55 million since 2024. In 2016, ​the figure was $877,000.

The survey also revealed that average hourly billing rate increased by 11%, from $1,114 in ⁠2024 to $1,242, according to Reuters.

#7625. Another Trump term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

President Donald Trump and his policies were a consistent and high-profile theme during the Supreme Court’s last term. The justices weighed in on several of Trump’s signature initiatives, from sweeping global tariffs and his efforts to limit the availability of birthright citizenship to his attempts to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission and Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors – as well as various important immigration cases. And that’s all before you get to the court’s interim docket, where Trump chalked up a number of significant victories.

As it currently stands, the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor, featuring two challenges to Trump’s immigration policies and a dispute over access to information about Trump’s U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE. But that could change soon: between Nov. 6 and mid-January, the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review filed by the Trump administration or Trump himself. Given the Office of the Solicitor General, which represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, has a high success rate – usually somewhere around 60% – for petitions that it files with the justices, Trump could once again end up dominating the term.

Immigration is already a hot topic on the court’s docket, but two immigration disputes could raise the prominence of the issue even more. When the justices meet for their Nov. 6 conference, one of the cases that they will consider is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a challenge to a Trump administration policy of quickly removing immigrants who cross the border illegally without giving them the chance to seek asylum.

Two federal courts in Washington, D.C., agreed with the challengers – a group of immigrants and three immigrants’ rights groups – that the policy violates federal immigration law. That prompted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer to come to the Supreme Court in August, where he argued that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit “threatens to dismantle” what Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin “describes as an ‘indispensable’ tool for controlling the border.”

Last month, the Trump administration asked the justices to weigh in on another dispute arising from its immigration agenda – this time involving the government’s efforts to detain and deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The government’s petition came in the case of one of those detainees, Badar Khan Suri, an Indian national who came to the United States for a postdoctoral fellowship at Georgetown University. The Trump administration has told the justices that they should also consider granting the petition for review filed recently by Mahmoud Khalil, an Algerian national who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria and became a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2024. The government contended that both men should be deported based on determinations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that their conduct – alleged support for the Islamic militant group Hamas, in Suri’s case, and participation in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” for Khalil – compromised U.S. foreign policy.

Attorneys for Suri and Khalil went to federal court in New Jersey and Virginia, asking judges there to review the legality of their detentions on the ground that (among other things) they had been detained in retaliation for their speech. As their cases come to the court, the question that the justices have been asked to decide is whether federal trial courts even have the power to consider such challenges, or whether (as the Trump administration argues) those claims are instead barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court, because they are also related to whether one can be deported. The federal courts of appeals have reached conflicting conclusions on the issue, which increases the likelihood that the justices will agree to weigh in.

Suri’s response to the government’s petition for review and the government’s response to Khalil’s petition are both due on Nov. 20. The justices will likely consider both petitions at a private conference sometime early next year.

In June, the Supreme Court granted the federal government’s petition for review in Genalo v. Black, agreeing to address whether there is a point at which a noncitizen has been detained so long that he or she has a constitutional right to a bond hearing and, if so, what standard the government must meet for him or her to remain in detention. That case was scheduled for oral argument in October, but it was dismissed in September because it was moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.

The Trump administration returned to the court later that month, asking the justices to grant a petition for review involving the same questions, which Sauer called “exceptionally important.” The case was filed by a citizen of the Dominican Republic, identified in court filings only as D.C., who has spent most of his adult life in the United States and has three daughters with a U.S. citizen. D.C. was detained on the same day that he finished serving a prison sentence, and the government sought to deport him.

In March 2026, when he had been in immigration custody for almost six-and-a-half months, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer agreed with D.C. that he was entitled to “an individualized bond hearing, with constitutionally adequate procedural safeguards.” The Trump administration is now appealing that decision to the Supreme Court without waiting for a federal appeals court to rule on the case. Sauer told the justices that “granting immediate review would allow the Court to consider” the questions it had already agreed to decide in Black during the 2026-27 term.

D.C.’s response is currently due on Dec. 8; if that deadline remains in place, the court would likely consider the government’s petition sometime in early to mid-January.

In Trump v. Thakur, the justices will consider a petition for review stemming from the 2025 decision to end research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, National Science Foundation, and National Endowment for the Humanities for researchers at the University of California. The researchers went to federal court, where they argued that the termination of those grants violated (among other things) their rights to free speech and fair treatment, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

A federal district court issued a preliminary order requiring the government to reinstate the grants. The government went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which upheld that decision with regard to the claims on the basis that the administration had ended the grants because of the recipients’ “perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints.”

The court of appeals rejected the government’s contention that it could terminate funding for programs that, in its view, are not in the public interest. “This overlooks that there is a critical distinction between creating or ceasing a particular program (or subsidy, or forum), on one hand, and discriminating against disfavored speaker viewpoints within a program (or subsidy, or forum), on the other,” the 9th Circuit wrote.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that “if left to stand, the Ninth Circuit’s decision will establish precedent forcing taxpayers to waste countless dollars on private projects promoting ideologies that their public stewards reject.”

Last week Sauer asked the Supreme Court to distribute the government’s petition, as well as the researchers’ brief opposing review, on Oct. 28, without waiting the 14 days normally prescribed by the court’s rules. This would allow the justices to consider the case at their Nov. 13 conference.

In United States v. Jackson, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to rule on the legality of Trump’s appointment of an acting U.S. attorney in Nevada. Sauer told the justices that the appointment of Sigal Chattah (as well as others around the country) was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.”

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

Three men who had been indicted on felony charges in Nevada after Chattah’s designation as the first assistant U.S. attorney sought to have, at a minimum, Chattah disqualified from appearing in the case as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.” The lower courts agreed that Chattah was not eligible to serve as the acting U.S. attorney, and that she could not play any role in the prosecution of the defendants’ cases.

In a 34-page opinion, Judge Eric Miller of the 9th Circuit wrote that the “text and structure” of the FVRA are “unambiguous: The statute does not permit the executive to fill an existing vacancy by designating a new first assistant.” Instead, he reasoned, the FVRA “provides that a first assistant automatically succeeds to a vacant office” only if the first assistant was first assistant when the principal office became vacant. The automatic-succession rule, he concluded, “does not apply to a first assistant” – like Chattah – “who never served under a validly appointed official.” Moreover, Miller continued, the attorney general cannot achieve the same result “by delegating all of the functions and duties of the U.S. Attorney to someone else.”

In a second petition, United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the Trump administration has appealed a ruling against it by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit in a dispute over the appointment of John Sarcone as the Acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York. When Sarcone obtained grand jury subpoenas for information from the New York attorney general’s office relating to its investigations of the National Rifle Association and Trump, the office sought to quash the subpoenas on the ground that Sarcone had not been validly appointed.

A federal district court granted that request, and the 2nd Circuit upheld that decision. Sauer came to the Supreme Court in September, where he told the justices that Jackson was a better case in which to consider the validity of Trump’s appointments because the grand jury that issued the subpoenas in the New York case had been discharged and, as a result, the subpoenas were no longer enforceable. He urged the court to hold the New York case until it acts on Jackson.

The defendants challenging Chattah’s appointment have until Nov. 5 to file their brief opposing review; the response of the N.Y. attorney general’s office is currently due on Nov. 2.

There are several other notable petitions pending.

In May 2025, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration’s request to temporarily enforce a ban on transgender servicemembers. In a different case just over one year later, a divided panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of an order by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., barring the Trump administration from expelling several challengers to the policy from the military. (At the same time, that panel lifted the part of the order that would have required the military to admit transgender people who want to join the armed forces.)

In its petition for review in United States v. Talbott, filed in August, the federal government asked the Supreme Court to review and eventually reverse the D.C. Circuit’s decision. Sauer called it “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The response from the challengers is currently due on Nov. 2.

In Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether and when a federal court can throw out an agency’s action or rule in its entirety – a concept known as “universal vacatur.”

The question comes to the court in a case that began as a pair of challenges (that were later combined) to rules issued to implement parts of a 2022 law that was intended to protect patients from surprise healthcare bills. A federal district court in Texas ruled for the challengers – the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies – but a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed that decision in part.

The case then went to the full 5th Circuit, which threw out some of the challenged provisions. The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court this month, asking the justices to take up the dispute. It pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, holding that federal courts do not have the authority to enter so-called universal or nationwide injunctions, which prohibit the government from enforcing a policy anywhere in the country. The same logic underlying that case – the idea that courts “can grant ‘complete relief’ to parties before the court but cannot, as a rule, reach beyond them” – should apply to such regulations, Sauer contended.

The challengers’ response is currently due on Nov. 13, although that deadline may be extended.

Petitions filed by Trump’s personal lawyers

Although the federal government filed all of the petitions discussed above, Trump is also seeking Supreme Court review in three petitions filed by his personal lawyers. The most recent petition is also the one that the justices could consider first: Trump v. Clinton, the president’s bid to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.”

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the lawsuit, finding (among other things) that Trump had brought his claims too late, and that many of the statements alleged to have been made by the various defendants were “plainly protected by the First Amendment.” Middlebrooks also sanctioned Trump and his attorney, Alina Habba, ordering them to pay nearly $1 million.

On appeal, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit largely upheld Middlebrooks’ decision and affirmed the sanctions orders. The full 11th Circuit rejected Trump’s request for reconsideration, prompting Trump – represented by Richard Klugh – to come to the Supreme Court on Oct. 9. He asked the justices to weigh in on two questions: whether the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended because of his unique role and responsibilities as president, and whether a court can fine the president and his lawyers for making the “substantial, unresolved argument” that the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended.

Through her longtime attorney, David Kendall, Clinton waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition. The case has been distributed to the justices for consideration at their Nov. 6 conference. The court is extremely unlikely to grant review without first calling for Clinton to file a brief opposing review.

In Trump v. CNN, the president is seeking to reinstate his defamation case against cable news giant CNN. Trump contends that when CNN used the phrase “the Big Lie” to describe his insistence that he had actually won the 2020 election, which had been stolen from him, it was attempting to link him with Adolf Hitler and Nazi propaganda – which, Trump said, was defamation.

A federal judge in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, dismissed Trump’s case. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the 11th Circuit upheld that ruling.

In his petition for review, which was filed in August, Trump contended that “CNN falsely and maliciously portrayed” him “as a knowing liar who fabricated objections to the 2020 election, lacked supporting evidence, and deliberately deceived the American people.”

And in July, Trump filed the second of two petitions arising from lawsuits brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store. The lawsuit leading to the second petition claimed that in June 2019, Trump had defamed her by calling her a liar – saying, among other things, that Carroll “was trying to sell a new book” and that her accusations were “totally false.” A jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million in January 2024.

The 2nd Circuit upheld the award in 2025, finding “ample evidence that Trump was recklessly indifferent to Carroll’s health and safety” and that “Carroll was subjected to ongoing and prolific harassment as a result of these statements, including a multitude of death threats and other threats of physical injury.” The full court of appeals in April declined to rehear the case.

Represented by a private lawyer, Robert Giuffra, Trump argued in his petition for review that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office, the $83.3 million award cannot be allowed to stand. “The threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next,’” Giuffra wrote.

The federal government filed its own petition backing Trump, in which it (like Trump) urged the Supreme Court to also decide whether the court of appeals should have granted then-Attorney General Bondi’s request to recertify that Trump made his statements as part of his role as president and therefore the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case.

Carroll’s response to both petitions is currently due on Oct. 30.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Another Trump term?, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 27, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/another-trump-term/

#7624. Journal of Free Speech Law: "Protecting the Thinking Process in Human-AI Interaction: The Forum Interstitiale Between Thought and Expression," by Caroline De Cock

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

International human rights law protects freedom of thought absolutely and freedom of expression subject to limitations. The relevant established doctrine calls the two sides of that line the forum internum and the forum externum. However, the line was drawn when thinking left no trace, and with current technological developments, it no longer holds.

Within the span of six months in 2026, a United States court ordered that 20 million ChatGPT conversations be provided as evidence under ordinary discovery rules, two federal courts reached opposite conclusions on whether a litigant's exchanges with a chatbot were protected at all, and the Supreme Court held that location records kept by a third party remain constitutionally protected. Records of where a person's body had been were protected, while records of how their mind worked were not.

The law currently has no category for the search query, the exploratory prompt, the unfinished draft, or the confession made to a machine. The U.S. answer has been a quarrel about privilege: Courts refuse to grant AI exchanges between users and chatbots protection because the machine is not a professional, like a doctor or a lawyer, and the industry asks for a new privilege because it claims the model behaves like one. Both the courts and the industry assume that protection depends on what the person is using, i.e., what the machine is. This Article argues that it depends on what the person who uses the machine is doing.

It proposes the forum interstitiale, a third zone between the two classical fora, which can protect the thinking process under a standard stronger than ordinary expression law but short of absolute. Every candidate analogy to interactions with AI chatbots in existing law is tested herein, from search queries and confidential dialogue to protected reading, aggregated records, the European law on correspondence and data protection, private diaries and drafts, and neural data. Each fails for the same reason, namely that the protection it offers relates to a relationship, a disclosure, a recording, an addressee, or a data type, and never to the function of the act as thinking.

The interstitial zone this Article proposes only flows upwards. It lifts acts abandoned by the current binary approach into protection and displaces nothing from the absolute core of protected thought. The Article also sets out what acts belong in the liminal zone, five elements of the protection standard, the duties those elements impose on AI providers, and a map of individual AI interactions across the three fora. This classification determines what records of thought can be demanded, kept, filtered, and used against the person who was engaged in the process of thinking.

NEXT: Prof. Francesca Gino's Contract and Discrimination Claims Against Harvard Business School Dismissed

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7623. Suspenseful not-exactly-horror movies to watch, this Halloween

I don’t know if I like horror or not, honestly. I definitely like it more than I used to? Still, I don’t really ever want to turn on a movie that’s going to scare me. I like thrills, maybe a few chills… that’s it. So, here are some good Halloween movies that are very suspenseful and even a bit spooky and maybe even a little scary… but that won’t traumatize you. I think?

I grouped them into three categories: old-timey suspense movies, movies that definitely have blood but aren’t GORY scary messes (the blood volume is offset by inventiveness or funniness or satire), and then movies that I could sit through but that are definitely too scary for some people.

NOT VERY SCARY, AS IN “SCARY IN AN OLD-FASHIONED WAY”:

I’m not talking about the insipid remake with Armie Hammer, but the original, Alfred Hitchcock’s masterpiece. The good people who read CrimeReads do not need me to tell them to watch Rebecca, but I’m underscoring it because watching a scene in which a house burns down might be the very thing you need, lately, idk.

I will never, never stop praising Charles Laughton’s only film, a masterpiece about a psychopathic serial-killer and self-appointed preacher (Robert Mitchum, always great, never better), who, when he gets out of jail, becomes obsessed with finding the money hidden by his lately-executed bank robber former-cellmate—a secret which is kept by the robber’s two young children. TELL ME this is not the most eye-widening plot you’ve ever heard. And now believe me when I say that it is shot gorgeously, too. The cinematography will make you scream. SWOOPING shadows. Ghostly UNDERWATER shots. Insane stuff.

My high school AP US History teacher Mr. O’Neill heartily recommended that I watch this earlyish-career Hitchcock movie, about a teenage girl (Teresa Wright) who becomes suspicious that her beloved Uncle Charley (Joseph Cotten) is a murderer, after he visits her family in their idyllic California town. It’s really excellent—Mr. O’Neill was correct.

Based on the novel by Boileau-Narcejac (a pair of writers, actually), this midcentury horror-noir from one of my favorite directors, Henri-Georges Clouzot, is the perfect Halloween movie. Simone Signoret and Véra Clouzot play the mistress and wife (respectively) of a sadistic schoolmaster (Paul Meurisse) who plan the perfect murder to rid their lives of him. But when the murder is done and his body vanishes, the tables begin to turn. It’s excellent, absolutely chilling feature—the best film Hitchcock never made (and, IMO, better than most films Hitchcock did make). (This is just an enthusiastic endorsement… I’m not knocking Hitchcock.)

Richard (Cornel Wilde) is a writer who believes he’s struck gold when he encounters Ellen Berent (Gene Tierney), a gorgeous young woman who is totally infatuated with him. Turns out, though, that she’s an obsessive psychopath. Whoops!

Park Chan-wook’s black comedy-thriller is one of the best movies about “hitting a breaking point” ever made. I love a satire about capitalism, and this movie, about a middle-class, white-collar worker who gets laid off and subsequently goes on a murder spree to get rid of anyone who might be competition for his old job, is pretty perfect.

I feel like no one saw Resurrection, an engrossing, chilling thriller starring Rebecca Hall and Tim Roth, and this is a crime. It might seem somewhat standard in plot—it is about a woman whose life is upended when a figure from her past returns—but it is punched up by fantastic performances: Roth’s sinister calmness and Hall’s detonating desperation. She also gives maybe the single best scene performance of the year: a seven-minute, one-take monologue that she delivers with her entire face. Incredible.

I’ll say upfront that M. Night Shyamalan’s Trap isn’t perfect. There are the kind of pitfalls that always seem to pop up in Shyamalan’s movies (a tendency to over-explain some things, some strange or stilted dialogue), but I find these things less “pitfalls” than funny markers of style. Shyamalan is an auteur in the truest sense of the word, and, in an era of endless sequels and unwanted franchises, I find it a breath of fresh air that he always seems able to turn out a new, original idea. And Trap, which is a movie about a serial killer who realizes that the FBI are closing in on him while he takes his tween daughter to a Taylor Swift-style pop concert, is not only a delightful and original premise, but it is also executed with such love and care that it feels almost impossible not to enjoy.

First and foremost, it is a father-daughter movie. Our protagonist, the slick murderer Cooper (Josh Hartnett), adores his young daughter Riley (Ariel Donoghue), and is so excited to be able to be with her to enjoy her favorite artist, the pop singer Lady Raven (Saleka Shyamalan). His clear love for her and his family plays out nicely against his increasing need for self-preservation; as the walls begin to close in, he clings tight to his daughter, and it’s clear that for maybe the first time, he’s beginning to worry if this will be a day his daughter won’t forget not for its specialness, but its potential to upend her life. And second, Shyamalan’s own daughter Saleka, herself a singer-songwriter and musician, plays such a large part in this film, that it is clear that Trap is a family-affair, behind the scenes just as much as in front of the camera. I find it incredibly charming that, at the start of Shyamalan’s career, he was marketed as an extremely mysterious figure with a dark imagination, and now, maybe years later, he is perhaps most famous for seeming to be a very loving father.

Oh, one more thing… in Trap, there is an FBI agent/criminal profiler who is leading the manhunt, and she’s played by the great Hayley Mills. Hayley Mills is the former child star who played the original twins in the original version of The Parent Trap (1961). So, like, I can’t stop thinking about how M. Night Shyamalan cast the original parent-trapper in the original Parent Trap to lay a parent trap to trap a parent in Trap.

Drian De Palma’s Blow Out is a clever re-imagining of Michelangelo Antonioni’s Blow Up (the film listed right above), only featuring an a movie sound engineer (John Travolta) accidentally recording a murder, rather than catching it on film. This film has a lot to say about what surveillance, scandal, and murder have to do with America—and thus it’s set in Philadelphia during the Fourth of July.

I loved this wonderful, twisty satirical film about our… cough… reliance on technology. I can’t say much more than that; but it’s an excellent film for today’s modern age.

Maybe you’re not interested in extremely well-made parodies of Gen-Z online culture, and maybe you are. But it would still be worth your time to watch Halina Reijn’s Bodies Bodies Bodies, about a group of narcissistic zoomers stuck in a mansion together during a hurricane, playing a murder-themed party game that somehow becomes real. The kids start to suspect each other, in ways that provide ample opportunities to satirize the “toxic” fake-woke culture permeating the zeitgeist and wielded by the most privileged among us.

I absolutely loved Strange Darling, JT Mollner’s wild and weird serial killer movie, which was shot all on 35 mm film by the actor-turned-cinematographer Giovanni Ribisi. And man, he’s a good DP. Strange Darling is as much as a visual treat as it is a narrative extravaganza, a fully controlled and impressive story told in an innovative way. It stars a superb Willa Fitzgerald as a young woman (simply called “the lady”) and an impressive Kyle Gallner (simply called “the demon”) and it drops us in the middle of their night, a night that has started as a one night stand and has twisted into a terrifying cat-and-mouse chase puppeted by a serial killer. The shot that plays during the opening credits, of Fitzgerald’s character running desperately across a green field in bright red scrubs, her ear having been blasted off by a shotgun, is one of the most arresting things I’ve seen at the movies in a while. And the movie only gets more, well, arresting from there.

Would a list about small-town crime movies be complete without an entry from David Lynch? No! Kyle MacLachlan is a young college student returning to his hometown for the season when he discovers a severed human ear in a cornfield (I KNOW!), and thus embarks on a strange mystery.

I loved this frosty, bloody, bone-chilling indie film, written and directed by Bridget Savage Cole and Danielle Krudy. It’s about two sisters (Sophie Lowe and Morgan Saylor) from a small, coastal New England fishing town. Shortly after the death of their beloved mother, they wind up having to cover up the terrible murder of a would-be assaulter. But as they attempt to conceal the crime, hoping friendly police officers and nosy neighbors do not suspect anything too fishy, they become drawn into their town’s dark underbelly, which turns out to be surprisingly matriarchal.

I loved this comic slasher film, starring Samara Weaving as a young woman marrying into a billionaire family dynasty without realizing they’re going to wind up attempting to sacrifice her at midnight on her wedding night. It’s a wonderful satire on elitism and class in America, and a fun (sometimes heavy-handed) take-down of patriarchal institutions in general. If you’re looking something to watch with a friend, I highly suggest this. I saw this with my friend Eleni in theaters, last summer, and we sat in the last row and ate doughnuts the whole time. The movie will make your blood run cold at times, but this memory warms my heart.

A sequel that is just as good as/if not better than its original, Ready or Not II pops into the days after the events of Ready or Not I. It’s very Halloween 2. In this sequel, after she’s made it through, she’s challenged by a powerful group connected to her in-laws’ family (also with a Satanic pact) to a DOUBLE OR NOTHING game of hide-and-seek, and they have to play, or they’ll kill her sister, Kathryn Newton! The actors in this group of deadly players include such luminaries as Sarah Michelle Gellar, Elijah Wood, Néstor Carbonell, Kevin Durand… and David Cronenberg. Yes, David Cronenberg. DO! A! DOUBLE! FEATURE!

I debated with a friend whether or not this Barton Fink is a proper crime movie (I think it qualifies for this list because it’s ALL about L.A. in the summer and it’s probably the sweatiest film ever made, plus there is also a vicious murder in the middle of it) but he thinks not a crime movie as much as a terrifying, vaguely supernatural movie about a mental breakdown. Still… decide for yourself.

No, this is not The Watcher, the incompetent Netflix series adapting that one article in The Cut. This is Chloe Okuno’s gutting, sensitive, all-too-real movie about a young woman who discovers that she has a stalker. When Julia (an amazing Maika Monroe) movies with her husband to Bucharest, she thinks that the man who often stares out at her from the apartment across the street could be the serial killer who has been decapitating women around the city.

Eileen! This thriller, which is basically perfect almost all of the way through, is based on the novel by Ottessa Moshfegh. Anne Hathaway rocks her portrayal of a sultry, secretive psychologist at a young men’s prison in Massachusetts. She, Rebecca, is the first bright spot in a while that Eileen (Thomasin McKenzie), who works in the prison, has experienced, and it’s not long before Eileen begins to grow veeeeeery interested in her. The movie builds well and is really interesting, but a late-in-the-film monologue from Marin Ireland brings the house down.

OKAY THIS ARE ACTUALLY DEFINITELY A BIT SCARY BUT YOU WILL PROBABLY BE OKAY (PROBABLY):

Late Night with the Devil is a fresh, bracing horror film from writer-directors Cameron and Colin Cairnes and producer-star David Dastmalchian. It has a crystalline premise. Get a load of this: a late night TV show host, desperate for better ratings, plans a broadcast that will catch audiences’ attentions. His program, which airs on Halloween night in 1977, includes appearances from psychics, paranormal debunkers, and a psychologist who claims to have been able to communicate with a demon inhabiting a possessed child. Oh, and… the possessed child, herself. She’s there too. So, of course, when the show commences, things go horribly wrong. The film unfolds crisply, playing with a cinéma vérité style, as if we’re watching a behind-the-scenes broadcast about the apparently-famed broadcast, which includes material never before seen. I love films that handle exposition creatively, and this one certainly does, though its sense of overarching structure does fade a bit as the film progresses (sometimes, later on, I wasn’t positive if we were watching the broadcast, the broadcast of the broadcast, or something else). Perhaps this is related, but at times (in the film’s revelatory third act, for example) it’s almost too economical; I would not have called the film heavyhanded if it provided a few more conclusive answers. Just a couple! I mean, the devil’s in the details! But these are quibbles. Overall, it’s a smartly-paced, original, and riveting horror movie. If you like scary movies of any kind, or if you like the very specific category of “movies about broadcast television,” this one’s for you.

I am a moderate horror movie fan married to an extreme horror movie fan, so my consumption of all things spooky is pretty constant throughout the year. Still, I can’t deny that it’s just more fun to watch something bone-chilling in the chilly days of October. This month, I recommend you find yourself a cozy blanket and a moderately brave loved one and watch The Invitation, a horror-thriller movie that takes place at a dinner party in the Hollywood Hills (I know—and it gets even scarier)! A man and his new girlfriend attend a dinner hosted by the man’s ex-husband and her new husband, along with a few other friends. Things get even more intense than you’d expect, and the final of the movie is one of the most haunting horror ending I’ve ever seen.—Jessie Gaynor

Suspiria (2018) As someone who prefers to peek into the cinematic world of horror every now and then (and especially in October), I couldn’t help but recommend Luca Guadagnino’s 2018 remake of the classic Suspiria, which cranks up palimpsestic, arthouse film aesthetics so high that you can occasionally forget you’re watching a scary movie. The film clocks in at almost three hours and features heavy-hitters like Tilda Swinton, Dakota Johnson, Alek Wek, Chole Grace Mortez, and Mia Goth. The muted wintery aesthetic is rightfully accompanied with slithering worms, broken bones, ghoulish breathing, the occasional jump-scare, and plenty of blood and guts to make your toes curl. And I mustn’t forget: the ending is so unexpected that you’ll feel you’ve just emerged from a fever dream (and that’s probably because—spoiler—it is and is not). Suspiria has all you need for, what will likely be, an intense night you won’t forget—or one you’ll hope not to remember. –Rasheeda Saka   The Invisible Man (2020) The Invisible Man updates the classic story of Griffin, a man who has turned himself invisible and winds up using this quality to deftly harm people. Yet unlike the 1933 film version (in turn based on H.H. Wells’s novel of the same name), Griffin is not a rampaging, murderous lunatic who endangers society, but a possessive and vengeful threat to one woman in particular. This theme rings a little familiar: don’t we hear often that women are more likely to be murdered by someone they know than by a random maniac? The new Invisible Man makes Griffin the abusive ex-boyfriend of our protagonist Cecilia (Elizabeth Moss). He seems to have died, but has really turned transparent, which makes his vicious stalking even easier to accomplish. Because of this, for a while, the new Invisible Man, written and directed by Leigh Whannell, seems like a straight-up, supernatural horror movie—in which a woman is haunted by a ghost rather than hunted by a person. The way the film allegorically uses genre in this way to starkly un-desensitize us (apologies for that turn of phrase) to abuse is generally pretty successful, but the film possibly makes its more intense criticism of patriarchal oppression through Cecilia’s attempt to prove that someone is literally stalking her. This is the least science-fictional and most gut-wrenchingly real part of the movie: that in attempting to prove that she is in danger, Cecilia would be fighting an uphill battle even if her assaulter were visible. And he’s not. (Available to stream on HBO Max.)

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads.
