#7571. What businesses should know about consent rules when calling consumers

Rules around obtaining consumer consent before calling or texting are in a state of legal and regulatory uncertainty – and companies should remain cautious.

Senosiain is an associate and Rollins is a shareholder at Gunster. Views are the authors’ own.

The Telephone Consumer Protection Act governs calls and text messages sent by businesses to consumers. One such rule is that businesses must obtain express written consent prior to sending text messages to consumers, if they are using an automated telephone dialing system or making calls using an artificial or pre-recorded voice, including the use of AI bots.

The TCPA also provides that businesses may not call or text consumers on the federal Do Not Call List unless prior express consent is given. Even basic telemarketing calls and text messages require prior express consent. Violation of the statute can trigger liability for up to $1,500 per call or text message sent.

Additionally, many states have their own version of the TCPA, deemed “mini-TCPAs,” that require compliance for all businesses who make calls to consumer-residents in that state, regardless of where the business is domiciled.

Many companies use lead generators which gather consumer consents for multiple businesses and then provide the companies with consent and contact information for those potential consumers. Lead generators who obtain proper written consent can be a very useful tool for companies. This was generally permissible under the TCPA.

However, in 2023, the Federal Communications Commission updated its TCPA rules requiring “one-to-one consent” which was to become effective Jan. 27, 2025.

The one-to-one consent rule provides that if a business uses an ATDS, artificial or prerecorded voice, the business must obtain prior express consent, one seller at a time.

Thus, it prevents lead generators from using a single consumer’s consent for multiple businesses. Additionally, the one-to-one consent rule provides that the consent must be clear and conspicuous, and the calls and texts initiated pursuant to the consent must be logically and topically associated with the interaction that prompted the consent. This rule applies to both text messages and phone calls.

On Jan. 24, 2025, the FCC postponed the 2023 order by a year, until Jan. 26, 2026. Later that same day the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals vacated the 2023 Order, thus eliminating the one-to-one consent rule.

The Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held “that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority under the TCPA because the 2023 Order’s new consent restrictions impermissibly conflict[ed] with the ordinary statutory meaning of prior express consent.”

Notably, the court ruled that the FCC exceeded its statutory authority at the outset, when it created the one-to-one consent rule. The court held that the 2023 Order’s one-to-one prior express consent restriction impermissibly conflicted with the ordinary statutory meaning of “prior express consent.” Thus, the Court vacated application of the 2023 Order, and remanded for further proceedings.

As a result, it is very likely that we will see other cases challenging TCPA regulations, especially as to the consent required before making a telemarketing call or text message using an ATDS.

It is unclear whether the FCC will revise its 2023 Order to comply with the Eleventh Circuit’s decision. In order to be prepared for this rule to come into effect, and in an abundance of caution, businesses who use lead generators to source potential consumers’ consent should ascertain that the lead generators are obtaining individual, one-to-one consent.

Businesses should also only contact consumers who provide this consent for telemarketing that is logically and topically associated with that which the consent was provided. Further, in addition to storing consumer contact information, businesses must retain the consent forms, information as to when consent was given, and through whom. Even businesses that do not use lead generators to obtain consent should continue to review their consent practices to ensure strict compliance with the TCPA and mini-TCPAs.

The TCPA requires prior express consent, and in many cases, prior express written consent, for calls and text messages made to prospective consumers. Regardless of any changes to the TCPA, the FTSA still requires that businesses obtain prior express written consent when making unsolicited telephone calls (including sending text messages) using an automated system. And lastly, to further protect your business, the consent form should have robust terms of service, including a class action waiver.

We continue to recommend that businesses ensure compliance with the TCPA, FTSA, and any other state regulations by always obtaining express written consent prior to contacting potential consumers via calls or text messages.

#7570. Court to hear argument in religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court will hear oral argument on Nov. 3 in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado, which argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because Colorado will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

The Catholic preschools say that they “have no objection to Colorado’s decision to allow over 1,000 … preschools to selectively serve the communities they are designed to serve.” Instead, the preschools emphasize, they “simply want the same accommodation extended to them.”

Colorado counters that the Catholic preschools “remain welcome to participate in” the universal preschool program. However, the state writes, if they do, they must be “subject to the same equal-opportunity requirements that apply to all other publicly funded preschools—public and private, secular and religious.”

Under the universal preschool program, families in Colorado can receive up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools. To be part of the program, preschools must meet state standards in areas such as employee training; they are also required to sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” Colorado does not allow them to refuse to serve LGBTQ families, because it believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs in the case are the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children. They went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy, arguing that making Catholic preschools’ participation in the universal preschool program contingent on accepting the agreement amounts to unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to create a religious exemption to allow them to participate in the program.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit ruled for the state. It acknowledged that in a line of decisions, the Supreme Court has held that “when a state offers subsidies for private education, it cannot categorically withhold those funds from religious institutions.” In the 10th Circuit’s view, however, those cases do not apply to the preschools’ challenge because Colorado “did not exclude” religious preschools from the universal preschool program. To the contrary, the court of appeals wrote, it “welcomed and actively solicited their participation” and it is not seeking “to prohibit funds from being used for religious purposes.” “The restrictions imposed by the nondiscrimination requirement universally cover enrollment policies and conduct, but they are not a targeted burden on religious use.”

The court of appeals also rejected the challengers’ contention that the nondiscrimination requirement is unconstitutional because it burdens their right to freely exercise their religious beliefs. In the court’s view, Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that normally do not violate the Constitution.

Although a regulation issued by the Colorado Department of Early Childhood contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catchall” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation, the court of appeals said that preference is not the kind of individualized exemption that would render the law not generally applicable, because the preschools are still required to comply with the nondiscrimination requirement.

The court of appeals also rebuffed the challengers’ argument that the nondiscrimination requirement is not generally applicable because the program permits schools to give preferences to low-income families and children with disabilities. As an initial matter, the court of appeals suggested, it was “not persuaded” that such preferences actually are exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement because they were intended to protect such children and families and do not discriminate against wealthier families or children without disabilities. But in any event, it continued, the nondiscrimination agreement is still generally applicable because the Supreme Court’s cases only prohibit the state from treating religious activity less favorably than comparable secular activity. And the preferences for low-income families and children with disabilities are not comparable, the court of appeals concluded, because – unlike the exemption that the challengers in this case seek – they do not “undermine[] the government’s asserted interest in ensuring equal access to preschools.”

The challengers came to the Supreme Court in November 2025, asking the justices to weigh in – which they agreed in April 2026 to do.

At the Supreme Court, the justices will review two main questions. The first is the scope of the court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction.

The challengers contend that under Carson, this case should be “an uncomplicated one.” Colorado, the challengers say, “knowingly excluded Catholic preschools solely on account of their religious exercise” – specifically, “their religious practices of ensuring that all enrolling families are supportive of the Catholic Church’s teachings on sex and marriage and of treating enrolled four-year-olds in accordance with their biological sex.” That exclusion, the challengers argue, places a burden on their ability to exercise their religion, in violation of the Constitution.

Colorado counters that Carson “applied the settled principle that government may not target religion for disfavored treatment.” What the preschools are seeking instead, it says, is a “new rule that would trigger strict scrutiny whenever public-benefits conditions incidentally burden religiously motivated conduct.”

The second question before the justices centers on what a challenger has to show to prevail on a claim that a law is not generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

In Tandon v. Newsom, the challengers contend, the Supreme Court made clear that, for purposes of Smith, “[a] law is not generally applicable if it ‘treat[s] any comparable secular activity more favorably than religious exercise’” – a test that the universal preschool program fails. Colorado created the universal-preschool program to ensure equal access for all preschool-aged children, they emphasize. Because the exemptions for low-income families and children with disabilities allow preschools “to provide families with unequal access based on protected characteristics,” the challengers argue, “they undermine Colorado’s asserted interest in equal access ‘in a similar way’ to” the religious accommodation that the challengers seek. Moreover, the challengers add, the program also fails the “general applicability” test under Smith because it gives Colorado discretion, through the preference system, to allow participating preschools “to discriminate in favor of LGBTQ families and other groups,” such as “‘gender-nonconforming children,’ ‘children of color,’ or members of ‘the LGBTQ community.’”

Colorado pushes back, telling the justices that the law creating the universal preschool program “expressly prioritizes specialized services for” children from low-income families and children with disabilities, based on the state’s “longstanding awareness that ensuring equal opportunity for these children often requires providing them with additional support.” But “allowing publicly funded preschools to provide” such services does not “allow any secular conduct that undermines Colorado’s equal-opportunity interests”; therefore, it says, the law is generally applicable for purposes of Smith.

Similarly, Colorado continues, the system of preferences, used to match preschools with families, that are “unrelated to the characteristics protected by the equal-opportunity requirements, by definition, are not exceptions from those requirements.” It is clear, the state stressed, that such preferences can be implemented “only when” they “do not violate the equal-opportunity requirements.”

Correction (Oct. 30 at 11:40 a.m.): A prior version of this article stated that “a participating faith-based preschool may prioritize the enrollment of families that belong to the same faith as that school.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7568. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7566. Judge advances McDonald’s McRib lawsuit that alleges deceptive marketing

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients. (Photo from Getty Images)

A federal judge in Illinois on Friday did not dismiss a proposed class action lawsuit accusing McDonald’s McRib of misleading customers about the sandwich’s ingredients.

The plaintiffs allege that the McRib, which costs $7, is shaped to look like ribs and misleads customers in ads to think that it contains rib meat instead of cheaper pork cuts.

In Chicago, U.S. District Judge April Perry of the Northern District of Illinois dismissed some claims, but she did not accept the McDonald’s argument that a reasonable customer could expect the McRib to contain rib meat. Perry said ads of the rib-shaped patties could possibly be an attempt to defraud, but more proof was needed, according to coverage by Reuters.

“Plaintiffs’ proffered understanding of ‘McRib’ is not unreasonable or fanciful,” Perry wrote.

McDonald’s contends that it does not use hearts, tripe or stomach as McRib ingredients, which the suit alleges. The fast-food giant, which has sold the sandwich since 1981, said distinctive product names do not fool reasonable consumers.

“This lawsuit distorts the facts, and ⁠the claims are meritless,” McDonald’s said in a statement.

#7564. Groups ask Supreme Court to leave lower court order in place halting border wall construction in southwestern Texas

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction. Eric Glitzenstein, a lawyer representing the plaintiffs, told the justices in a 40-page filing that granting the federal government’s request to lift that order would allow the Trump administration to “immediately resume blasting, bulldozing, road construction, and other border barrier-related construction across one of the most remote and ecologically and culturally significant landscapes in the United States.”

The dispute centers on three waivers of various environmental and conservation laws that then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and her successor, Markwayne Mullin, issued earlier this year to authorize construction of the border wall in the Big Bend region, including areas in Big Bend National Park. Noem and Mullin relied on a provision of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 that gives the Secretary of Homeland Security the power to “waive all legal requirements” necessary “to ensure expeditious construction” of border walls and roads. With the waivers, Noem and Mullin determined that additional border barriers are required in the Big Bend area because it “is an area of high illegal entry.”

The plaintiffs in this case – an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church – went to federal court to challenge the waivers’ legality. On Oct. 2, U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone temporarily barred the Department of Homeland Security from continuing construction on the border wall in the Big Bend region “until and unless” the government complies with environmental and other applicable laws.

In a written opinion issued on Oct. 14 to explain her reasoning, Cardone concluded that the challengers were likely to prevail on their claim that under the major questions doctrine – the idea that if Congress intends to give a federal agency the power to make decisions of vast economic or political significance, it must say so explicitly – the DHS secretary did not have the authority to issue the waivers.

As an initial matter, Cardone rejected the government’s contention that she did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claims because they arose from a statute, while IIRIRA only allows federal courts to hear challenges to waiver decisions if they involve the Constitution. The major questions doctrine, she said, is a “constitutional … rule” based on the idea that “courts should expect Congress to speak clearly when it delegates major lawmaking authority to the executive.”

Turning to the question of whether the major questions doctrine barred the waivers, she observed that both the government and the challengers “appear to agree that the waiver of all legal requirements to construct a border wall in the Big Bend Sector is of ‘major economic and political significance.’” The key issue, she continued, is thus whether Congress clearly gave the DHS secretary the power to issue the Big Bend waivers. It did not, she wrote. She emphasized that another provision of IIRIRA authorizes the DHS secretary to “take such actions as may be necessary to install additional physical barriers and roads … in the vicinity of the United States border to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” When that provision is read together with the waiver provision, she said, it means that the DHS secretary can only waive legal requirements for “construction ‘to deter illegal crossings in areas of high illegal entry.’”

But the Big Bend region is not, she contended, such an area: although it “comprises over 25% of the U.S.-Mexico border,” it accounts for only a tiny percentage (“between 0.3% and 2.2%”) of all of the people apprehended crossing the border. This means, she said, that “if the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector, and the waiver authority would apply to the entire U.S.-Mexico border. If that were the case, Congress could have simply authorized construction ‘to deter illegal crossings.’” The major questions doctrine instructs courts to avoid “interpretations that would render limiting language meaningless,” Cardone concluded.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court on Oct. 21, asking the justices to pause Cardone’s order and to grant review and summarily reverse it. First, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer argued, the district court did not have the power to consider the challengers’ claim based on the major questions doctrine because their complaint specifically alleged that the DHS secretary “lacked ‘clear congressional authorization’ … to issue the waivers” under the IIRIRA – a statutory claim that “Congress denied district courts” the authority “to entertain.” But in any event, Sauer continued, “[e]ven assuming that the Secretary’s waiver authority implicates a question of ‘vast economic and political significance,’ Congress did clearly authorize the Secretary both to build border barriers and to waive legal requirements in order to facilitate their expeditious construction.”

In their brief on Thursday, the challengers insisted that the major questions doctrine applied to their claim, stressing that “the decision to waive myriad federal, state, local, and tribal laws across vast geography for the purpose of building border infrastructure, even through national and state parks where border crossings are miniscule, is a truly ‘extraordinary’ assertion of power.” “Whatever authority Congress delegated, it did not clearly authorize the sweeping exercise of power asserted here, and” the government’s “actions therefore amount to a constitutional violation of the major questions doctrine.”

The challengers also argued that DHS will not suffer any permanent harm if the construction is temporarily blocked – one of the factors that courts consider in deciding whether to award temporary relief. To the contrary, they noted, before Cardone issued her order halting construction, “in response to intense local opposition,” DHS “voluntarily paused construction for weeks in vast portions of the project area.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7563. Torrential rains spell disaster across Southwest

The increased rainfall could improve drought conditions, but a Colorado climate expert says the winter runoff will play a larger role.

PHOENIX (CN) â Communities across the Southwest are still underwater as the region comes out of one of the wettest weekends on record.

Torrential storms fueled by global climate change and the strongest El NiÃ±o on record dumped more than six inches of rain across the high country of Arizona, in some places accounting for more than half the annual rainfall in just three days. From Friday to Sunday, Arizona received more rain by total volume than any other state in the country.

The storms battered the entire Four Corners region, setting records and prompting Colorado Governor Jared Polis to request an emergency declaration through the Federal Emergency Management Agency for the southwestern counties of Archuleta and Rio Grande.

âDevastating flooding has damaged homes and businesses, washed away roads, and disrupted the basic services Southwestern Colorado families depend on,â Polis said Saturday. âThe damage documented so far exceeds what state and local resources can address alone.â

The San Luis Valley, straddling Colorado and New Mexico, received four times its typical October precipitation in just four days, according to Colorado state climatologist Russ Schumacher.

âMuch of southern Colorado had their wettest September to October period on record, and now November is off to a very wet start as well,â Schumacher told Courthouse News. âThe flooding on some rivers was worse than what was experienced just 10 days ago.â

President Donald Trump already partially granted an emergency declaration in New Mexico for flooding that began last week.

Ten storm gauges across the three states recorded new records.Â While recent storms exacerbated existing effects in Colorado and New Mexico, Arizona was hit the hardest just in the last three days.

In eastern Arizona at the foothills of the White Mountains, the small town of Pinetop-Lakeside recorded 6.2 inches of rain over the three-day period, resulting in powerful floods that washed out streets and even collapsed a bridge.

Indigenous communities, including the Navajo and Hopi communities, have been particularly hard hit and warned not to return due to the risks of contaminated water, downed power lines and potential gas leaks.

In central Arizona, the city of Prescott declared a state of emergency Monday morning, activating its Emergency Operations Center. Yavapai Countyâs emergency management service opened a shelter in conjunction with the Red Cross for those displaced by flooding.

âItâs been such a large area thatâs been devastated by the water its gonna take a while to get under control,â a county representative said on the phone.

Verde Valley Fire Chief Danny Johnson told 12News that first responders conducted at least a dozen swift water rescues on Sunday alone.

The county announced evacuation orders for multiple communities including Winslow, Cottonwood, Camp Verde and Sedona, and both the White Mountain and San Carlos Apache tribes.

To the south, law enforcement rescued eight people from Sabino Canyon near Tucson on Sunday, according to the Coronado National Forest. Two others were rescued just outside that area. A National Forest representative said there were no injuries.

Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs declared a statewide state of emergency Monday afternoon after pressure from multiple Republican lawmakers. She has not yet requested FEMA assistance.

According to the weather forecasting tool Weather City, Arizona has received 103% of its average annual rainfall to date. The southernmost county of Cochise has recorded 136%. This October was the second wettest on record for the city of Phoenix.

The storms are expected to subside across the four corners region this week, providing some immediate relief from the surging floodwaters. While the damage has been devastating, long-term effects could mean good news for regional drought conditions.

âThe drought situation has turned around in a big way in southern Colorado, but at the expense of the communities that have been affected by multiple rounds of flooding,â Schumacher said.

An Instagram user recorded footage of waterfalls cascading into the partially empty Canyon Lake, one of the main surface water reservoirs for Arizonaâs Salt River Project. But reservoir storage across the region is still low.

Lake Powell has risen 14 feet over the last month but is still 13 feet lower than a year ago. Lake Mead has only risen by a foot so far. Schumacher said it will take a few more days for the most recent rain in Colorado and New Mexico to reach Lake Powell.

James Heffner, a senior hydrologist at the Arizona Department of Water Resources, said Mead may continue to fill because of declining downstream demand in the coming days.

Thanks to above-average rainfall in September and October, high soil moisture in Arizona means the land is primed for winter runoff that could help refill aquifers.

“We’re off to a great start in terms of precipitation,â Heffner said. âHowever, the Upper Colorado is a snow-dominant system and what happens in terms of snowpack is far more important to runoff into the reservoirs.â

The rainy season has been fueled in part by what experts have referred to as a âSuper El NiÃ±oâ that carried moisture from warming Pacific waters through the American Southwest.

Rainfall also received a boost from tropical storms like Hurricanes Polo and Trudy, the former being the longest-lasting Category 5 storm to ever stir the Pacific. Still, the research group World Weather Attribution estimated global climate change did more to fuel the historic storm than the El NiÃ±o.

âEl NiÃ±o is a big part of the story,â Schumacher said. âThe precise role of climate change will be a topic of research going forward, but the fact that the Pacific water temperatures are so warm right now is a result of the combination of El NiÃ±o and overall warming.â

But Kyle Ann Sebastian, media manager for the Union of Concerned Scientists, warned not to put too much stock in the Super El NiÃ±o and the recent storms busting the region’s crippling drought.

âThe Southwest has been in a multiyear megadrought that wonât be addressed through one month of extreme rainfall,â she said. âOngoing groundwater depletion is a huge issue even when you get heavy rainfall. This is also classic precipitation whiplash for the Southwest â heavy rainfall on drought-parched lands is a recipe for flash flooding.â

#7562. ‘Judge Stone’ by Viola Davis and James Patterson wins inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Legal Fiction

Viola Davis (left) and James Patterson appeared in New York City in March for a discussion of their book, “Judge Stone,” which was chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

Judge Stone, by acclaimed actor Viola Davis and prolific author James Patterson, has been chosen as the winner of the inaugural Scott Turow Prize for Excellence in Legal Fiction.

The prize, which is being awarded by the ABA Journal, the University of Miami School of Law and the University of Miami College of Arts & Sciences, was determined by a panel of judges that featured former ABA Presidents Deborah Enix-Ross and Carolyn Lamm, California Court of Appeal Justice Lee Smalley Edmon and Turow himself.

A public poll hosted by the ABA Journal also chose Judge Stone as the favorite for the prize from among the field of three finalists, which also included A Pair of Aces by Marie Benedict and Victoria Christopher Murray, and Grave Danger by James Grippando.

The Turow Prize aims to honor the work that best illuminates the role of lawyers in society and their power to effect meaningful change. It is a successor to the prestigious Harper Lee Prize, which the Journal and the University of Alabama previously awarded to outstanding works of legal fiction, including novels by John Grisham, Michael Connelly and Grippando.

Judge Stone is a legal thriller about a Black woman judge from a small town in Alabama who presides over a controversial case. It is the first collaboration between Davis and Patterson.

Davis is one of a select group of celebrities who are “EGOT” winners for taking home Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony awards. In 2025, she was honored by the Golden Globes with the Cecil B. DeMille Award for “outstanding contributions to the world of entertainment.”

She won an Emmy for TV’s How to Get Away with Murder and has appeared in numerous films, including Academy Award–nominated Doubt, The Help and Fences (for which she received the Oscar). She won two Tonys (for Fences and King Hedley II) and a Grammy for best audiobook, narration and storytelling recording for her memoir, Finding Me. She also took home a Screen Actors Guild Award for her role in Ma Rainey’s Black Bottom.

In his long career, Patterson has created notable characters and series including Alex Cross, the Women’s Murder Club, Jane Smith and Maximum Ride. He’s written true stories about the Kennedys, John Lennon and Tiger Woods, and has coauthored No. 1 bestselling novels with Bill Clinton, Dolly Parton and Michael Crichton. He’s received an Edgar Award, ten Emmy Awards, the Literarian Award from the National Book Foundation and the National Humanities Medal, according to jamespatterson.com.

Named in honor of pioneering attorney and international bestselling author Scott Turow—the “father of the modern legal thriller”—the Turow Prize seeks to unearth compelling works of fiction that illuminate the dynamics of law, the justice system and the human experience.

Turow’s 13 fiction and two nonfiction books, including Presumed Innocent and the current Presumed Guilty, have sold over 30 million copies worldwide and been adapted for film and television.

Davis and Patterson will receive a cash prize and a signed copy of Presumed Innocent at the award ceremony and reception on Nov. 19 hosted by the University of Miami, along with the exclusive right to feature the prestigious Turow Prize logo on their winning book’s cover.

#7560. Judge scolds ICE over warrantless arrests in Oregon, orders compliance

"Indeed, the sole ICE officer who testified admitted to falsely stating facts in official agency documentation about the basis for an arrest. There is no telling how many other agents in Oregon engaged in similar misconduct," U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai wrote.

EUGENE, Ore. (CN) â A federal judge on Monday ordered federal immigration authorities to comply with an earlier injunction blocking warrantless arrests, after finding an officer fabricated evidence to justify an arrest.

âThis case underscores what happens if people were not called to testify under oath in a courtroom, if as a society we do not demand that government agents explain their actions, and if the public fails to shine a spotlight on what is happening under cover â people with authority know they will not be held to account,â wrote U.S. District Judge Mustafa Kasubhai in a 50-page opinion.

Kasubhai issued a preliminary injunction in February blocking U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement from making warrantless arrests in Oregon unless officers determined an individual posed a flight risk. The order set new rules and parameters for making arrests that complied with the law.

However, the plaintiffs, two men who say they were arrested in Oregon and taken to a Washington state processing facility more than 100 miles away, said ICE was not complying with the injunction.

The plaintiffs, who represent a class of Oregon immigrants arrested without a warrant or probable cause, accused ICE of assessing flight risk only after making warrantless arrests, failing to document the circumstances of those arrests, underreporting them and withholding documentation.

Over a two-day evidentiary hearing in September, ICE denied violating the court order. Kasubhai disagreed.

âThe court finds that ICE agents in the District of Oregon have continued to conduct warrantless arrests without adequately making and documenting the requisite particularized finding of escape risk,â the Joe Biden appointee wrote. âDefendants have also failed to comply with the courtâs order to appropriately document and disclose warrantless arrests.â

From Feb. 5 to July 31, federal immigration officials arrested 574 people in Oregon. Of those, 504 were noncustodial arrests, meaning they likely occurred without a warrant. ICE reported only 13 warrantless arrests during that period.

However, testimony from the co-directors of the Deportation Data Project and Portland Immigrant Rights Coalition showed officers conducted significantly more than 13 warrantless arrests, Kasubhai determined.

Based on testimonies from people stopped or arrested over the summer, the court also found that ICE inaccurately reported warrantless arrests.

One individual, identified as H-D-G-H-, was on his way to fish when ICE deportation officer J.G. arrested him. The two gave conflicting accounts of the arrest, and the court found H-D-G-H- credible and J.G.âs testimony false.

That conclusion was bolstered by J.G.âs admission that his written account of the arrest was inaccurate. He testified that he wrote the narrative âas if I â¦ already knew who the person was, but I did not.â J.G. maintained that despite the false narrative, the arrest was lawful.

âThe court gives no weight to this account,â Kasubhai wrote. âThe evidence here clearly establishes ICE officers did not conduct an arrest pursuant to a valid warrant.â

As part of the preliminary injunction, the federal defendants are required to provide documentation every 30 days describing the warrantless immigration arrests that occurred in Oregon, and Kasubhai found they failed to properly do so.

âThese produced documents, as scant a sampling size as it is, reveal defendantsâ falsification of I-213s, misstatements of material facts when evaluated against credible testimony under oath, use of boilerplate language that casts significant doubt on ICE agentsâ meaningful investigation of necessary facts, and perhaps the least of the worst transgressions, sloppiness,â Kasubhai wrote.

Kasubhai noted that the presumption of regularity directs courts to assume government officials acted in good faith and followed required procedures.

âThis presumption no longer holds for defendants. The evidence in this case proves as much,â Kasubhai wrote. âDefendants are held to the same expectation as any other litigant before this court. One must earn credibility by acting with integrity.â

Kasubhai ordered ICE to continue transmitting the terms of the preliminary injunction to officers and employees to ensure compliance. The court also ordered the defendants to produce past documentation to the plaintiffs, as well as body camera footage for arrests after Sept. 1 and any arrest documents requested by the plaintiffs.

âWe are grateful to the Oregonians who stood up in court and shared their stories,â Isa PeÃ±a, director of strategy at Innovation Law Lab, said in a statement.

PeÃ±a said Innovation Law Lab will continue fighting for Oregonians harmed by ICE’s lawless actions.

“The people who have been unlawfully taken from their families, pulled out of their cars on their way to work, or had their windows smashed deserve to know ICE is being held accountable,â said Jordan Cunnings, legal director at Innovation Law Lab.

The defendants did not respond to a request for comment before press time.

#7559. The November argument session begins on Monday

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It was a relatively quiet week at the court, as the justices – and the SCOTUSblog team – prepared for the November argument session to begin next week. On the interim docket, the court decided one immigration-related dispute and moved closer to being able to decide another.

On Thursday, an environmental group, a local landowner, and a group formed to preserve a church urged the Supreme Court to deny the Trump administration’s request to be allowed to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. For more on their filing, see the On Site section below.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court denied a request from three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. There were no noted dissents.

The court’s November argument session will begin next week. On Monday, the justices will hear argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

Congress may be “the battleground in the 2026 midterm elections,” but the Supreme Court is playing a role in many races, according to USA Today. Republican and Democratic candidates alike are highlighting “disputes about the high court’s membership, its size and its ethics” and calling on voters to keep these battles in mind when they head to the polls next week. In particular, candidates are raising the possibility of a Supreme Court vacancy during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office and emphasizing that the party that controls the Senate will be able to determine whether another Trump nominee is confirmed to the court.

U.S. District Judge Maame Ewusi-Mensah Frimpong has “barred immigration agents in Southern California from stopping people based on racial stereotypes,” citing what she described as “a mountain of evidence” showing that agents are “targeting people who appear Latino,” according to the Los Angeles Times. “The injunction … requires agents to establish individualized reasonable suspicion before detaining someone for immigration enforcement.” The Times noted that the evidence cited by Frimpong in her new order “had not yet been turned over by the government when the Supreme Court last year stayed the judge’s earlier order barring stops based solely on race or ethnicity, language, location or employment, either alone or in combination.” Frimpong acknowledged the Supreme Court's decision in her new order, but emphasized that the court “had not explained its reasons for granting the stay.” “This Court cannot be faulted for failing to follow guidance that was never given,” the judge wrote. The Trump administration has indicated that it will appeal Frimpong’s order to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.

On Wednesday, Utah “filed criminal charges against prediction market operator Kalshi and two of its executives, months after a federal judge rejected Kalshi’s effort to prevent Utah from enforcing its strict anti-gambling laws against the activity,” according to the Associated Press. “The charges include 13 counts of violating the state’s prohibition on gambling and another charge involving profiting off illegal activity.” The AP noted that “[t]he felony charges could represent a new tactic in how states try to assert regulatory authority over the fast-expanding activity, a clash that appears headed to a showdown at the U.S. Supreme Court.”

Last week, the University of North Carolina School of Law “tested whether AI could replicate the reasoning of US Supreme Court justices” by staging “a simulated Supreme Court argument based on an actual case the high court heard in 2025,” according to Reuters. Participants found that although the three AI justices used in the test drew the same conclusions as the real-life justices, “deciding the case the same way the actual court did,” the bots did not excel at mimicking their behaviors during oral argument. “The AI justices asked questions and hypotheticals of the law students who argued the case, but their interactions felt robotic and they didn’t interrupt or interject the way the real justices do.” “There’s still this huge gap in it actually feeling human,” said Nicole Downing, the law school’s assistant dean for AI, to Reuters.

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak explored the Trump administration’s battle against what it describes as “rogue activist judges,” a category that has come to include judges who expressed frustration with government lawyers or criticized the administration’s actions in media interviews. Liptak noted that the Supreme Court held, in a 1994 opinion from Justice Antonin Scalia, that “[e]xpressions of impatience, dissatisfaction, annoyance and even anger” are “within the bounds of what imperfect men and women, even after having been confirmed as federal judges, sometimes display” and do not necessarily establish “bias or partiality.”

The plaintiffs challenging the Trump administration’s efforts to build a border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place an order by a federal trial judge in El Paso temporarily halting the construction.

The court will hear oral argument on Tuesday in a challenge brought by Catholic preschools. The schools argue that their exclusion from Colorado’s universal preschool program is a form of religious discrimination in violation of the First Amendment, because the state will not provide them with an exemption from rules that would require them to admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

(SCOTUSblog Plus) Earlier this month, the concept of cruel and unusual punishment briefly captured the country’s attention after the state of Tennessee on Sept. 30 tried and failed to execute Christa Pike. The botched execution drew attention to a range of past rulings on the death penalty, while also highlighting a number of unresolved issues in this fraught area.

In his Controlling Opinions column on Wednesday, Richard Re reflected on Justice Samuel Alito’s effort in his new book to discourage judicial “insecurity” – that is, “a judge’s self-conscious worry that he might be advancing his own policy preferences under the guise of impartial adjudication.” According to Re, “what Alito labels insecurity is better understood as a form of humility and self-awareness,” impulses that are laudable, not problematic.

As it currently stands, the 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor. But that could soon change, because by mid-January the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review from the Trump administration or Trump himself.

In his Justice, Democracy, and Law column on Tuesday, Edward Foley explored a growing battle over the division of authority between states and the federal government when it comes to “determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs.” One such case involves the issue of alleged noncitizen voting in California, which may soon arrive at the Supreme Court.

In her In Dissent column on Monday, Anastasia Boden explored 1926’s Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty, in which the Supreme Court, after rehearing the case and “a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions,” paved the way for modern zoning. Boden noted that “[t]hree justices dissented, though they never said why.”

Sarah Isgur and David French zoom in on the cases prosecutors have brought against political enemies of the Trump administration. Then, they review the latest news from the battle over a Washington, D.C., golf course before tackling the administration’s sue-and-settle case in Texas.

The election is upon us, and worries about possible anti-democratic actions have many on alert. Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka peer ahead to see what to watch out for and review the relevant constitutional law and history.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John McKinley, who served on the court from 1838 to 1852.

With the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act of 1837, Congress added two more seats to the court. The first went to Justice John Catron, and the second went to Justice John McKinley, whose confirmation created a nine-justice court. While the seat itself was an honor, its duties were less so, as McKinley would discover.

McKinley was born in May 1780 in Culpeper County, Virginia. His family soon moved to Kentucky, where he taught himself law, passed the bar in 1800, and practiced in both Frankfort and Louisville. After moving to Alabama around 1818, McKinley grew wealthy from land speculation, partnered with Andrew Jackson in the Cypress Land Company, and helped found the city of Florence, Alabama. Jackson himself called McKinley “the most prominent man” in the state.

McKinley entered the Alabama Legislature in 1820, and, after backing Jackson for the presidency (he had previously supported Henry Clay), won a U.S. Senate seat in 1826. In the Senate, McKinley advocated for bankruptcy policies “favorable to small farmers.” However, his vote to override Jackson’s Maysville Road veto (the Maysville Road Bill essentially proposed federal stock purchases for internal improvements, like state roads) raised doubts about his loyalty, and he was not reelected in 1830. After one term in the U.S. House and another in the state legislature, he won a second Senate term in 1836, only to leave the seat within two months due to his Supreme Court appointment.

In 1837, the Eighth and Ninth Circuits Act expanded the court to nine justices, and Jackson’s advisers pushed McKinley for one of the new seats, but Jackson preferred his friend William Smith instead. When Smith declined, the pick then fell to the newly inaugurated President Martin Van Buren, who went with McKinley. Van Buren gave McKinley a recess appointment in April 1837, and the Senate confirmed him by voice vote that September.

After his nomination, McKinley wrote to then-House speaker James Polk that he had “accepted the appointment, although it is certainly the most onerous and laborious of any in the United States.” The new 9th Circuit included Alabama, Arkansas, Mississippi, and eastern Louisiana and required eight circuit terms a year. McKinley told Polk he would travel more than 5,000 miles annually, although McKinley later reported a figure closer to 10,000. The duties also likely ate into his finances (the justices were required to personally pay for their own circuit court duties) and took a toll on his health (he later had a paralyzing stroke on his way to Jackson, Mississippi).

Even before his first term started, McKinley asked Van Buren in person about changing the new 9th Circuit, but the president left the issue out of his next annual State of the Union, upsetting McKinley. Following McKinley’s first full term, the justices disbanded in March 1838 to “confront some 6,000 cases on their cumulative circuit dockets,” according to Steven Brown, who wrote McKinley’s first full-length biography. McKinley’s share from the 9th Circuit alone made up 4,700 of those.

Brown detailed one of the more interesting stories from McKinley’s extensive circuit duties in a 2011 Journal of Supreme Court History article. In April 1839 while holding circuit court in Jackson, a fight spilled into the courtroom and an officer of the court (who had been called “a stupid jackass” by McKinley for not bringing in the court marshal) pulled McKinley’s nose. Newspapers reported that the justice swore never to return to Jackson, and McKinley referenced the “gross personal indignity” in a letter to Van Buren.

In his 1839 State of the Union address, Van Buren told Congress that the circuit’s schedule and distances made it “impossible” for its judge to keep up. McKinley missed much of his circuit duties, along with the entire 1840 term, due to illness. Combined with his failure to hold court in Arkansas for almost five years, states in his circuit felt “neglected,” and the Mississippi Legislature called for McKinley’s impeachment. Congress eventually reorganized the circuits in August 1842, relieving McKinley of Mississippi and Arkansas; beginning in 1843 he rode the reconstituted 5th Circuit, which covered Alabama and Louisiana.

As for McKinley’s actual approach to cases, he was strongly for states’ rights, supporting them “over the authority of the federal government.” During his time on the court, McKinley wrote 19 majority opinions, four dissents, and two concurrences by one count, 22 opinions by another, and 23 by a third, the lowest per-term rate of his era. One of his opinions for the court was in 1845’s Pollard’s Lessee v. Hagan, where he held that new states enter the union on equal footing with the original 13, including ownership of the lands beneath navigable waters. Four years later in the 1849 Passenger Cases, McKinley argued in his concurrence that the federal government, not the states, controlled immigrants arriving from overseas until they became permanent residents of the states.

Increasingly ill after a stroke in 1842, McKinley died in Louisville in July 1852 at age 72, after 14 relatively difficult years on the court. He was replaced by Justice John Archibald Campbell, also from Alabama.

JUSTICE O'CONNOR: "A light bulb exploded."

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "I think we're... I think it's safe."

CHIEF JUSTICE ROBERTS: "It's a trick they play on new Chief Justices all the time."

— Central Va. Community College v. Katz (2005)

Poland's constitutional court is in chaos: A pro-EU government installs judges by force, suspends its old leadership and the hard-right opposition calls it a coup.

(CN) â For Europe’s far-right populists, Poland has become the scene of a coup. For their liberal opponents, the country is seeing a long-overdue restoration of democracy.

The centerpiece to this drama is the Constitutional Tribunal in Warsaw, Poland’s constitutional court â the same court that rocked Europe in 2021 by declaring European Union laws secondary to Poland’s constitution. Four years later, the EU’s highest court hit back by declaring the court illegitimate, ruling it had been illegally captured by the country’s ousted far-right government.

On Friday night, with protesters aligned with Polish nationalists keeping watch over the court’s front gates, seven justices appointed by Poland’s ruling pro-EU centrist government entered a side door to the court under police escort.

They then took hold of the court’s website and declared the suspension of the court’s president and vice president, justices aligned with the previous hard-right government led by the Law and Justice party, also known as PiS.

The announcement ignited a furious response from the Law and Justice side.

âAs of today, Poland has become a police state, and from there itâs a straight path to authoritarianism, and then to totalitarianism,â JarosÅaw KaczyÅski, the Law and Justice leader, declared outside the court.

Bogdan ÅwiÄczkowski, the suspended chief justice, raced to the court too. After his supporters cut through a fence with a power tool, he tried to enter the court, but he was met with rows of riot police. ÅwiÄczkowski declared an illegal âcoup dâÃ©tatâ was underway.

At around 1 a.m., Polish President Karol Nawrocki showed up at the court, escorted by his security team.

The president, who is aligned with Law and Justice, was flying to Senegal for a diplomatic trip when the chaos erupted in Warsaw. He ordered his airplane to turn back mid-flight.

Back in Warsaw, Nawrocki forced his way through rows of police and even tussled with Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a newly appointed judge in charge of court takeover, before he entered the court. Videos showed him arguing with newly appointed judges.

Outside the court, the president declared the takeover a breach of the constitutional order and he called for urgent, cross-party consultations among parliamentary leaders.

Meanwhile, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, the leader of the center-right Civic Platform, defended the operation and accused Nawrocki of unlawfully intimidating judges.

âRestoring the rule of law is our duty,â he declared. âAfter years of PiS-led lawlessness, this is a difficult process, sometimes painful, and it requires decisive action. There is no other way.â

Over the weekend, far-right figures, led by France’s Marine Le Pen, joined the fray by denouncing Tusk and accusing Europe’s liberal establishment of resorting to antidemocratic measures to silence and target their opponents on the right.

On Sunday, Le Pen said what happened in Poland was a âforcible takeover of a constitutional body.â

âThe proliferation of such strong-arm tactics within the European Union itself is beginning to raise serious questions,â she said on social media.

The European Commission, meanwhile, issued a carefully worded statement that supported the actions of the Tusk government. It cited a European Court of Human Rights ruling in May that said the Polish Parliament’s appointments to the constitutional court should not be hindered.

Nawrocki has stymied the court by blocking judges appointed by Tusk’s government. He’s done that by refusing to administer swearing-in oaths. Instead, newly appointed judges were sworn in by Parliament.

Since seizing power in December 2023, the Tusk government has refused to recognize the court’s legitimacy.

By Monday, the standoff between Nawrocki and Tusk remained intense with no resolution in sight.

The court, meanwhile, faced uncertainty too.

Korwin-Piotrowska said she planned to carry out the court’s business and reportedly planned to hold a meeting of its judges Tuesday. But Polish media reported that some judges might not attend.

Alberto Alemanno, a law professor at HEC Paris, said Europe’s highest legal authorities â the European Court of Justice, the European Court of Human Rights and the Council of Europe â have ordered Poland to fix the court.

âThe law is clear;â Alemanno said. âPoland must have an independent Constitutional Tribunal.â

However, he said overhauling the court must be done properly.

âRespect for the rule of law cannot condemn a country to accept institutional capture indefinitely,â he said. âBut restoring it is no blank check to disregard legal constraints.â

He also questioned the appointment of Maciej Berek, a close ally of Tusk.

âHow can Tusk demand a politically independent court while appointing one of his closest associates to it?â he said. That, he said, âcontradicts the pledge to depoliticize the court.â

Still, he said Friday’s operation âwas not a coupâ but aimed âto restore a lawful court, not to capture it.â

As for Nawrocki, Alemanno said his refusal to accept new judges amounted to an abuse of office.

Aleks Szczerbiak, a political scientist and expert on Poland at the University of Sussex, said legal scholars in Poland were divided about the legality of the Tusk government’s actions. Progovernment law experts side with Tusk while antigovernment ones go the other way, he said.

âInterestingly there are some liberal legal scholars who have been very critical of Law and Justice but don’t support the government’s actions on Friday,â he said.

In the end, the Tusk government will likely be able to overhaul the court, even if that means resorting to the police and security services, he said.

But using force could backfire if Poland’s ultranationalists return to power, he added.

âA right-wing government will use exactly the same tactics and justifications against a reconstituted tribunal,â he said. Such a government could refuse to recognize the courtâs rulings and force judges off its bench.

Ideally, the two sides will find common ground to tamp down tensions and arrive at a â‘constitutional reset’ compromise agreement,â he said. âBut I can’t see any prospect of this at the moment.â

#7557. Judge tosses DOJ’s suit against Harvard over race-related admissions data

The government sought that data as part of an investigation into whether Harvard has engaged in discrimination by considering race in its student admissions process.

(CN) â A federal judge dismissed a Trump administration lawsuit against Harvard University on Monday, icing an effort to compel the Ivy League college to turn race-related admissions records over to the government.

The Department of Justice filed the suit in February after it claimed Harvard failed to cooperate with a probe into whether it considers race in its student admissions process â running afoul of the administrationâs stance on diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives.

But in a 10-page ruling, U.S. District Judge Myong Joun found the government was too quick to sue. The Joe Biden appointee in the District of Massachusetts sided with Harvard in ruling the DOJ filed suit without first taking steps to secure the schoolâs voluntary compliance with its demands for admissions data.

âThe government â¦ has not supplied a sufficient basis for the judicial relief currently sought,â the judge ruled.

Jounâs findings only address the limited question of whether the DOJ â and the Department of Education â can currently ask the court to compel Harvard into turning over the data the agencies seek.

âThe ruling does not determine whether Harvard has discriminated, whether the agencies may lawfully seek appropriately defined applicant-level data or whether Harvard may ultimately be required to provide such data,â he clarified.

He dismissed the complaint without prejudice, opening the door for the government to sue again if it can truly prove Harvard will not comply voluntarily with its demands. Then and only then, Joun said, can it ask for the courtâs intervention.

In a statement to Courthouse News, DOE spokesperson Ellen Keast said Harvard has a âwell-documentedâ history of discrimination, citing a 2023 Supreme Court ruling that gutted affirmative action.

âWhen the government asked for admissions data to determine whether Harvard has changed its ways, the school refused and a Democrat-appointed judge is now shielding Harvard from accountability. Students should be judged on their merit and accomplishments, not the color of their skin, and the Trump administration will work tirelessly to ensure Harvard abides by obligations to uphold the law.â

Harvard and the DOJ didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.

In its initial lawsuit filed Feb. 13, the government claimed Harvard âis not complying with a federal investigationâ into whether its admissions process is discriminatory. The DOJ claims it is part of a broader probe into the schoolâs compliance with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color and national origin in programs that get federal financial assistance.

âHarvard has failed to disclose the data we need to ensure that its admissions are free of discrimination â we will continue fighting to put merit over DEI across America,â then-Attorney General Pam Bondi said in a February statement announcing the suit.

But Harvard claimed this was just another attempt from the government to strong-arm the school into being friendlier to the Trump administration. Harvard argued it was responsive to the DOJâs demands but was sued nonetheless because of its refusal to cede to the administration on issues like antisemitism.

The college filed its motion to dismiss on June 4, claiming it has endured a âgovernment-initiated onslaughtâ since President Donald Trump reclaimed the White House.

âPresident Trump has publicly expressed his beliefs that âHarvard has lost its way,â that it âhas been hiring almost all woke, radical left, idiots and birdbrainsâ and that âHarvard is a JOKE.â The rest of the executive branch has followed the presidentâs lead,â Harvard claims in the filing.

Harvard has indeed been embroiled in litigation with the Trump administration since early 2025, but federal courts have largely sided with the school.

In September 2025, a federal judge found the administration’s $2.6 billion cuts to Harvardâs research funding unlawfully retaliatory. U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs, a Barack Obama appointee in Massachusetts, called the funding freeze an “ideologically motivated assaultâ on one of the nationâs top colleges and concluded the administration was doing the same to other prestigious institutions around the country.

Earlier this year, a judge shot down another complaint the DOJ brought against Harvard. In that suit, the government accused the school of âtolerat[ing] antisemitic mobs of students, faculty and visitorsâ during pro-Palestine demonstrations. U.S. District Judge Richard Stearns, a Bill Clinton appointee in Massachusetts, found the government fell short of proving systemic antisemitism on Harvardâs campus.

#7556. Fifth Circuit questions whether Chinese citizens can challenge Texas property ban

Two Chinese nationals say Senate Bill 17 unconstitutionally blocks them from making further purchases of Texas real estate. The state says their plans are too speculative and lack constitutional rights.

(CN) â Two Chinese citizens living abroad asked the Fifth Circuit on Monday to revive their challenge to a Texas law barring people linked to China and other designated countries from buying most real property in the state.

Min Huang, who lives in Shanghai, and Qiong Dai, who lives in New Zealand, own rental properties in the Houston area and want to buy more. They argue Texas Senate Bill 17, which took effect in September 2025, unconstitutionally blocks additional purchases.

With limited exceptions, the law restricts individuals and entities connected to China, Russia, Iran and North Korea, countries flagged in U.S. intelligence assessments, from acquiring interests in Texas real estate.

In December 2025, a lower court dismissed the plaintiffsâ claims, finding that foreign citizens outside the United States generally lack constitutional rights. U.S. District Judge Alan D. Albright, a Donald Trump appointee, stayed the rest of the case pending the Fifth Circuitâs decision in a related challenge, Wang v. Paxton.

On Monday, attorney Justin Sadowsky told the appellate panel the Constitution protects the plaintiffsâ planned purchases because they would travel to Texas on visitor visas to complete them, the property is in Texas and enforcement would occur in Texas courts.

âI think there are three grounds for people having constitutional rights in the United States,â he argued. âOne is for actions that take place in the United States. Two is over property that they have within the United States. And three, when actions are taken by courts in the United States against a third party, they have constitutional rights regarding those courts’ decisions.â

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod, a George W. Bush appointee, questioned how the appeals court could help the two Chinese citizens after a lower court dismissed their claims and whether people living overseas have a constitutional right to buy Texas property without setting foot in the United States.

Sadowsky said the case remains alive because a third plaintiffâs claims have not been dismissed, though he acknowledged the appeal could become moot if they are. He argued the law targets the property itself, giving buyers a protected interest once they purchase it, and that the Constitution protects transactions involving U.S. property even when buyers remain abroad.

U.S. Circuit Judge Carl E. Stewart, a Bill Clinton appointee, asked whether the plaintiffsâ plans to purchase were speculative. Sadowsky said they have the same development interest as anyone else.

âPeople who have purchased properties, who have plans to purchase properties, will in fact execute purchasing properties,â he said, also pointing to newly proposed attorney general regulations creating an enforcement task force and reporting requirements as evidence of a willingness to enforce the law.

For Texas, Assistant Solicitor General Benjamin Mendelson argued that the plaintiffs lack standing because they âalleged no specific plans to purchase any real estate in Texas.â Citing related cases, he said the standard is whether the event is imminent, not merely probable.

âThe standard is not a reasonable probability that an event will happen,â he said. âThe standard is that the event is certainly impending.â

Mendelson further argued that sovereign immunity bars the suit, that foreign citizens abroad have no cause of action under the equitable doctrine of Ex parte Young and that the plaintiffs lack a âsubstantial connectionâ to the United States sufficient to assert constitutional rights.

âA proposal doesnât do anything,â he said, adding that no one has been arrested or prosecuted under the statute and that a settlement in an unrelated case does not equate to enforcement.

Elrod asked whether the state has any interest in who owns land within its borders. Mendelson focused on the jurisdictional defects, while Sadowsky, in rebuttal, contended that national origin discrimination would trigger strict scrutiny and that standing should not require a completed transaction that would immediately moot the case.

The panel also included Senior U.S. Circuit Judge Carolyn D. King, a Jimmy Carter appointee who participated remotely. It took the case under submission without indicating when it would rule.

#7555. Executive Assistant / Corporate Administrator at Canonical

Canonical is a leading provider of open source software and operating systems to the global enterprise and technology markets. The company is founder led, profitable and growing. We are hiring Executive Assistants and Corporate Administrators to join our Corporate Operations team. We ensure that the business runs smoothly and that travel, expenses and events are efficiently and correctly managed.

We look for positive team players who are self-driven and results oriented, with excellent attention to detail. The best candidates show that they are forward planners, reliable and determined, and keen to assume responsibility for projects, processes and policy. We are a unique global business, so we are not looking for candidates with extensive experience so much as excellent organisers and communicators who are keen to develop skills and strive for continuous improvement.

This team plays a crucial role in the overall operation of the business. They run significant business operations and processes, supporting the respective department leads but also taking central responsibility for logistics, expenses, travel and scheduling. They are the secret to our success! We look for confident and effective people who have good judgment and the self-assurance to hold firm on a point of policy regardless of the seniority of people on the other side of a discussion. If you like to take responsibility and you like to ensure that things are done properly and efficiently then you will enjoy the role tremendously.

Location: This is a global operation, we have open roles in teams in all time zones.

We revisit compensation annually (and more often for graduates and associates) to ensure we recognise outstanding performance. In addition to base pay, we offer a performance-driven annual bonus.
